# He Who Fights With Monsters: Compendium (spoiler level 3, Books 1-13)

Exported from the compendium by `src/tools/export_levels.py`. A derived copy: it is not a source, and the compendium files are the place to correct anything. It holds 379 documents cleared to level 3. Facts carry the reference form "Book N, ChX LY" where the book text shows them; "notes" and "wiki" mark the lower tiers. Lines that cite a later book or name a later-level term were held back; see held_back.txt.

## World Primer: the Worlds of *He Who Fights With Monsters*

This primer is the foundation of the compendium. It explains the setting in plain language and summarises the facts that come up again and again. Later documents expand every section. Where a fact only becomes true later in the story it is marked **(Later: Book N)**.

---

### 1. The setting in one page

The series follows Jason Asano, an ordinary Australian who is pulled out of his world by an accident and arrives, hairless and alone, in **Pallimustus**: a world very like Earth in size and shape, but soaked in magic. There, people absorb **essences** (crystallised magic), which give them supernatural abilities, and grow through **ranks** by hunting **monsters** and training. Adventurers, guilds, gods and rulers all depend on this system.

Pallimustus has a twin, **Earth**, which was made from the same template but has much less magic, so its people do not know magic exists (at first). The two worlds are linked, and the link matters more and more as the story proceeds. Above both worlds sits a larger cosmos of **great astral beings**, **gods**, **astral kings** and other powers who rarely interact directly with mortals but shape their lives.

In a roleplay you can set a story anywhere from the beginning (a rural iron-rank adventurer in Greenstone) to the end (a gold-rank world-defender at the edge of a cosmic war). The chief factors that change from period to period are: who knows what, how powerful the leading characters are, and what the dangers are (a Builder cult, a monster surge, messengers, vampires, Knowledge's plan).

---

### 2. Two worlds

#### 2.1 Pallimustus

Pallimustus is an alternate Earth whose continents are similar but not identical. Key differences: Africa is separate from Eurasia; a large landmass in Southeast Asia pushes into Australia and consumes New Zealand; Iberia and Arabia are missing; Sri Lanka is huge (Book 1, Ch1 L65) and is called Pranay (Book 2, Ch34 L58). The Mediterranean equivalent is the **Gramid Passage**, which joins directly to the Indian Ocean (Book 6, Ch47 L703). It has two moons (Book 1, Ch1 L23). The year has twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days for the solstices, equinoxes and new year, and the year begins in spring (Book 1, Ch22 L19); the week has six days (Book 6, Ch10 L41). Time units (hours, minutes) match Earth's (Book 1, Ch22 L20).

The planet has a thin membrane to the astral, so magic is dense. Features of the world that follow from this:
- **Astral spaces** (pocket dimensions) attached to the planet through apertures such as waterfalls and caves.
- **Natural manifestations**: essences, awakening stones and monsters appear spontaneously.
- **Monster surges**: cyclical events (every ten years, Book 1, Ch31 L71) when magic spikes and monsters pour out. A surge is the world venting excess magic. The series' major surge begins in Book 7, about five years overdue (Book 7, Ch1 L56), which the books connect to a magical link to Earth that had been bleeding Pallimustus off. **(Later: Book 4-7)**
- Animals include **heidels** (horse-sized, scaled, two-headed and horned, Book 1, Ch17 L106) in place of horses.

Because magic is concentrated regionally, **magic level** varies by place. Greenstone is low-magic: "mid-iron" density, which Clive calls very low (Book 3, Ch34 L60). The wiki calls Vitesse much denser (wiki; no book figure), and the place files give what the books say about Rimaros and others. Astral spaces and surges can be higher still. Magic level affects what monsters appear, how quickly people can advance, and even what technology works.

#### 2.2 Earth

Earth is the same template with a more rigid dimensional membrane, which the World-Phoenix reinforced billions of years ago, so it has less ambient magic (Book 4, Ch68 L79, L97; Book 4, Ch2 L11). Earth's hidden magical world has three powers:
- **The Cabal**: ancient, secretive, built around old magic and vampires, controlling old money. Its leaders include messengers hiding from other messengers. **(Later: Book 4, 10-11)**
- **The Network**: a coalition of secret societies that uses essences and monster cores. It maintains the **Grid** that detects "dimensional incursions" and keeps Earth's magic in check. It names ranks by category, matched to the spirit-coin colour: category one is iron, two bronze, and a silver-ranker is category three (Book 4, Ch21 L31-33; Book 4, Ch31 L48); it grades events by category as well (Book 4, Ch5 L13-16). It says "luminous" for holy (Book 4, Ch19 L36) and "affinity gems" for quintessence (Book 4, Ch23 L26).
- **The Engineers of Ascension (EOA)**: a technology-and-body-modification faction preparing for the revelation of magic.

Magic has been quietly leaking onto Earth for a long time and "goes public" during the story. By Books 5-6 the Grid fails, monsters pour in, **transformation zones** change cities and their people into other races, and vampires take Europe. **(Later: Book 5-6, 11, 13)**

#### 2.3 The link between the worlds

A link made roughly five hundred years ago siphons magic from Pallimustus into Earth: an Earth outworlder who had joined the fake Purity's church returned home with magic Knowledge had bargained from the messengers (Book 13, Ch1017 L19-21). The siphon delays Pallimustus's monster surges, and the delay makes the eventual breakthrough more dangerous (Book 4, Ch68 L131-135). Repairing it is one of Jason's central tasks. Its completion creates a **bridge** that will become a true doorway between the worlds, which is the key to the Book 13 conflict. **(Later: Book 4-13)**

---

### 3. How magic works (the basics)

#### 3.1 Essences

An **essence** is a manifestation of pure magic in the form of a small glass cube or crystal. Absorbing one (by ritual, or simply by holding and consuming it) imbues the person with five related **essence abilities**, one awakened at once and the rest later. A person can hold **four essences**; the fourth usually forms a **confluence** from the first three.

Essences come in rarities (Common, Uncommon, Rare, Epic, Legendary), and no essence is simply better than another: a Duck essence in skilled hands can beat a Fox. Essences are named for their concept or animal (Fire, Wind, Blood, Dark, Sin, Dragon, Swift, Rat, Spider, Sword, Technology...). They show up in monster loot, are given by gods, and are collected and traded.

#### 3.2 Confluence essences

When three essences are absorbed a **confluence essence** manifests, determined by the combination. In the early books the outcome for a combination is fixed and recorded by the Magic Society (see `03_Magic_and_Adventuring/Confluences.md` for the cites); by Book 12 the fixed combinations "are starting to add variety" (Book 12, Ch10 L91). Examples: Dark + Blood + Sin = Doom (affliction specialist); Earth + Fire + Potent = Volcano; Magic + Might + Wing = Dragon; Swift + Balance + Wind = Mystic. A confluence can be refused, but then cannot be replaced. Some confluences (Death, Corrupt, Sacrifice, Undeath, Succubus...) are **restricted** by the Adventure Society.

#### 3.3 Awakening stones

Each essence holds five abilities; absorbing the essence awakens one, and the rest require **awakening stones**, which are consumable crystals. The Magic Society grades a stone one to five stars by how often it appears (see `03_Magic_and_Adventuring/Awakening_Stones.md`); the stone's theme steers what it awakens; the essence matters most, but race, knowledge and personality also influence the result. Gods and astral beings sometimes give stones to followers.

#### 3.4 Abilities

Essence abilities come in types: **special attacks**, **spells**, **special abilities**, **auras**, **conjurations**, **summons and familiars** (often needing a ritual) and **rituals** in their own right. Abilities improve in rank as the user advances: an ability that begins as a single effect gains extra effects at each rank (Jason's Leech Bite, for instance, adds new afflictions at each stage). Abilities have mana and stamina costs and sometimes cooldowns. Many abilities inflict **afflictions** (lasting harmful conditions) or grant **boons**; the series gives them specific names.

#### 3.5 Attributes

Every person has four base **attributes**: **Power**, **Speed**, **Spirit** and **Recovery**. They rise as essence abilities advance and are the measure of raw ability. A person cannot advance until all attributes have reached the next rank (Book 5, Ch25 L26-27).

#### 3.6 Quintessence, spirit coins and other magical materials

- **Quintessence** (called **affinity gems** on Earth) appears as gems of an essence's theme (for example Dark Quintessence Gems, Book 1, Ch6 L15; crafting material, Book 1, Ch7 L68) and is used in crafting.
- **Monster cores** are crystallised magic from monsters. Eating one raises abilities slightly; this is the fast path to advancement but it stalls most people around silver and makes gold very hard.
- **Spirit coins** are the currency of the magical world. They are concentrated magic that a ranked person can consume to sustain themselves. See section 7.
- Other staples: crystal wash (cleaning solution used after monster fights), healing unguents, recovery potions, skill books, dimensional bags.

#### 3.7 Rituals, formations and artifice

Beyond essence abilities there is "external magic": **ritual magic** (circles of chalk, ink or silver powder with chants), **formations and arrays** (large-scale rituals such as the Network's Grid), **alchemy** (potions, ointments), **artifice** (magical items, weapons, vehicles), and **skill books**, which impart skills by flooding the reader with text (they require consciousness and are strenuous).

#### 3.8 Familiars and summons

A **familiar** is a deliberately created creature bonded to its owner, normally via a ritual. A **summoned familiar** can merge with the summoner and dies with them; a **bonded familiar** survives its owner but cannot vanish into them. Familiars can have their own abilities. Jason's three familiars (Shade, Colin, Gordon) are central to him. Other examples: Stash (Humphrey), Onslow (Clive), Shimmer and Gemini (Belinda).

---

### 4. Ranks and power

Ranks measure the quality of a person's magic and are a social class system as much as a power scale.

| Rank | Earth term | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Normal (unranked) | Category 0 | Ordinary people, including those with some essences |
| Iron | Category 1 | Four essences absorbed (Book 1, Ch15 L100). Digestion changes (Book 2, Ch34 L73); can live on spirit coins; sense auras |
| Bronze | Category 2 | All abilities unlocked and at bronze; much tougher |
| Silver | Category 3 | Can fight through blows that would be lethal to a bronze-ranker (Book 5, Ch1 L38); some abilities allow flight at silver (Book 2, Ch9 L30-31); the usual ceiling for core-users |
| Gold | Category 4 | No need to breathe (Book 2, Ch34 L73); centuries-long life (Book 1, Ch22 L58) |
| Diamond | Category 5 | The peak of mortal power; few exist; rumoured not to die of old age |
| Transcendent | none | Gods and astral beings, effectively unkillable |

Facts that recur: people of a higher rank **suppress** those of lower rank ("tyranny of rank"); essence users age slower: bronze-rankers can live well past a hundred, silvers can double that, gold-rankers live for centuries, and it is rumoured that diamond-rankers cannot die of old age (Book 1, Ch22 L58); ranking up involves a "purge" in which impurities are expelled (often messy) and the body changes; advancing without monster cores is slower but leaves greater potential. **Half-transcendence** means peak diamond combined with transcending mortal nature.

Roles in society: iron and bronze make up most adventurers; silver are elite; gold are rare and politically important; diamonds are sovereign powers ("everyone gets one world-changing action", according to their etiquette). Title and respect follow rank.

---

### 5. Auras

An **aura** is the physical, intangible projection of a person's soul and will. It grows with rank. People learn to **project**, **retract** and **suppress** it; stronger auras can suppress weaker ones. Auras can carry emotions, blanket areas, reveal lies, or physically move matter at very high levels (messengers do this routinely). Uncontrolled gold-rank auras injure unranked people. Techniques include blending into a crowd (making an aura read as part of the ambient background) and masking (messenger devices that fake or block auras). **Titles** earned from deeds (Giant Slayer, Resolute, Indomitable, Godless Prophet...) alter a person's aura. **Soul crests** (see section 10) provide personal identification.

---

### 6. Monsters and surges

**Monsters** are magic made sentient without a soul. They manifest spontaneously where magic is dense, last from days to weeks, become more aggressive near the end, and dissolve into **rainbow smoke** leaving loot (cores, coins, materials, ointments, items). Monsters have ranks matching the quality of their magic. They range from hamsters and eels (lesser) to hydras, dragons, kraken and leviathans. Some are intelligent (the Dinosaur King, springclaw gorillas) and some come from specific origins (construct creatures, vorger from the deep astral, apocalypse beasts such as the sanguine horror and the world-taker worm).

Not every creature that looks like a monster is one: **magical creatures** (natural animals with magical traits) and **creatures** (Tartarian brutes, nagas) have souls and leave no rainbow smoke.

Adventurers hunt monsters because monsters left alone grow dangerous, produce loot and cores, and threaten settlements. The Adventure Society posts notices and contracts. Typical dangers: ambushes, tyranny of rank, afflictions, packs. Typical loot rules: usually only the one who kills or the party members get the loot (the System later automates this).

A **monster surge** is the world's pressure release. Magic density spikes, monsters of higher rank manifest, astral spaces open and the Society moves to "surge protocols" (contracts become orders). A surge lasts months. **(Later: Book 6-8)**

---

### 7. Economy, materials and daily life

- **Spirit coins** exist in lesser, iron, bronze, silver, gold and diamond forms. 100 lesser coins make one iron coin; each higher rank is ten times the last (Book 1, Ch36 L72; Book 1, Ch61 L65), so a gold coin equals about 100,000 lesser coins. A ranked person can eat a coin of their rank to restore resources; eating a higher coin temporarily raises them to that rank, with severe backlash. Coins from Jason bear his face and the words "PRODUCT OF JASON / G'DAY, MATE!" (Book 1, Ch2 L50-53).
- **Spirit coin farms** in low-magic regions are a major industry (Greenstone's biggest export).
- **Lodging, food and travel** vary by region: Greenstone has a loop terminal that opens onto a street of temples (Book 1, Ch45 L4). Only the wealthiest residents of Old City have magic-driven indoor plumbing (Book 1, Ch71 L7). Vitesse's cloud palace has lush plants growing out of its walls and columns (Book 2, Ch40 L3). Rimaros has islands floating in the sky (Book 7, Ch7 L3).
- **Cloud constructs** (Jason's cloud flask, Emir's cloud palace) are magical buildings and vehicles made from cloud substance.
- **Communication**: the Magic Society's **water link** (Book 2, Ch6 L5) and the **sky link** communication tablets, whose inventor appears in Book 12, Ch14 L19 (the Sky Link Company, Book 12, Ch56 L4). **Transport**: heidel wagons, skyships, skimmers, portals (limited by rank and distances).
- **Daily staples** noticed by the series: crystal wash, healing unguents, strawberry-schnapps-flavoured recovery potions, elf and celestine fashion, tea, stews and sandwiches (Jason's cooking is a recurring feature). A recovery potion tasting of strawberry schnapps appears in Book 1, Ch6 L50, and crystal wash in Book 1, Ch32 L52.

---

### 8. Peoples (natures)

Each **nature** (race) has exactly six inherent **racial gifts** (Book 1, Ch15 L65) that can evolve with a blessing from a great astral being.

- **Humans**: the most common; faster advancement and special-attack affinity; the only native race of Earth that can use essences.
- **Elves**: spellcasters and healers; life and magic affinity; long-lived.
- **Leonids**: lion-headed, strong and fast (e.g. Gary).
- **Celestines**: metallic hair and eyes, skin from alabaster to dark; astral and holy affinity; not a natural race: two outworlders who have a child produce a celestine (Book 5, Ch44 L72); excellent portal users.
- **Draconians**: scaled, fire-breathing, claim dragon descent.
- **Smoulder**: earth-and-fire folk; the **brighthearts** are a magical sub-species adapted to the deep.
- **Runics**: blue-black skin with glowing runes.
- **Merfolk, goblins, valash** (humans turned into them by transformation zones, Book 9, Ch45 L57), **lehenik** (Nik's kind, from a word for "first", Book 11, Ch23 L42).
- **Outworlders**: people from another world whose souls rebuilt a body. They have unusual gifts (interface, quest system, inventory, map, "mysterious stranger" language adaptation) and cannot be easily tracked.
- **Messengers**: winged, gestalt beings who are not essence-users (see section 9).

---

### 9. The wider cosmos

#### 9.1 The astral and the cosmos

Clive explains the cosmos as **dumpling soup** (Book 1, Ch69 L85): worlds are dumplings in the soup, which is the astral, the source of all magic. Astral spaces are congealed magic attached to a world; the **deep astral** is pure magic where a physical body cannot survive. **Universes** begin as seeds. **Interstice** is the oldest and largest city-world, with administrators and no rulers, where great astral beings do business in physical reality (Book 3, Ch69 L219-222). The cosmos is kept in order by the **Rules of Intrusion** (Book 12, Ch63 L7; "Laws of Intrusion" in Book 13, Ch1017 L44), which govern entry into worlds that have not opened to the cosmic community. **(Later: Book 2-4, 8, 11-12)**

#### 9.2 Great astral beings (GABs)

Great astral beings are cosmic-scale transcendents who embody aspects of the cosmos. They operate through **prime vessels** (mortal avatars). Named GABs: the **World-Phoenix** (dimensional integrity, formerly the Boundary), the **Builder** (construction; the post was transferred to a new mortal after the old Builder was sanctioned), the **Reaper** (death's finality), the **Keeper of Moments/Sands** (time), the **All-Devouring Eye** (annihilation), the **Celestial Book** (magic's understanding), **Seeker of Songs**, **Whisper in Corners**, **Legion** (life), the **Word in the Silence**, and other nameless functionaries. They once sat under a **Cosmic Throne** and then sundered it. In Book 11 the throne is left empty as a neutral arbiter (Book 11, Ch65 L8), and in Book 12 Jason learns it "could never be restored to what it was", with an echo of him imprinted on it (Book 12, Ch1 L34). **(Later: Book 11-12)**

#### 9.3 Gods

**Gods** are concept-based beings outside physical reality who manifest avatars, speak with Akashic Speech and give followers essences, stones and miracles. Each is bound to a world. Gods named in the books include Knowledge, Healer, Dominion, Hero, Death, Fertility, Hearth, Destruction, Discord, Undeath and Pain, with Purity (or Disguise) a special case; see `02_Cosmology_and_Powers/Gods_and_Churches.md`. Gods cannot enter another god's domain, cannot affect Jason inside his realm, and cannot sanction one another lightly. **Churches** are major institutions (the Church of the Healer provides healing; Dominion backs rulers; Knowledge has an archive and an army; Purity was a long-running fraud: its true god was replaced by a deceiver). **(Later: Book 8, 10-13)**

#### 9.4 Astral kings, messengers and the Council of Kings **(Level 2-3)**

An **astral king** is a being whose soul has become a small universe. Most astral kings began as **messengers**, a servant race grown on birthing trees, bound by a brand placed in the soul that enforces rank limits (Book 10, Ch4 L53-55; Book 11, Ch25 L49-51). **Messengers** are gestalt beings (body and soul fused), tall, winged, hierarchical and arrogant, who believe themselves the highest life in the cosmos. They are not essence-users; their power comes from their astral king. The **Council of Kings** is the ruling body of astral kings. The **Unorthodoxy** are free messengers hiding from the Council. Jason himself becomes a different sort of astral king, an **astral nexus**, with a **prime avatar**. **(Later: Book 8-12)**

#### 9.5 Authority and sanctioning **(Level 3)**

**Authority** is the fundamental power of transcendent beings (their flesh, blood and soul), and is currency in the cosmos. **Sanctioning** is a punitive or self-imposed transformation of a transcendent being's authority, for example the old Builder's replacement or Purity's self-sanctioning. The authority concept is central to the final books.

---

### 10. Souls, death and resurrection

- The **soul** is the person; the body is its expression. Healing magic uses the soul as a blueprint. **Soul scars** are permanent. **Soul crests** are magical tattoos printed on the soul, which appear on the body (Book 2, Ch70 L34-42).
- **Death**: the soul lingers near the body for seconds to an hour; gold-rank healers can reverse death inside that window. Great astral beings could resurrect people but the Reaper and the World-Phoenix object. Gods changed magic so resurrection is harder. **(Later: Book 7)**
- **Outworlders** are souls that wandered into the deep astral and rebuilt a body on arrival.
- **Reincarnation** exists: a soul renews as a different person (e.g. Gary).

---

### 11. Societies and institutions

- **The Adventure Society**: global monster-hunting organisation. Members wear badges that track kills and locate the body. Stars (1-3) rate judgement, not power. It runs notice boards, contracts, orders, field assessments and branch offices run by directors. A **Continental Council** supervises branches. **Guilds** (Burning Violet, Sapphire Crown...) are elite organisations whose members receive resources.
- **The Magic Society**: records essences, regulates spirit coin farms, runs the water link, researches magic, and holds the "living document" of essence combinations.
- **The Alchemy Association**: guild of alchemists.
- **The Church** (plural): a collection of religious organisations; the Healer's church is the largest.
- **The Red Table**: a blood cult with branches in remote areas (Book 1, Ch18 L5; Book 7, Ch55 L75).
- **Noble houses and monarchies**: kingdoms (the Storm Kingdom, Estercost), duchies, city-states. Diamond-rank rulers exist.
- **Indentured servitude** is a legal norm in many places (criminals' labour sold). It becomes a flash-point in Book 12. **(Later: Book 12)**

---

### 12. Geography at a glance

- **Estercost**: kingdom with capital Cyrion (largest city), **Vitesse** (city of flowers; Remore Academy), and the colony city **Greenstone** (low-magic delta city; Jason's early home).
- **The Storm Kingdom** (Rimaros): city-of-islands in the Sea of Storms, ruled by a gold-rank Storm King; adventurer island Livaros, quiet Arnote, trade island Provo (the three public islands, Book 7, Ch7 L70).
- **Yaresh**: elf rainforest city, with a natural array beneath it.
- **Boko**: desert academic city north of Greenstone (destroyed in Book 12, Ch33 L3).
- **Other regions**: Zartos (celestine underground city), Pranay (Sri Lanka-like; Jayapura), Kurdansk (Dreisil), the Dragon Lands (Antarctic analogue), Sadi Andali (lawless slave markets), Girlano (cartel-ruled), Segurado, Hornis, Kazlahk, Rakesh (first mentions: Zartos, Book 1, Ch16 L49; Dreisil, Book 6, Ch47 L390; Rakesh, Book 6, Ch47 L623; Hornis, Book 1, Ch102 L11; Girlano, Book 8, Ch24 L22; Segurado, Book 12, Ch24 L6; Sadi Andali, Book 12, Ch50 L126; Kazlahk, Book 11, Ch68 L1377; Jayapura, Book 2, Ch69 L66). The descriptions are from the place files.
- **Astral spaces and zones**: the City of Fallen Echoes (Book 2, Ch42 L96), the desert astral space (Book 1, Ch24 L34), Cardinas and the natural array (Book 10, Ch72 L31), transformation zones (Book 5, Ch44 L48-49; Book 6, Ch47 L3).
- **On Earth**: Casselton Beach (Jason's hometown), Asano Village, Saint-Étienne (France) and Nitra (Slovakia) domains, Sydney, Makassar, Broken Hill, the Australian artefact site.

---

### 13. History in outline

1. **Before the series**: the original Builder creates Earth and Pallimustus from a shared template; he is sanctioned and replaced by a new mortal Builder. Five hundred years ago Knowledge, Disguise (impersonating Purity) and an Earth outworlder (the Network's founder) set up the link and the Network; the Order of the Reaper is crushed by the churches. **(Level 3 reveal)**
2. **Books 1-3**: Jason arrives (age 23); adventures in Greenstone; the Builder cult's star seeds; the contest for the Scythe of the Reaper; the cult's boarding vessel; Jason dies and returns to Earth.
3. **Books 4-6**: Jason on Earth; the Network, Cabal and EOA; the Grid fails; Makassar; transformation zones; Slovakia and France; vampires; Jason and Farrah return to Pallimustus.
4. **Books 7-9**: the great surge; the Builder's invasion platforms and the One Day War; Jason's soul-space becomes an astral kingdom; the messengers and the Battle of Yaresh.
5. **Books 10-11**: the Cardinas expedition and the Death Pact; Undeath and the transformation zone; Gary's death; the aftermath of the sundered Cosmic Throne (Book 11, Ch64-65); Jason's interface becomes available to everyone with essences (Book 12, Ch1 L36).
6. **Books 12-13**: Jason's prime avatar; Boko; the abolition of the System in slave-law regions; the return to Earth; vampire war; Knowledge's plan (Book 13, Ch1015 L78); at the end Jason walks to the standing stones at Ascension's Gate (Book 13, Ch1024 L153).

See `08_History_and_Timeline/Master_Timeline.md` and the per-book timelines for the verified chronology.

---

### 14. Recurring facts worth remembering

- Jason's powers revolve around **afflictions** (long-lasting debilitating effects). Many characters' signature lines are used as incantations ("Feed me your sins", "Mine is the judgement, and the judgement is death").
- **Team Biscuit**: a familiar picked the team's name (Book 10, Ch47 L78; the wiki credits Stash); Jason's biscuits are a running joke (Book 1, Ch78).
- **Cloud houses** are a signature aesthetic; so are floral shirts, board games and pop-culture references.
- **Humour and pop culture**: Jason's Earth references (Knight Rider, Airwolf, Voltron...) are part of the tone.
- **Morality**: Jason refuses to treat people as tools; mercy and autonomy recur as themes; his world-changing actions have costs.
- **Gods and wishes**: gods often grant boons that are traps; "poison pills".

---

### 15. Running a scene at a given period

When setting a roleplay, decide **era** and **scale**:

| Era | Setting | Typical scale | Key dangers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Early (Book 1-2) | Greenstone, delta, desert astral spaces | Iron-rank | Blood cult, crime lords, Builder cult, monster surge precursors |
| Mid (Book 3) | Greenstone to the Reaper-trial astral space | Bronze | Star seeds, kidnapping, energy ghouls |
| Earth (Books 4-6) | Australia, Asia, Europe | Bronze to silver | Network politics, EOA, monster waves, vampires, transformation zones |
| Rimaros (Books 7-8) | Storm Kingdom | Silver | Builder fortresses, Order of Redeeming Light, royal politics |
| Yaresh (Books 9-10) | Elf rainforest, natural array | Silver | Messengers, worms, Undeath, elemental horrors |
| Zone and aftermath (Book 11) | Transformation zone, Earth | Silver to gold | Undeath, reality collapse, vampire war |
| Return (Books 12-13) | Pallimustus tour and Earth | Gold | Messenger kings, pirates, Elizabeth's blood weapons, Knowledge |

Era choice and spoiler handling are covered in `10_Roleplay_Support/Era_Selection.md` and `10_Roleplay_Support/Spoiler_Management.md`.

---

### 16. Glossary of core terms

**Adventurer**: someone who hunts monsters and takes contracts. **Affliction**: a lasting harmful condition. **Astral kingdom**: Jason's soul realm. **Aura**: projection of the soul. **Awakening stone**: crystal that awakens an essence ability. **Boon**: a lasting beneficial condition. **Cloud flask**: Jason's bonded item that makes cloud houses. **Confluence**: the special fourth essence. **Core**: crystallised magic from a monster. **Essence**: crystal of magic. **Gestalt**: body and soul fused. **GAB**: great astral being. **Grid**: Earth's detection network. **Hegemon**: Jason's title and aura power. **Messenger**: winged servant of an astral king. **Outworlder**: person from another world. **Prime avatar**: a physical anchor for an astral being's power. **Quintessence**: crafting gems of an essence's theme. **Rank**: iron through diamond. **Sanction**: punitive change of a being's authority. **Spirit coin**: currency of magic. **Star seed**: Builder implant that puppets its host. **System**: Jason's interface made universal. **Voice of the Will**: a bonded avatar of an astral king's will.

## Astral Kings and Messengers

### 1. Summary

Astral kings rule their own universes. Most are messengers' masters: the messengers are their servants, invaders of worlds, and carry the astral king's message. In Book 8 Jason discovers that he himself is an astral king, which makes him both a political danger among the messengers and an unusual ally to them.

### 2. Astral kings

- **What they are**: "what amounts to sentient miniature universes" (Dawn to Jason, Book 8, Ch67 L53); they forge "their very souls into physical universes, creating domains where their power was unassailable and all-but-unlimited" (Book 9, Ch95 L15). The wiki's added claims about immortality and control over whether inhabitants can die are not confirmed.
- **Prerequisites**: "you're an astral king because you have an astral kingdom... because you possess an astral throne and an astral gate" (Book 8, Ch65 L88); the "astral throne, astral gate and soul forge trifecta" (Book 10, Ch1 L52). The wiki's mention of transcendence is not confirmed. Jason's body is a gestalt of physical and spiritual (Book 9, Ch62 L30: a healer observes that he "was not a dual-entity comprised of body and soul, but a gestalt physical and spiritual being", like messengers).
- **Original astral kings** guided messengers when they came into being, as a parent guides a child; they were not themselves messengers. Boris explains (Book 11, Ch25 L51) that back then there were no limits on rank, because rank limits are a function of the brand, which did not exist. When messengers transcended and became astral kings, they instituted the brand and enslaved their own kind; war and rebellion followed, the free lost, and the defeated went into hiding. The Unorthodoxy descends from the free.
- **Most astral kings are messengers**: Jason is told (Book 9, Ch23 L44) that "the vast majority of astral kings are messengers".
- **Voices of the Will**: servants who carry the bestowed power of an astral king. Jason's familiars hold the source end of that power (Book 9, Ch62 L30-34), which shocks a healer: no silver-rank should possess it, and she realises Jason is a silver-rank astral king. Colin can awaken as a Voice of the Will after hibernation (Book 9, Ch69 L55-59).

### 3. Jason as an astral king (spoilers)

After the Astral Throne and Astral Gate appear (Book 8, Ch49 L105), Jason's spirit realm becomes an astral kingdom. The place-level description is in `06_Places/Astral_Spaces/Spirit_Vault_and_Astral_Kingdom.md`. His familiars gain bonded, eternal forms. He tells Arabelle that being an astral king puts him on a different path from anyone he cares about (Book 9, Ch41 L81).

### 4. Messengers

- **Nature**: gestalt beings whose body and soul are one thing; Jason explains (Book 9, Ch52 L60) that because auras are projections of the soul, their gestalt nature gives them aura abilities that body-soul dual beings do not have. A messenger seen in Book 9 "looked like a celestine with alabaster skin and long hair of spun gold... His eyes were solid gold orbs" (Book 9, Ch52 L5). Messengers can hide their wings, reduce their size and diminish their beauty (Book 13, Ch954 L4), and have hidden on Earth for millennia.
- **Belief and the instinct to kneel**: Book 10 has a chapter titled "The Instinct to Kneel" in which Hess confesses to feeling it (Book 10, Ch16 L48); Dawn tells Jason that messengers are messengers of astral kings, whose message is "Kneel", and that astral kings rule through them rather than invading in person (Book 8, Ch64 L72-80).
- **Rank**: the books confirm that rank limits are a function of the brand (Boris, Book 11, Ch25 L51), that Fal Vin Garath is a silver-rank messenger master and Jes Fin Kaal a gold-rank Voice of the Will (Book 9, Ch56 L5-8). A silver seal on messengers is mentioned in Book 9 (Vesta Carmis Zell "felt one of her seals disappear", a silver-rank seal, when Jason frees Tera; Book 9, Ch102 L66-67), and diamond messengers can begin to resist the brand (Book 11, Ch25 L53). Whether messengers are strictly capped at silver is not established.
- **Social order**: servants races (Benella and others) are subject to messengers; masters may treat them as they please so long as it does not impinge on other messengers (Book 9, Ch56 L5).
- **Methods**: Garth's isolation (duel) power (Book 11, Ch29 L31), aura masks, the world-taker worm and other apocalypse beasts (Book 10, Ch6 L11; Book 9, Ch62 L23), and the natural array's changes that devolve intelligence (Book 9, Ch104 L84). That messengers enslave essence users to dig for the array is from earlier notes and was not rechecked.
- **Resurrection**: does not work on messengers or anyone like them; their life is not just physical and is tenacious (Jason, Book 9, Ch65 L23).
- **Birth**: Jason says messengers are "budded, not born" and are "actually plants, which is kind of crazy" (Book 12, Ch67 L23).

### 5. The Unorthodoxy

Full account in `The_Unorthodoxy.md`; the Council of Kings has its own file, `The_Council_of_Kings.md`.

Dissenting messengers who want to live without astral kings. Boris Ket Lundi tells Jason (Book 11, Ch24 L86) that he is Unorthodoxy and that his astral king's allies do not know; Book 12 confirms that Navise Den Rigal, a Voice of the Will, serves a minor astral king who is secretly one of the Unorthodoxy's rare astral kings, and that Boris was slipped into the service of Vesta Carmis Zell. Marek Nior Vargas leads a breach force against Yaresh in Book 9, has misgivings about the operation and the politics, and later brings his people into Jason's realm; whether Marek leads the Unorthodoxy is unchecked. Tera Jun Casta is a branded messenger whose brand Jason removes (Book 10, Ch42 L7: it was the brand of her astral king master, Vesta Carmis Zell, and it traumatises her).

### 6. Jamis Fran Muskar

The Council of Kings is, in Book 10 (Ch15 L3), "the closest thing the messengers had to central leadership"; a group of prime avatars, each belonging to a different member, watches the Builder's agents preparing to move a planet. Many astral kings stand outside it (Book 11, Ch24 L86). Jamis Fran Muskar is an astral king whose avatar attends the Book 10 scene; his avatar stands out because its wings have been completely absorbed into his body (Book 10, Ch15 L6), and in Book 12 he angrily accuses messengers of defying "the explicit instructions of the Council of Kings" (Book 12, Ch33 L51-55). In a scene with Vesta Carmis Zell he says that when a certain task is complete the price is paid and Zithis Carrow Vayel, the Builder, will have fulfilled his debt to them (Book 10, Ch15 L9). What the debt is remains unexplained in the text I checked.

### 7. Dangers and hooks

Messenger diplomacy, an enslaved population in a rainforest, a defecting messenger asking for sanctuary, an astral king's message. Hooks: a messenger envoy expects Jason to kneel; a Voice of the Will visits a human city.

### 8. Open questions

- Whether the silver cap is a fixed rule or varies by king.
- The Council of Kings' composition.
- How the seal and brand operate in detail.

---

## Authority and Sanctioning

### 1. Summary

Authority is what great astral beings and gods are made of, and the thing that lets them shape the cosmos. It cannot be taken by force and must be traded, it comes in a safe set state and a dangerous potential state, and it is guided by will. Sanctioning is how transcendent beings change one another: their authority is turned against them, or they change themselves with it. The books treat it as the cosmos's only real punishment, because an immortal cannot be killed.

### 2. How it works

- **What it is**: great astral beings are the most powerful entities in the cosmos, and "the nature of both themselves and their power was known as authority" (Book 8, Ch52 L9). Authority is "the fundamental power of the cosmos", and everything in physical reality is underpinned by it to some degree (Book 8, Ch57 L25).
- **Two states**: set-state authority has been put to a purpose, which makes it fixed, defined and safe ("clay turned into a bowl"); potential-state authority is the unworked clay, "except the clay is actually enriched uranium" (Book 8, Ch57 L25, L35).
- **Jason's domains**: his spirit domains are made of set-state authority, which he calls "the treehouse that I'm allowed to play in" (Book 8, Ch57 L25, L66). His spirit realm is also an aspect of his authority (Book 8, Ch57 L27). He thinks that if his domains broke down into potential-state authority it would kill him (Book 8, Ch57 L70).
- **Transformation zones**: they are "areas of set-state authority breaking down into potential-state authority", the domes being the world sealing them like scabs (Book 8, Ch57 L62).
- **It must be traded**: Jason says authority "has to be traded" and the Builder agrees (Book 8, Ch54 L18-19). The great astral beings' dealings are "striking bargains and making pacts", and pacts are about trading authority (Book 8, Ch52 L51, L88).
- **It cannot be taken**: when the diamond-ranked Shako touches the tablet holding Jason's authority he is thrown away with a sonic boom (Book 8, Ch52 L59). Jason says Shako could no more take it than "burn down the cosmos" (Book 8, Ch52 L70), and tells him "That isn't the kind of power you can just take" (Book 8, Ch52 L72). Shako has none of his own: "It is not my place" (Book 8, Ch52 L56-57).
- **Holding it is dangerous to a mortal**: the authority Jason holds feels like a cancer that would likely destroy him if he did not get rid of it soon, which he suspects is what burns through vessels so quickly (Book 8, Ch54 L15-16). Gods and great astral beings know at once when a mortal outside a spirit domain carries it (Book 8, Ch52 L11-12).
- **Shown to the holder**: it resonates with the great astral beings and gives Jason insight into how authority and the beings made of it work (Book 8, Ch54 L17).

- **Will guides authority**: "Will is critical to the use of authority." Overcoming another's will to interfere with their authority is extremely difficult but not impossible, which is why gods have to team up to punish one of their number, and so do great astral beings (Book 11, Ch33 L140).
- **Affinity**: authority is flavoured by its holder. The Builder's is about forging reality and the World-Phoenix's about dimensional forces, so authority can be changed only so far (Book 11, Ch33 L155-157). Jason used authority taken from the Builder for the cloud flask and his astral throne, and authority taken from the World-Phoenix for his astral gate (Book 11, Ch33 L157).
- **Mortals and authority**: mortals use it through intrinsic-mandate magic, which Jason reaches through his familiar Gordon (Book 11, Ch33 L152-153).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Who can hold it**: Shako tells Dawn she is "on the cusp of claiming your own authority" (Book 8, Ch53 L24). She says she is now a hierophant, no longer among the servants but "my own agent" (Book 8, Ch53 L29).
- **Jason's special case**: he accepted a power the great astral beings gave him, meant to let him do what the World-Phoenix needed, with set-state authority only (Book 8, Ch57 L33-35).
- **Inside a spirit domain**: even gods cannot spy on Jason there, as if it were territory from which they are excluded (Book 8, Ch52 L11).
- **Shade's authority**: Shade makes use of "authority accumulated over tens of thousands of years" for his self-sanction (Book 11, Ch68 L2206).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **The Builder's tablet, Book 8**: Jason breaks down the Builder's door and holds a sliver of authority as a tablet. He refuses to let Shako take it, offers it to the Builder in a trade, and gets the way into the fundamental realm opened once; the Builder takes the authority back (Book 8, Ch52 L58-70; Book 8, Ch54 L54, L60-61, L99).
- **The original Builder**: the other great astral beings sanctioned him for the twin-universe experiment by taking his authority and giving it to a mortal (Book 13, Ch1017 L11). Dawn says even hierophants are not told the secrets of the Builder's ascension and his predecessor's sanctioning, which are widely held to explain his erratic behaviour (Book 8, Ch19 L40).

- **The new Builder's conditions**: when the other beings gave him "the sanctioned authority of original Builder", they set conditions, including the power to revert his mind to the state it was in at sixteen, as a messenger (Book 11, Ch68 L450-454). The Builder-and-nameless problem is described by Raythe and Velius (Book 11, Ch65 L61).
- **The Boundary becomes the World-Phoenix**: the Boundary "wanted to be more than it was" and sanctioned itself. The Cosmic Throne resisted, and the sundering freed the World-Phoenix from the pressure to be turned back (Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795).
- **Shade sanctions himself**: Shade spends accumulated authority, and the window reads that he "has sanctioned himself" and become a Shadow of the Hegemon. Jason is then "in a state of self-sanction" and "has accepted external sanction", and the familiar contract becomes permanent (Book 11, Ch68 L2205-2218). The Reaper warns "Sanctioning can so easily go wrong" (Book 11, Ch68 L2220).
- **Hero's planned self-sanction**: Gwydion says Hero has decided to sanction himself, something he has considered for longer than any of them has lived (Book 11, Ch68 L707).
- **Purity**: his instability was coming to a head about five hundred years ago and he was likely to sanction himself, "essentially retiring himself and being reborn", until Knowledge persuaded him to leave a divine relic instead (Book 13, Ch1017 L15-16).
- **Undeath's avatar**: Jason sanctions the echo of Undeath's authority that drives an avatar. Gordon works the intrinsic-mandate magic, Jason guides it with will, and he reforges the god's authority with ghost fire into a divine weapon, at risk of Undeath taking root in his soul (Book 11, Ch33 L140-157; Book 11, Ch35 L43-48).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **"Sanction" is not the affliction.** The holy affliction Sanction reduces healing and cannot be cleansed while Penance is on the target (Book 12, Ch67 L339). A character who knows the affliction thinks sanctioning is that; Jason says "what I'm talking about is a different kind of sanctioning. It's how entities like gods and great astral beings punish their own kind" (Book 11, Ch33 L9-13).
- **Sanctioning is not killing.** "You can't kill an immortal, but you can sanction them, which means to change them in some way" (Book 13, Ch1017 L11).
- **Sanctioning is not painting over.** Jason guesses it might be "taking someone and slapping a new person over the top"; Dawn tells him to stop watching heist movies (Book 8, Ch55 L31-32).
- **Authority can be ordered over.** Shako tells Jason "Hand it over, Asano" (Book 8, Ch52 L53), but the tablet throws him away, and the Builder concedes that authority must be traded (Book 8, Ch54 L19).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Book 8**: Jason holds authority for the first time and trades it back (Book 8, Ch54 L99).
- **Book 11**: he learns to use another's authority against it, and Shade's self-sanction makes the familiar bond permanent (Book 11, Ch35 L43-47; Book 11, Ch68 L2217-2218).
- **Book 13**: the limits are stated. Knowledge tells Jason that even as a great astral being he "will not have the authority to sanction a god. That is for other gods to do", and Jason answers that he said he would kill her (Book 13, Ch1024 L141-142). Dawn, as a new transcendent, "can't be killed, only sanctioned" (Book 13, Ch992 L63-64).

### 7. Using this in a story

Keep authority scarce, specific and expensive. A mortal who comes by a scrap of it is in danger from the holder and from every great astral being who notices; any deal over it is a trade, not a gift. A sanction should change its target in a way the story can show: a role lost, a mind reverted, a self remade. When a character says "sanction", check whether they mean the affliction or the act. Jason's confrontations with gods stay about will and trades until the rules, as stated in Book 13, are changed by someone with the standing to do so.

---

## The Cosmic Throne and the Sundering

### 1. Summary

The Cosmic Throne was the ultimate authority that regulated the great astral beings. They broke it long ago, replaced it with a web of pacts, and in time regretted it. Jason is asked to repair it during his transition to astral king, and to leave it empty. He does so at the end of Book 11, which sets a new status quo for the cosmos and, as a side effect, makes his interface the System.

### 2. How it works

- **What it was**: "the power that regulated cosmic forces, keeping the great astral beings adherent to their respective purposes" (Book 11, Ch64 L24). Transcendent entities have effectively infinite power, and authority is "the right for a transcendent being to employ their infinite power in a specific way", which keeps the cosmos in balance; the throne was "the ultimate authority" (Book 11, Ch64 L24-25).
- **A neutral arbiter**: the throne must be left empty, "a neutral arbiter without will, only purpose", as it was before the sundering (Book 11, Ch65 L8-9). Raythe and Velius want someone who will claim the ultimate authority and then give it up without ever exercising it (Book 11, Ch65 L6).
- **The rules it enforces**: "The rules of the cosmos are enforced by something called the Cosmic Throne. It was damaged long ago, but the throne has been restored and the rules are more dangerous to bend, let alone break" (Book 12, Ch63 L9). Knowledge says the rules "have been put back in place. By you, no less" (Book 13, Ch1024 L141).
- **Gods are bound by it**: gods are bound to their worlds and last only as long as the planet they are attached to; Knowledge's crossing to Earth was only possible through the circumstances of the Builder's twin universes, which "would never have happened while the Cosmic Throne was intact" (Book 13, Ch1021 L69-71).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Those who stood aside**: the great astral beings agreed to pacts instead, but not all took part. The Keeper of Moments opposed the sundering from the beginning and refused to participate (Book 11, Ch64 L47), and the Keeper, the All-Devouring Eye and the Word in the Silence "have ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering" (Book 11, Ch64 L49).
- **The nameless**: the original pacts did not include the nameless great astral beings, whom the named ones treated "as nobility sees servants" (Book 11, Ch65 L59). Without the throne's oversight they are "unbound from the strictures of their duties" (Book 11, Ch65 L58) and are unhappy at its restoration, but will not hunt Jason (Book 12, Ch1 L26).
- **Servants cannot do it**: "No servant of the great astral beings can be used. The pacts prevent it" (Book 11, Ch64 L83), so Dawn and other minions cannot repair the throne.
- **The chosen candidate**: the repair needs someone in one of a short subset of transcendental processes, including becoming an original, with a pre-existing connection to the Sundered Throne (Book 11, Ch64 L85-89). The great astral beings believe the All-Devouring Eye created Gordon specifically for this outcome (Book 11, Ch64 L91).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **The sundering and its cost**: after the throne was sundered some regretted it and others "revelled in their newfound freedom", including the Builder, who had always been bound by strict rules and began to experiment (Book 13, Ch1017 L9). The twin universes of Earth and Pallimustus were "a step too far", the sort of thing the throne had prevented, and the others sanctioned the Builder (Book 13, Ch1017 L9-11).
- **The pacts and why they failed**: the old Builder was sanctioned and the new one brought into the pacts together with the nameless, but this addendum "was not an effective curb on the behaviour of these late additions" (Book 11, Ch65 L61). The nameless cause many lesser problems that "fester in the dark", cascading "towards infinite anarchy" (Book 11, Ch65 L62-64).
- **The offer**: Raythe and Velius ask Jason to repair the throne while he is transcending, and the Reaper speaks through Velius to say that many of those who took part in the sundering now think revisiting it would be prudent (Book 11, Ch64 L58-66).
- **The risks**: connecting to the throne exposes his soul to intrusion, and his soul becomes a liminal space that others can enter while he is connected (Book 11, Ch65 L20, L28). The World-Phoenix, which prefers things as they are, will be his antagonist (Book 11, Ch65 L34-36).
- **Restrictions released**: after the sundering the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations, so that each had only one possible confluence; Jason's repair starts to unravel the restrictions (Book 11, Ch68 L1574-1580).
- **The World-Phoenix**: before the sundering the Boundary sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix and the throne resisted, "a constant fight to not be turned back into what I was" (Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795). When the throne is restored it takes the World-Phoenix's current state as the new baseline, so the pressure ends (Book 12, Ch60 L16).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **"The throne is a weapon."** It is meant to be empty; its danger is the ultimate authority, "a power that no one and nothing should have" (Book 11, Ch65 L3).
- **"Restoring it undoes the sundering."** It cannot: "The throne could never be restored to what it was. Part of you was imprinted upon it" (Book 12, Ch1 L34).
- **"Jason will rule the cosmos."** He is asked to leave it empty (Book 11, Ch65 L8). He mocks the idea in a threat to the Reaper that he will use the Cosmic Throne to give everyone in the universe ten free resurrections (Book 11, Ch68 L2409).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Book 11, the repair**: the throne room stands at the end of a hallway in a castle at the boundary of reality. The throne is split as if cleaved by an axe, the gap filled with blue and orange light, and Gordon's orbs shine and sing (Book 11, Ch68 L2522-2524). The great astral beings gather in their own prime vessels, including Raythe and Helsveth (Book 11, Ch68 L2526-2528). Jason says he is not going to make a fundamental change to the cosmos "right?" and every person with essences or their potential sees "Don't Panic. Everything is going to be fine. Welcome to the System." (Book 11, Ch68 L2533-2540).
- **Book 12, the aftermath**: his mortal aspect barely endures the task and he falls off the throne (Book 12, Ch1 L3, L22). The restoration set "a new status quo based on things as they were at the moment of restoration" (Book 12, Ch1 L28). The strictures the beings placed on the cosmos after the sundering are now being released (Book 12, Ch1 L30).
- **Book 13, the rules back in force**: Knowledge notes that the rules are in place again and that Jason, even as a great astral being, will not have the authority to sanction a god, which only gods can do (Book 13, Ch1024 L141).

### 7. Using this in a story

Treat the throne as the cosmos's fixed constitution: it limits what even great astral beings may do, and breaking the rules has consequences nobody in the books can name. Because it is empty, no one can bargain with it, and the way to get around the rules is a loophole, a pact or a trade. A story in which a character wants to "use the throne" is a story about a temptation Jason is expected to refuse.

## Gods and Churches

### 1. Summary

Gods are transcendent beings outside physical reality, each focused on a single concept (Dominion, Healer, Knowledge, Death and more). They manifest avatars, speak with Akashic Speech, give followers essences and awakening stones that they can take back (Book 1, Ch21 L57; Book 3, Ch61 L11), and work miracles (Book 10, Ch82 L72). In Jason's words in Book 8, "gods are like regional managers of full-blown universes". Churches are their institutions.

### 2. What gods can and cannot do

The churches as institutions have their own files in `../05_Organisations/Churches/`: Healer, Knowledge, Purity, Dominion, Death, Undeath and Hero.

- **Sight**: gods cannot see into an astral space that is not part of their world. In Book 10 a goddess says she cannot see into the astral space Jason is holding prisoners in; in Book 8 a priest says his god cannot see inside a building hidden from the gods (Book 10, Ch31 L69-75; Book 8, Ch43 L48-53).
- **Domains**: gods cannot enter another's spirit domain ("higher rules for higher beings", Book 6, Ch24 L86); gods cannot reveal other gods' deceptions, being bound by rules of interplay (Book 8, Ch48 L22-26).
- **Miracles**: "if you want a miracle, you need one of my servants or a grand sacrifice" (a god to Jason, Book 10, Ch82 L72).
- **Death certification**: the Church of Death certifies deaths; in Book 7 an official is shown a certification that Jason has died four times "so far", and in Book 10 Jason shows Hana Shavar the card (Book 7, Ch17 L104; Book 10, Ch38 L73).
- **Essences and stones**: gods bestow divine versions of regular essences and divine awakening stones (Book 1, Ch21 L57; Book 2, Ch13 L60). They return to the god: freed cult captives with divine essences are weaker because the power "was not consumed by the process but returned to their god" (Book 3, Ch61 L11), and ex-clergy stripped of divinely gifted essences suffer a "debilitating imbalance in the body and soul" (Book 4, Ch11 L16). When the Healer casts out priests who exploited their healing, Dominion offers to take them into his service (Book 1, Ch95 L90-94).

### 3. Gods named in the books

Gods and churches the text names in the form "god of" or "Temple/Church of", by first mention: Knowledge (Book 1, Ch44 L68), Roads and Journeys (Book 1, Ch45 L4), Hero ("heroes", Book 1, Ch45 L39), Purity (Book 1, Ch65 L130), Fertility (Book 1, Ch82 L73), the Healer (Book 1, Ch94 L3), Revels (Book 1, Ch112 L96), Deceit (Book 2, Ch13 L103), Death (Book 2, Ch25 L67), Dominion (Book 2, Ch66 L105), Trade (Book 3, Ch69 L872), Undeath (Book 7, Ch9 L99), Lust (Book 7, Ch20 L54), War (Book 10, Ch9 L10), Liberty (Book 10, Ch28 L56), Destruction (Book 10, Ch66 L103), Disguise (Book 11, Ch4 L85), Pain (Book 12, Ch26 L80), Chastity (Book 12, Ch46 L89) and Rivers (Book 12, Ch13 L5). The fan wiki's list of 43 names is given in full below, as a wiki-tier supplement. Undeath, Destruction and Disguise "have only hidden strongholds that are constantly being hunted" (Book 10, Ch85 L40), and Undeath priests are "the most reviled people in our world" (Book 10, Ch78 L32). In Book 1 Jason sees temples such as the Temple of Roads and the Temple of the Healer on the Divine Square (Book 1, Ch45 L4-9).

### 4. Gods and churches in the story

Each of the following has its own file in `Gods/`: Knowledge, Death, the Healer, Hero, Purity and Disguise, Dominion, Undeath, Fertility, Hearth, Destruction and Pain and Discord. The notes below are the short form.

#### The Healer
God of medicine and healing. The Greenstone temple was corrupt and had to be corrected by divine intervention; Neil makes a stand in the temple in Book 1, where a priest tells those who stand against the church that they are no longer welcome (Book 1, Ch94 L3-7). After the revelations about Purity, "the church of the Healer has taken over from Purity in dealing with the star seeds" (Book 3, Ch21 L73); a Healer priest, Carlos, specialises in soul damage from star seeds (Book 8, Ch17 L45). Hana Shavar, an elf and High Priestess of the Healer, is in charge of operations that use Jason's cloud palace as a base after the messenger attack (Book 10, Ch3 L29; the city's priestess, Book 9, Ch74 L43); during the attack she avoided Jason's bunker and sent her priests into Emir Bahadir's (Book 9, Ch80 L6-13); Carlos Quilido is a Healer priest who joins the Cardinas expedition (Book 11, Ch67 L6).

#### Dominion
The god of rulership. A believer says "Dominion issues the divine right to kings and nobles" (Book 1, Ch45 L18), but Dominion tells Jason "There is no divine right of kings. Mortals choose and I try to help them not make a complete mess of things" (Book 12, Ch13 L67). His church is the most prominent outlier in keeping low-ranking essence users under its thumb (Book 3, Ch69 L859), and he tells his new clergy "There is no service in my church... you will obey or suffer" (Book 1, Ch95 L94). He tells Gary "That is where monarchs come from. I love them most of all. I'll be keeping an eye on you, Gareth Xandier" (Book 1, Ch95 L104), and a character says in Book 9 that he likes "the ones who refuse to kneel" (Book 9, Ch41 L11).

#### Purity and Disguise (Level 2/3)
Book 10 states that the Order of Redeeming Light was created by Disguise, a god masquerading as Purity: its Flames of Redemption are an extreme modification of lesser vampirism, and the order was founded only after Disguise took on Purity's mantle (Book 10, Ch39 L46-49, Arabelle and Carlos). Jason tells Melody Jain that her god is "an illusion. A disguise" (Book 10, Ch40 L16). In Book 8 Carlos Quilido tells Jason his theory that the gods may have sanctioned Purity long before, and that rules of interplay stopped them telling their clergy (Book 8, Ch48 L40-60). In Jason's Book 13 briefing, Purity, who embodies several contradictory meanings, was unstable about five hundred years ago and likely to sanction himself; Knowledge interfered; and a relic of Purity's divine power was left behind (Book 13, Ch1017 L14-24). Purity's most zealous worshippers carry many purgation tools (Book 7, Ch35 L39); the wiki's claim that the doctrine treats humans as the "pure" state is not used here.

#### Knowledge (Level 3 for the plot)
In Book 1 Jason meets the goddess as a woman with colourful clothes and Mediterranean features, beautiful yet "detached and untouchable" (Book 1, Ch46 L16); she knows everything anyone in her world knows, including Jason, so she knows "Mario Kart shortcuts" (Book 1, Ch77 L10). In Book 13 Jason tells his allies that she has been preparing to invade Earth for half a millennium and used him as a key part of the plan; the briefing says she promised the messengers' leader a chance to invade Pallimustus and claim Purity's relic, and that around a third of the priests and priestesses of Knowledge are her spies (Book 13, Ch1017 L14-20). When Gabrielle Pellin refuses to believe it, a cube leaves her chest into Knowledge's hand, Gabrielle seizes, and Travis catches her (Book 13, Ch1023 L139). Jason answers Knowledge's claim that she will be "the one true God" of his world with "The next time we meet, Goddess, will be the day you die" (Book 13, Ch1024 L153).

#### Death (Level 3)
The goddess of death appears to Jason in the Cardinas death chamber as "a stocky, middle-aged woman with a colourful dress" with the warmth of "a matronly tavern keeper" (Book 10, Ch82 L62). Her pact seals any ability to resurrect himself or another, persists through any change in his nature, and is enacted by the goddess guiding his soul to change itself, without her gaining access to it. In return he gains the title Keeper of the Cycle: abilities that apply afflictions also apply ghost fire, mana drain degrades the animating force of undead, and allies in his aura are affected by ghost fire while he suppresses undead (Book 10, Ch83 L75-78). In Book 12 Gordon suggests asking Death to return the resurrection power Jason gave away (Book 12, Ch6 L18-22), and Death does: "I will return what was taken, Jason Asano, now that it cannot be used for its original purpose" (Book 12, Ch8 L10), the reality material forming Jason's prime avatar (Book 12, Ch8 L19).

#### Hero (Level 3)
The god of heroes is "the only core deity not to have subordinate gods" (Book 1, Ch48 L92). Those who make the ultimate sacrifice are offered the Cup of Heroes (Book 10, Ch89 L54; Gary drinks it, Book 10, Ch86 L59, and says "I'm only a demigod", Book 11, Ch1 L9). Almost a year later Gary is a haggard figure kept alive by Hero's power (Book 11, Ch68 L703-708). Gwydion tells Gary that Hero has decided to sanction himself, something he has considered for longer than anyone has been alive (Book 11, Ch68 L707-709). When Gary drinks it, his hammer, fire and iron essences become divine versions and his forge confluence is replaced by a Demigod essence (Book 10, Ch86 L67-70), not a "Hero" essence.

#### Undeath (Level 3)
Hana Shavar says (Book 10, Ch78 L38) that the Church of Undeath lies dormant for generations and strikes when its god has "saved up his chances to intervene", bringing "dark miracles". Garth Larosse, a zemravore and priest of Undeath, leads the church's priests in Cardinas (Book 10, Ch88 L58-63; Book 11, Ch29 L3-5). Undeath is one of the gods with only hidden strongholds (Book 10, Ch85 L40).

### 5. Churches in practice

Churches provide healing, ritual rooms, scribes and, in some cases, armies. A church can be corrupt or reformed by divine intervention. The Church of Knowledge funds the Magical Research Association (Book 12, Ch1 L58).

### 6. Dangers and hooks

A fraudulent god, hidden temples, divine bargains with a price, a god's claim on a follower. Hooks: a temple raid, a divine gift with a catch, a priest who learns that their god's authority is a mask.

### 7. Open questions

- The count and full list of gods against the book text (the text-scanned list above is not exhaustive).

## Great Astral Beings

### 1. Summary

A great astral being (GAB) is a cosmic-scale transcendent: an aspect of the cosmos that embodies a concept such as construction, finality of death, time, entropy or dimensional integrity. They are not gods and are not bound by gods. Clive describes them in Book 1 as similar to gods but belonging to no world: they exist between worlds in the deep astral, "gods to the gods, although you wouldn't catch any gods saying that". They do not rule worlds directly. They act through **vessels**: mortals chosen to host them, and **prime vessels**, who carry the fullest part of their power. GABs cannot interact with physical reality directly; they recruit others to act for them (Clive on the Builder, Book 2, Ch21 L112).

### 2. Key facts

- **Authority**: they generate it intrinsically. See `00_Cosmology_Overview.md`.
- **Mortal form**: great astral beings enjoy mortal bodies (Book 11, Ch68 L2526). A vessel can be possessed; Clive notes it is possible, if far from ethical (Book 3, Ch57 L4). Diamond-rank vessels of the great astral beings can withstand the strain and keep their selves, unlike the disposable vessels the Builder uses; eventually the soul can no longer cope and the vessel passes on the role, with no lingering effects and a stronger soul as a result (Book 3, Ch69 L1036-1040).
- **No fear of gods**: Clive says a GAB is one of the few beings that need not fear a god's retribution, since the gods of Pallimustus cannot see into an astral space that is not part of their world (Book 3, Ch62 L33).
- **Sanctioning**: see section 4.
- **Pacts**: after the Sundering, pacts between GABs restrict their direct meddling. Dawn tells Shako in Book 6 that by killing Jason he violated the compact between the Builder, the Reaper and the World-Phoenix (Book 6, Ch18 L79-80).

### 3. Named great astral beings

Each has its own file in `Great_Astral_Beings/`: World-Phoenix, Builder, Reaper, Celestial Book, Legion, All-Devouring Eye, Keeper of Moments, Seeker of Songs, Whisper in Corners and Word in the Silence.

| GAB | Concept | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| The Builder | Construction, forging reality | Original Builder sanctioned; new Builder is the mortal messenger Zithis Carrow Vayel (sixteen-year-old diamond-ranker when recruited; Book 10, Ch26 L55). Vessels have included Shako and Erigo Fin Desca (prime vessel after Shako was taken by the Sundered Throne; Book 10, Ch15 L5). |
| The World-Phoenix | Dimensional integrity | Formerly the Boundary; it sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix because it wanted to be more than its role, the Cosmic Throne resisted, and the Sundering freed it (the World-Phoenix's own account to Jason, Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795). Female in mortal form; prime vessel Helsveth (Book 11, Ch68 L2527-2530). Dawn is a hierophant. |
| The Reaper | The finality of death | Its followers' order of assassins used the Way of the Reaper martial art (Book 1, Ch50 L41); that the Reaper gave it to them is from the wiki and not confirmed. Shade is one of its shadows (Book 11, Ch68 L2209). Its vessel in Book 11 is the celestine Velius (Book 11, Ch64 L9; Ch22 L11). |
| The Keeper of Moments (of Sands) | Time | Prime vessel Raythe (Book 11, Ch64 L9); polices time travel; stood apart from and against the Sundering. |
| The All-Devouring Eye | Entropy, annihilation | Stands apart; the avatars of doom belong to it and were loaned to the Throne (Book 11, Ch34 L97, L103). A messenger says Jason "has grown in ways only the All-Devouring Eye anticipated" (Book 11, Ch22 L29); Gordon comes from its realm (Book 8, Ch55 L92-93).
| The Celestial Book | Understanding the nature of magic | Against the Sundering (Book 11, Ch65 L75); Clive venerates it (Book 1, Ch85 L51). |

| Whisper in Corners | (not detailed) | Came around to fight the sundering's consequences. |
| Legion | "Administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself"; its realm abuts the All-Devouring Eye's (Book 8, Ch55 L92) | Came around (Book 11, Ch65 L75). |
| Word in the Silence | (not detailed) | "Ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering", with the Keeper and the All-Devouring Eye (Book 11, Ch64 L49). |

Raythe tells Jason that only "the nameless" will stand with the World-Phoenix against him (Book 11, Ch65 L55). Velius explains that the nameless are "entities that govern the functions of the cosmos. Life, death, time, matter... the functionaries of all that is", "very happy with the removal of the Cosmic Throne's oversight" and "unbound from the strictures of their duties"; the original pacts did not include them (Book 11, Ch65 L57-59). In Book 12 Jason is told the nameless "are unhappy, as they would be with anything short of complete cosmic anarchy" (Book 12, Ch1 L26).

### 4. Sanctioning

Sanctioning is an extreme change to a transcendent being's nature through a shift of authority, usually punitive. Book 8 (Ch55 L25-31): Jason and Dawn reason that the original Builder was sanctioned, perhaps by "slapping a new person over the top", and Dawn says there are secrets about the Builder's ascension and his predecessor's sanctioning that even hierophants are not privy to (Book 8, Ch19 L40). Examples in the text: the Boundary sanctioned itself into the World-Phoenix (Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795); Shade sanctioned himself into a Shadow of the Hegemon (Book 11, Ch68 L2209-2214); Hero decided to sanction himself (Book 11, Ch68 L707-709); Purity was likely about to sanction himself when Knowledge interfered, and the wiki says he expended his authority on a single artefact (Book 13, Ch1017 L14-16; wiki). "You don't kill gods, you sanction them." Only a god can sanction a god. See `Authority_and_Sanctioning.md` for the full account.

### 5. The Builder (Level 1; notes to 3)

- **Obsession**: "obsessed with physical reality while, by its very nature, being unable to co-exist with it", it is building a world of its own in the deep astral from stolen astral spaces; because an astral being cannot interact with physical reality directly, it "recruits people to carve off the astral spaces connected to their world, then it steps in and claims them" (Book 2, Ch21 L106-112).
- **Methods**: cults; **star seeds**, the means by which great astral beings "send their followers" power instead of essences and stones, which turn a heretic's remnant power into a means of exploding themselves (Book 2, Ch21 L26-30) and which are "transcendent-rank objects" not purged by an essence ability or simple ritual (Book 2, Ch21 L36); cultists and captives "exploded into crystal stars" (Book 2, Ch59 L113); constructs such as golems and clockwork animals; Clockwork Kings, gold-rank native creatures of the Builder's world, dragon-like and not monsters, whose cores make the cult's clockwork cores (Book 2, Ch25 L37-45).
- **Cult**: its cultists in Greenstone summoned Jason by accident while trying to summon a Clockwork King.
- **History**: the original Builder crafted twin universe seeds, Earth and Pallimustus; was sanctioned and replaced.
- **Book 8 settlement**: the Fundamental Realm Authority Token enters Jason's inventory in Book 8, and his ability to access the fundamental realm is lost (Book 8, Ch49 L89-91); he looted it from the destroyed artefacts (Book 8, Ch50 L94-95), and Dawn tells him he will need to give it back (Book 8, Ch51 L68-70). The separate item the World-Phoenix crafted in Book 6 is for establishing the link (Book 6, Ch18 L124). The deal that ends the Builder's invasion is not checked.

### 6. The World-Phoenix (Level 2/3)

- **Role**: guardian of dimensional integrity; gave Jason the World-Phoenix Token and Nirvanic Transfiguration.
- **Identity**: formerly the Boundary; resisted by the Cosmic Throne when changing, and freed by the Sundering. She speaks of the Boundary in her own words in Book 11 (Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795).
- **Relationship to Jason**: sent Dawn; in the Rumble in the Jungle, the soul-space battleground where Jason's team stands against the nameless great astral beings (Book 11, Ch68 L171-175).
- **Prime vessel**: Helsveth (Book 11, Ch68 L2527-2530).

### 7. Hierophants

A hierophant is a former prime vessel who still serves a great astral being. Book 3 describes the World-Phoenix's cult: its head, the First Servant, was the great astral being's primary vessel, and former vessels end up as peak existences, even among their rank. Dawn is the World-Phoenix's hierophant; Soramir tells Jason (Book 7, Ch60 L27) that the Hierophant is allowed to intervene in the world a single time.

### 8. Dangers and hooks

GABs rarely appear in person. Their reach is felt through cults, vessels, relic wars and rules. Hooks: a cult of the Reaper, a Builder platform in the sky, a hierophant's request, a time-keeper's agent policing a link.

### 9. Open questions

- Exact stance of the Reaper in the Sundering (see the Cosmology Overview).
- Whether the "nameless functionary" GABs are described in the books or only the wiki.
- The origin of the pacts between GABs.

## The Council of Kings

### 1. Summary

The Council of Kings is the nearest thing the messengers have to central leadership: a loose body of the strongest astral kings, the heirs of the side that won the old war against free messengers. It guides but does not rule, many astral kings stand outside it, and its members are rivals who cooperate. Its de facto leader is Jamis Fran Muskar.

### 2. How it works

- **What it is**: "the closest thing the messengers had to central leadership", represented in Book 10 by a collection of prime avatars, each belonging to a different member (Book 10, Ch15 L3).
- **Membership**: it "ostensibly represents the strongest of the astral kings", with many others outside it, "even a few powerful eccentrics who have declined to be part of our little group" (Book 10, Ch15 L40). The council does not know how many astral kings stand outside it (Book 11, Ch24 L86).
- **Authority**: "The Council of Kings may guide us, but you do not rule us" (Book 12, Ch33 L55). Jamis says he is a member and that some consider him its leader, "although it has no such thing" (Book 12, Ch35 L11). Tera Jun Casta calls him "the closest thing we have to a true, singular leader" (Book 13, Ch999 L77).
- **Not absolute**: the council's power is not absolute, as what happened in Boko already shows, and controlling it is "a delicate affair" (Book 12, Ch35 L81).
- **Rivalry**: "Every person here is an enemy to everyone else in this room, yet we work together regardless" (Book 10, Ch15 L50).
- **Messenger structure**: astral kings rarely mix their forces, to protect the culture of hierarchy. Large operations are coordinated by meetings of Voices of the Will, the commanders of each king's local forces (Book 12, Ch26 L18).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Vesta Carmis Zell**: she sits in the Book 10 meeting, where Jamis tells her she is the only astral king in the room not focused on the larger goal and not some "personal project" (Book 10, Ch15 L30). In Book 9 she calls the council after Jason frees Tera (Book 9, Ch102 L69). By Book 13 she is "on the outside of the Council of Kings, particularly after her losses on Pallimustus" (Book 13, Ch999 L77).
- **Outside the council**: at a Book 12 meeting of Voices of the Will, the Voices belonging to council members are absent (Book 12, Ch26 L20). The council has instructed the forces not to provoke Jason (Book 12, Ch26 L29), and one Voice says none of their kings belong to the council (Book 12, Ch26 L30).
- **Hypocrisy**: Jamis says his people have a détente with the originals: "We avoid them, and those associated with them. They, in turn, do not interfere with us", and the arrangement keeps the messenger masses from seeing it (Book 13, Ch1000 L38). A few rebel astral kings fit within the council's ideological framework, so long as they do not highlight it (Book 13, Ch1000 L40).
- **Private agents**: Jamis has agents on Earth that the council cannot access (Book 13, Ch1000 L34-36).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **The Builder's planet-move**: prime avatars of council members watch the Builder's world engineers move a planet, and one of them wants to destroy Erigo Fin Desca as a traitor until Jamis stops him (Book 10, Ch15 L3, L16-19).
- **Jamis on Jason**: he tells Vesta he does not fear the rise of another original and will not annihilate every potential threat, since "our species would spend their entire lives roaming the cosmos, smiting silver- and bronze-rankers" (Book 10, Ch15 L43, L57).
- **Boko**: Jamis rebukes messenger commanders for defying "the explicit instructions of the Council of Kings" (Book 12, Ch33 L52, L65) and later meets Jason, saying he would offer him a seat on the council if he would take it (Book 12, Ch33 L71).
- **Jamis's offer**: empowered by the council, he offers the withdrawal of a significant number of occupying forces in return for Jason not campaigning against the messengers (Book 12, Ch35 L66). Jason points out that the territories are the ones now useless to their goals, and Jamis admits it (Book 12, Ch35 L68-70).
- **The squeeze on Earth**: the council saw no value in poking at the great astral beings and avoided Earth, which was central to the scandal that saw the original Builder sanctioned (Book 13, Ch954 L7).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **"The council commands all messengers."** It does not, as Book 12 shows when kings and Voices defy it (Book 12, Ch33 L52-55).
- **"The council is united."** Its members are rivals who work together and fall out, as Vesta does (Book 10, Ch15 L30, L50).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Book 9**: Vesta convenes the council over Jason (Book 9, Ch102 L69).
- **Book 10**: the council watches the Builder's task, with Jamis restraining Vesta (Book 10, Ch15 L3-62).
- **Book 12**: the council has told its forces not to provoke Jason (Book 12, Ch26 L29), is defied at Boko (Book 12, Ch33 L52), and Jamis meets Jason (Book 12, Ch35).
- **Book 13**: Jamis reappears with a request and a threat, and the council's ignorance of the Unorthodoxy colony on Earth is part of what Jason trades on (Book 13, Ch1000 L36, L74).

### 7. Using this in a story

Use the council as an alliance of rivals. Any messenger action has to be read against the council's instructions and its members' private agendas. Jamis is the best face for it: polite, curious, amused, and capable of threats delivered as courtesy. A story that needs a messenger threat can pit one king against another before it pits any of them against Jason.
