## The System

### 1. Summary

The System is the interface of windows, ranks and messages that Jason carried alone from Book 1. When he restored the Cosmic Throne, an echo of him was imprinted on it, and his interface became available to everyone in the cosmos with essences or the potential to get them. He administers it through the System Administrator gift, with limits, and in Book 12 withdraws it from regions that keep slavery or indenture.

### 2. How it works

- **Before**: in Books 1 to 10 the interface is one of Jason's outworlder gifts, a private window, inventory and quest log; see `../03_Magic_and_Adventuring/Unusual_and_Unique_Magic.md`.
- **The announcement**: on every world with magic, every person who has essences or the potential for them sees a screen saying "Don't Panic. Everything is going to be fine. Welcome to the System", in whatever medium the species uses to communicate (Book 11, Ch68 L2535-2540).
- **Why**: "The throne could never be restored to what it was. Part of you was imprinted upon it. An echo of you, spread across the cosmos", and "You made your interface available to everyone with essences or the potential to get them" (Book 12, Ch1 L34-36).
- **What it does by default**: it lets people view their own information and nothing more, but species gift evolutions and essence abilities are expanding the base effects, as they did for Jason (Book 12, Ch1 L38).
- **How it arrives**: the System waits for a moment of safety before revealing itself to an individual (Book 12, Ch1 L44). Most deaths come from reactions to the System, not the System itself: religious furore, superstition, and mass killings to keep the new power from teaching oppressed people (Book 12, Ch1 L46).
- **Where it runs**: it imprints itself on devices such as mirage chamber projectors, and people love the integration (Book 12, Ch20 L21-22).
- **Terms**: the prime avatar's sheet uses "nature" instead of "race", and Shade suggests the term now has to cover the breadth of individuals the System serves (Book 12, Ch8 L100-102).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **The System Administrator gift**: it gives access to all aspects of the system, with extras such as maps, voice and image chat, party and raid groups and assessing creatures and objects, which Jason can grant to others (Book 12, Ch67 L197). It represents his relation to the System, akin to a great astral being's, with most control sealed until he reaches full transcendence (Book 12, Ch10 L14).
- **Limited control**: Jason says he has limited ability to manipulate it, around his avatar and in his domains, and cannot "use it like it's my personal toy"; there are rules and they apply to him (Book 12, Ch42 L92). In Book 13 he still lacks full control of it and a lot is autonomic (Book 13, Ch1020 L9).
- **Jason's perception**: the prime avatar quiets his perception of those connected to the System, "a cosmos worth of muted mumbles" that is sealed away so it does not destroy his mind (Book 12, Ch8 L70-71).
- **Not everywhere**: it is withdrawn from regions that keep slavery or indentured servitude (see below).
- **Disbelief**: Anna Tilden suggests the System might be some cosmic force reaching Earth that Jason is leveraging early access to, and Jason answers with a System Administrator window: "I'm being as open as I can, Anna" (Book 12, Ch42 L99-101).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Quick recognition**: the System is "swiftly linked" to Jason by the organisations that had studied his abilities, and the Adventure Society sends Miles to find Clive (Book 12, Ch1 L54).
- **The withdrawal**: Jason sends letters to the powers holding Earth expatriates, saying the matter is not a negotiating position and that to have the power and do nothing is an abdication (Book 12, Ch50 L13-16). A System message says the Administrator will "shortly withdraw System access" in regions operating with slavery, indentured servitude or similar legal systems, with no System functions, alternate functionality for integrated abilities and diminished or failed rituals, for an indeterminate period (Book 12, Ch50 L28-29).
- **The reaction**: a mob gathers outside Jason's palace in Cyrion after the System goes dark (Book 12, Ch51 L3). The Queen of Estercost and others ask Vandrick to arbitrate "your withdrawal of the System" (Book 12, Ch51 L13).
- **The diamond-ranks' position**: Vandrick tells them that the diamond-rank community holds that the System "is yours to administer" (Book 12, Ch51 L59). Every new diamond-ranker gets one big world-changing action, and Jason's is using the System to push the abolition of slavery (Book 12, Ch51 L76-77). He is told to handle mortal affairs like a mortal and immortal affairs like an immortal (Book 12, Ch51 L82-84).
- **The cost**: a Cyrion house adventurer says Jason's ideals about slavery "mattered to no one until you took away the System" (Book 12, Ch52 L24), and warns him that he has made many enemies by taking it away (Book 12, Ch52 L30). A speaker for a trading house notes that the loss of the System was already an issue, though they can live without it (Book 12, Ch53 L34).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **"The System is a natural cosmic phenomenon."** Anna's fear that it is "some cosmic force" is answered by Jason's window (Book 12, Ch42 L99-101).
- **"Jason can pick who gets it."** The withdrawal covers whole regions at once, and access is reviewed region by region on his return (Book 12, Ch50 L29).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Book 11**: the System appears across the cosmos when the throne is restored (Book 11, Ch68 L2535-2540).
- **Book 12**: it is linked to Jason within days (Book 12, Ch1 L54) and withdrawn from regions with slavery (Book 12, Ch50 L28).
- **Book 13**: a System alert reads "[System Administrator] has identified a dimensional infraction and initiated an intervention action. The Hegemon has arisen. Beware his wrath," and everyone old enough for essences sees it (Book 13, Ch1014 L28-30; Book 13, Ch1020 L6-7). Jason says the system is part of him "like a spleen" (Book 13, Ch1020 L11), and four teams are linked by his interface in a raid (Book 13, Ch958 L51). Knowledge refers to him as "The System" in his coming role as a great astral being (Book 13, Ch1024 L141).

### 7. Using this in a story

Treat the System as part of Jason that everyone can use. Anything that appears in a window can be traced to his will or his autonomic reflexes, and he does not control it all. It is both a gift and a point of leverage: a power that can be withdrawn is a power that people fight over, and a character who sees it as impersonal is wrong.

---

## The Unorthodoxy

### 1. Summary

The Unorthodoxy is the messenger resistance: the descendants of the free messengers who lost the old war, who live in hiding without the brand and the indoctrination. They are few, scattered and short of allies, but they have astral kings of their own and hidden birthing planets, and a secret way of drawing extra power at their rank. Boris Ket Lundi is their agent on Earth and Pallimustus.

### 2. How it works

- **Origin**: Boris says that originally astral kings guided newborn messengers to form their own marks, and there was no rank limit because limits are a function of the brand. When messengers who had transcended became astral kings they instituted the brand and enslaved their own kind. There was war, the free lost, and the defeated went into hiding. "In time, the leaders of the enemy became the Council of Kings. We became the Unorthodoxy" (Book 11, Ch25 L49-51).
- **The orthodox view**: messenger society teaches that the Unorthodoxy is a scant few in the hidden crevices of society. Boris says most of that is inaccurate (Book 11, Ch25 L47). Orthodox messengers hunt them diligently (Book 11, Ch42 L28), and an orthodox commander worries that talk of a traitor astral king is the thinking that leads to the Unorthodoxy and a purge (Book 12, Ch26 L27).
- **Numbers and hiding**: "the Unorthodoxy is scattered and lacking in allies. We hide because we lack the strength to fight, and nothing ever changes" (Book 10, Ch79 L100). They use different methods in each place so that losing one site does not expose them all (Book 11, Ch42 L28).
- **Birthing planets**: messengers are still allowed to find their own marks only on Unorthodoxy birthing planets (Book 11, Ch42 L24-26). Earth does not have enough magic for the birthing trees (Book 11, Ch42 L29-30).
- **Astral kings of their own**: Boris says the Unorthodoxy has astral kings, "slipping back into the general population" among too many to track (Book 11, Ch25 L56-57). One is the king of Navise Den Rigal, a Voice of the Will (Book 12, Ch26 L19).
- **The secret**: Unorthodoxy messengers have learned to tap their own potential, stalling at a rank in return for "overcharged mana" to enhance abilities. It is hidden from rank-and-file messengers and is "one of our key weapons" (Book 11, Ch40 L111-113).

### 3. Members and associates

- **Boris Ket Lundi**: a gold-rank agent kept below diamond so he can move without attention. He had a brand placed by one of their astral kings to deceive Vesta Carmis Zell (Book 11, Ch25 L53-55), says he was never put through messenger indoctrination (Book 10, Ch79 L102), and claims the Unorthodoxy founded the Cabal (Book 10, Ch79 L98). He spent millennia scouting hidden colonies (Book 13, Ch954 L6).
- **Marek Nior Vargas**: he hopes that Jason's freeing of messengers will turn "dead wood" into "raging inferno" (Book 9, Ch103 L114) and talks of suborning astral kings (Book 9, Ch103 L121). Jason supports the Unorthodoxy in principle but says Marek would turn his people into child soldiers (Book 11, Ch2 L38) and worries about "victory or death energy" (Book 11, Ch2 L75). Marek's people subordinate themselves to Boris (Book 11, Ch49 L71).
- **Erigo Fin Desca**: formerly Unorthodoxy, he says he has moved on and that there is little point fighting an oppressor that can turn you into a mindless drone (Book 10, Ch15 L14-15).
- **Navise Den Rigal**: a Voice of the Will whose king is secretly Unorthodoxy, and who slips Boris into Vesta Carmis Zell's service (Book 12, Ch26 L19).
- **Tera Jun Casta**: freed by Jason, she lives with Boris and his Unorthodoxy messengers despite her views on them (Book 11, Ch68 L2480), and is angered by messengers who want to join (Book 11, Ch40 L58).
- **Freed messengers**: the messengers in the Cardinas zone are not ready for the Unorthodoxy, since Jason's aura contradicts what they were taught (Book 11, Ch42 L8-9), and Boris's own silver-rankers are the difficulty (Book 11, Ch42 L11).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Boris reveals himself**: he tells Jason's team he is with the Unorthodoxy, that the Cabal was founded by his people, and that his astral king saw what Vesta's plans would do to Pallimustus' membrane and sent him (Book 10, Ch79 L82, L98).
- **The Earth colony**: Boris scouted Earth as a site for hidden colonies, and the Council of Kings left the world alone because it was central to the scandal that got the original Builder sanctioned (Book 13, Ch954 L6-7). Jamis says he has agents there that the council cannot reach (Book 13, Ch1000 L36), and threatens to reveal the colony unless Jason trades (Book 13, Ch1000 L65-74).
- **Boris and the founder's familiar**: Boris worked with the Network founder's familiar to betray the founder (Book 13, Ch954 L9).
- **Refugees**: Jason arranges for freed messengers to be sheltered, as there are large and extremely secret Unorthodoxy enclaves on Earth (Book 11, Ch67 L18).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **"The Unorthodoxy is a handful of malcontents."** Boris says it is far larger than taught, and Jali says if messengers learned how many there are, society would fracture (Book 11, Ch25 L47; Book 11, Ch44 L14).
- **"The Unorthodoxy is a rebellion."** Marek says it is far from one, since "you cannot rebel against those without whom you will die" (Book 9, Ch103 L117).
- **"The Unorthodoxy cares about Pallimustus."** Jason says the Unorthodoxy doesn't care about this world, and Boris replies, "No, we care about you" (Book 10, Ch79 L99-100).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Book 9**: Marek sees Jason's work as a way to show his people they can live without astral kings (Book 9, Ch103 L114-121).
- **Book 10**: Boris approaches Jason (Book 10, Ch79 L82-100) and Erigo, the Builder's new vessel, admits he was once part of it and has moved on (Book 10, Ch15 L14-15).
- **Book 11**: Boris explains the Unorthodoxy's history and astral kings (Book 11, Ch25 L47-57).
- **Book 12**: a Voice who serves a secret Unorthodoxy king hides her allegiance (Book 12, Ch26 L19).
- **Book 13**: the Earth colony becomes a bargaining chip with the Council of Kings (Book 13, Ch1000 L65-76).

### 7. Using this in a story

The Unorthodoxy is a movement that survives by being invisible. A story that needs messenger allies can use it, but each ally has a cost: secrecy, a brand to remove or a past they do not trust. The tension between a freed messenger who is ready and one who is not is more interesting than an alliance, and Boris is the best voice for the mix of cheerful bluster and cold calculation the books give him.

---

## Death

### 1. Summary

The god of Death on Pallimustus governs the passage of souls into the astral, and is distinct from the Reaper, the great astral being who is "very big on the finality of death". The church certifies deaths and returns, opposes Undeath, and is dryly protective of the order of things. The deity changes guise, and the books speak of both a goddess and a lord.

### 2. Facts

- **Domain**: the Reaper is "very big on the finality of death. Some consider it the true god of death, as all our god of death governs is the passage of the soul into the astral" (Book 2, Ch25 L67). Where there is no god of death to guide the soul into the astral, it drifts into the Reaper's grasp on its own (Book 3, Ch69 L189).

### Books 4 to 9

- **The god and the Reaper work in balance**: the Goddess of Death and the Reaper "each have their areas of authority and they work with an ebb and flow" (Book 7, Ch60 L100). The Reaper's cult may not trespass on the local god's domain (Book 4, Ch3 L30).
- **Precautions against dying**: Death keeps a close eye on resurrections. A priest tells Jason that the goddess knew "each time you had fallen and each time you had returned" the moment he entered her sphere, and has asked that he be more careful (Book 7, Ch9 L123, L125).
- **Certification**: the Church of Death confirms that returned adventurers are who they claim, and its paperwork helps with registration (Book 7, Ch7 L64; Book 7, Ch11 L83; Book 7, Ch17 L105).
- **Alignment with a cult**: the Church of Death is "closely aligned" with a cult that works with it, doing public-facing things while the cult is the hidden hand (Book 9, Ch27 L87).

### 3. Later developments (spoilers)

- **Three guises**: in Book 10 Death appears to Jason as "a stocky, middle-aged woman with a colourful dress" with the warmth of a matronly tavern keeper, instead of the stern-faced man who normally appears in that region (Book 10, Ch82 L62, L65). To Miriam Vance he appears as a pale male elf in grey Yaresh clothing with a voice "cold and hollow as an empty tomb" (Book 10, Ch85 L12). In Book 12 she is a woman with plain features, pale skin and a grey dress with a faded blue flower pattern (Book 12, Ch8 L4).
- **The miracle**: Jason says prayer isn't his thing, and Death calls his prayer "very mediocre". She says a miracle needs one of her servants or a grand sacrifice, and she has no interest in the sacrifice of lives (Book 10, Ch82 L61-72). She declines his two resurrections as "not enough" (Book 10, Ch82 L77-78). The miracle that follows burns the undead to ash with ghost fire (Book 10, Ch85 L5).
- **The pact**: Jason makes a pact with the Pallimustus goddess of death, enacted by her guiding his soul to change itself, with no access to it (Book 10, Ch83 L64, L69). He gains power to diminish undeath energy, which makes his aura anathema to the priests of Undeath (Book 11, Ch28 L16). Death's ghost fire is the model for the weapon he forges (Book 11, Ch35 L45-46).
- **A talk with Miriam**: Death tells Miriam to stand, "You still command this battle" (Book 10, Ch85 L15), and explains how Disguise moved slowly to take over Purity (Book 10, Ch85 L33).
- **Giving back**: in Book 12 Death returns the resurrection power Jason had traded, saying holding it back would be "petty... unbecoming at our level" and thanking him for stymieing Undeath (Book 12, Ch8 L8-13). She says the gods will pass with their planet, "yet you will remain" (Book 12, Ch8 L15).
- **Limits**: Death's remit "does not reach beyond this planet, which itself will have its time" (Book 10, Ch82 L76).

### 4. Using this in a story

Death is patient, fair and unimpressed. She is tired of people who will not stay dead and relieved when someone else deals with Undeath. A scene with her should feel like a meeting with a good-natured official whose job is also the end of everything. Her church is a bureaucracy of certificates, funerals and quiet help against the undead.

---

## Destruction

### 1. Summary

Destruction is a god of the hidden kind, worshipped by those who want to destroy rather than rule. His church is small, secretive and well hidden, and its allies include the Church of Undeath. In Book 10 he takes an interest in the natural array under Yaresh, whose catastrophe or whose tree-turned-apocalypse-beast would serve him, and he speaks to Amos Pensinata through a prisoner priest.

### 2. Facts

- **The hidden kind**: Carlos explains that many gods fall into two camps: those with temples anywhere there are people, and "the gods whose priests dwell in the hidden places. Gods who you pray to not because of something you want, but something you want to avoid. Pain, Discord, Deceit" (Book 8, Ch48 L51). Destruction is not on his list, but the Book 10 priests work in the tunnels and the temples are hidden (Book 10, Ch66 L101); the wiki also counts Destruction among the hidden gods (wiki).
- **The priests under Yaresh**: captured priests are found with a messenger communication orb in the tunnels of the natural array (Book 10, Ch66 L84-86).
- **The voice of the god**: when Amos Pensinata presses a captured priest, "a new aura shrouded the prisoners, unmistakable in its divinity", and Destruction's voice rumbles "like an avalanche": "The souls of my priests are mine to toy with, not yours" (Book 10, Ch66 L90-93). Jason, as a nascent astral king, is unaffected by the god's will (Book 10, Ch66 L94-97).
- **His reply to a threat**: "You threaten the god of destruction with destruction? There is nothing you can do to me... Destroying my temples only fulfils their ultimate purpose... There are always those hungry for power to replace them... Those who hunger for power, not to dominate but to destroy" (Book 10, Ch66 L103). The priests explode (Book 10, Ch66 L104).
- **His aim**: Miriam says the god has taken an interest (Book 10, Ch73 L54). Jason suspects his goal is not the array blowing up but the tree: "he wants it to become some kind of apocalypse beast that devours every living thing on this planet" (Book 10, Ch73 L55). Emir adds that Destruction "wasn't too fazed by us taking out his priests" (Book 10, Ch78 L22).
- **Allies**: "The Church of Undeath is one of the few reliable allies the Church of Destruction has" (Book 10, Ch78 L27). Undeath's priest Jeff has a grandmother who is a high priestess of Destruction (Book 10, Ch88 L85).
- **The limits of the god**: Jason argues that if Destruction had the power to wipe them all out, he would have done so instead of talking (Book 10, Ch75 L25). Death will not say what Destruction had planned, since it is another god's affair (Book 10, Ch67 L34).
- **Outcome**: the god of Destruction was hoping for a seeping wound in reality from the transformation zone (Book 11, Ch41 L97). Jason tells the Undeath priests to step back and take stock "who won and who lost" (Book 11, Ch62 L18).

### 3. Using this in a story

Destruction is the god who does not need to win a fight: he needs his people to be hungry, and there will always be hungry people. His church is not a conquering army but a cult of saboteurs and fanatics, and a story that confronts it should expect to lose temples and win nothing permanent. He is best at pushing a larger catastrophe, as at Yaresh, rather than acting in person.

---

## Dominion

### 1. Summary

Dominion is the god of rulership, the god "of deciding who gets to be king". He is young, handsome, sneering, charming and frank, he is the god most interested in Jason, and he turns up in person more often than any other. His church is the outlier among churches in keeping low-ranking essence users under its thumb. For all his menace he gives Jason surprisingly honest advice.

### 2. Facts

- **The temple and the creed**: a believer in the Divine Square calls it the temple of Dominion and says "Dominion issues the divine right to kings and nobles. It is he who determines who rules, and who serves" (Book 1, Ch45 L15-18).
- **First appearance**: at Jory's clinic he comes to take the Healer's cast-out clergy, "young and handsome, but with a look of disdain and faint cruelty", with an aura like a wave of fire (Book 1, Ch95 L87). He tells those who join: "There is no service in my church... under me, you will obey or suffer. Or both, as I choose, because you will not enter my service. You will belong to me" (Book 1, Ch95 L94).
- **Jason and Gary**: "I love that guy," Dominion says of Jason, because "the ones who won't kneel are always the most fun" (Book 1, Ch95 L101). He tests Gary with his gaze, laughs when Gary stands, and says "That is where monarchs come from. I love them most of all. I'll be keeping an eye on you, Gareth Xandier" (Book 1, Ch95 L103-104). He asked after Jason by name (Book 1, Ch97 L7).
- **Thanks in person**: at the priest camp he comes with other gods in purple and gold robes with a simple golden crown, and tells Jason "You never disappoint" (Book 2, Ch65 L75-76). Jason calls him a "work acquaintance", someone he would not take for after-work drinks (Book 2, Ch66 L104-106).
- **His church**: the church of Dominion is the most prominent outlier among churches in keeping low-ranking essence users under its thumb (Book 3, Ch69 L859).

### 3. Later developments, Books 8 to 9

- **Oppression-friendly**: on Jason's lawn, Jason asks if he has somewhere to oppress, and he replies "I don't oppress. I'm just oppression-friendly" (Book 8, Ch56 L47-48). He compliments Jason's pagoda: "You're coming along nicely, Mr Asano" (Book 8, Ch56 L53-54).
- **Interest in Jason**: a priest says he can see why Dominion is so interested in him (Book 8, Ch43 L60), and Jason is warned that Dominion may have an agenda for him (Book 8, Ch59 L36).
- **Absent priests**: a character complains that she has never met a priest of Dominion, despite thinking power and control were the Church of Dominion's remit (Book 9, Ch49 L28-29).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **The sin essence**: Jason's sin essence brought out the authoritarian tendencies that got Dominion's attention (Book 10, Ch66 L43). The goddess Liberty "likes to keep a wary eye on Dominion's favourites" (Book 10, Ch31 L61).
- **A voice in the meeting**: Dominion interrupts a call with the Yaresh authorities, and Jason calls his offer "half-arsed power-plays" (Book 10, Ch16 L76-87). A speaker notes that "the god of dominion—the god of deciding who gets to be king—showed up for a chat, and not for the first time" (Book 10, Ch18 L129).
- **Jason's view**: "Dominion is still kind of a dick, though" (Book 10, Ch83 L55), and the power becomes who he is, "not good for anyone. Except the god of dominion, maybe" (Book 11, Ch2 L81).
- **Advice**: after Jason handles a fanatic poorly, Dominion appears by the arm-shaped temple, saying "It's religion. Showmanship is part of the deal" (Book 12, Ch13 L47). When Jason asks for guidance, he suggests giant banners with his face (Book 12, Ch13 L56). He tells Jason "There is no divine right of kings. Mortals choose and I try to help them not make a complete mess of things" (Book 12, Ch13 L67). A gift from Dominion helps Jason contain his presence (Book 12, Ch17 L27).
- **Not what people think**: a character says Jason told her Dominion isn't what most people think, and that Dominion said Jason should let people find their own solutions to indenture (Book 12, Ch49 L82-84).
- **His priests**: Brian, a priest of Dominion, serves as Jason's ally in the Cyrion crisis, saying that his church does not venerate power but "the establishment of power over others. Rulership. The exercising of authority", and that slavery, a subordinate god's domain, is "a petty tyranny" (Book 12, Ch52 L50, L72).

### 5. Using this in a story

Dominion should be fun and dangerous in equal parts. He is charming, speaks his mind, never lies about what he wants, and enjoys defiance more than obedience. A scene with him should leave the character a little more informed and a little more worried. His church is the grim counterpart to his personality: strict, hierarchical and unforgiving.

---

## Fertility

### 1. Summary

Fertility is the god of growth and birth, and his church is far more practical than its murals suggest. It grows children in vats, bridges races so that mixed couples can have children, supplies food in surges, and in Book 12 is the thing the brighthearts most need to rebuild their people. Its temples are covered in murals of people being fertile, which Jason notes with some alarm.

### 2. Facts

- **The murals**: Jason avoids pairing with "the god of fertility? The one with all the provocative murals?" (Book 1, Ch82 L73), and Farrah describes the temples as covered "in murals of people... being fertile" (Book 10, Ch8 L41).

### 3. Later developments, Books 6 to 9

- **Priestesses**: a priestess of Fertility is among those Humphrey's team meets (Book 6, Ch47 L910).
- **Food in a surge**: the Temple of Fertility keeps secure stations in outlying areas with infrastructure to grow large amounts of food quickly in a small space, critical to stopping fortress towns starving during a surge (Book 7, Ch21 L3-5). Jason leaves its main doors with his storage space loaded with supplies (Book 7, Ch21 L3).
- **Children without a partner**: the church can let people have a child without ever touching one another, growing the child in a jar, which is how most aristocrats do it (Book 7, Ch39 L74). A speaker says there are Gellers everywhere and that one would have to ask the Church of Fertility about that (Book 7, Ch45 L106).
- **Mixed-race births**: one person says the church allowed an elf and a human to have children and purged his father's "impurity" to produce him (Book 8, Ch17 L12), and describes another birth made possible with the church's help (Book 8, Ch20 L18).
- **Records**: a church record-keeper finds how the church helped Melody Jain have a child, which her order's overseers never knew (Book 9, Ch27 L26).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 12 (spoilers)

- **A messenger of the god**: a priestess in the full robes of the Church of Fertility, with young acolytes, arrives at Jason's door saying "My god told me that Jason Asano was in here" (Book 10, Ch1 L88-89).
- **Feeding Yaresh**: after the messenger attack the Fertility church supplies all the food for the refugees and its priestess runs Jason's relief building, which he turns into a multi-storey food court (Book 10, Ch8 L37).
- **In vats**: a character was "cracked out of the vat" by the church before he learned to walk (Book 11, Ch52 L54), and a speaker says he might have to recruit a priest of Fertility and one of Knowledge for a complicated plan (Book 11, Ch46 L29). He is advised to prioritise meeting the church of Fertility (Book 11, Ch63 L14).
- **Velius's cover**: Velius, a prime vessel of the Reaper, works on Earth as a fertility doctor, in a role normally filled by the church of Fertility, knowing all its magic that does not need divine influence (Book 11, Ch68 L776-778).
- **The brighthearts**: the church supplies the thing the brighthearts need most, children. In only a few years the streets are teeming with them (Book 12, Ch6 L27). The brighthearts' leader says excluding the Church of Fertility from the main city is especially contentious, since "we were brought to the brink of extinction, and they are vital to rebuilding our population", and Jason offers to withdraw his dominion over parts of the city so the temples can be built (Book 12, Ch7 L46-48).

### 5. Using this in a story

Fertility is the unromantic god of life: logistics, food and births, with a surface of ancient frankness. His church solves problems that other churches cannot, so it is rich in leverage. Use its people to supply, to rebuild and to quietly keep records, and keep its murals as a running joke that the characters take less seriously than visitors do.

---

## Hearth

### 1. Summary

Hearth is a god of home and shelter. The books show only its church at work: its priests organise people who have lost their homes, alongside the church of Refuge. This file records what the text says.

### 2. Facts

- **The Healer's Hearth ritual**: Neil asks whether a procedure is "the Healer's Hearth ritual" (Book 9, Ch67 L33), suggesting a ritual named for Hearth is used by the Church of the Healer.
- **Organising refugees**: after Boko's destruction, Jason says "The priests of Hearth and of Refuge will be organising the people. Who wants to settle permanently, who wants to find a new home, and who wants to wait for the reconstruction of Boko" (Book 12, Ch39 L103).
- **In Jason's kingdom**: the clergy in his astral kingdom stay for his journey to Earth. The first contingent came from the churches of Hearth, Refuge and Dominion, and others joined as the work expanded, mostly for the logistics of a population in the tens of thousands (Book 13, Ch951 L33).

### 3. Not in the text

No scene shows the god, a temple, a named priest or its relationship with other gods. The wiki lists Hearth and Refuge as gods first mentioned at the Boko refugee scene (wiki).

### 4. Using this in a story

Hearth is the church for displaced people: a temple that finds rooms, food and a place to belong. Use it for refugee stories, new settlements and logistics, and give it a calm, practical priesthood.

---

## Hero

### 1. Summary

Hero is the god of heroes, the only core deity without subordinate gods. He appears in the books almost only through the Cup of Heroes, a miracle that makes a dying hero a demigod at a terrible price. Hero is regretful about it, and by Book 11 plans to sanction himself to give mortals a gentler option.

### 2. Facts

- **Name and rank**: Jason notes "the god of heroes is called Hero. They really stick to that straightforwards naming convention" (Book 1, Ch45 L39). Hero is "the only core deity not to have subordinate gods" (Book 1, Ch48 L92).
- **Appearance**: a leonid larger than Gary's demigod form, with a divine aura (Book 11, Ch68 L310).

- **The Cup of Heroes**: when Gary goes out to die against the undead, Hero appears and tells him his choice, not his life, was the sacrifice: "You believed that you came here to die. People keep thinking that what the gods want in sacrifice is their lives, but that is not the case" (Book 10, Ch86 L45). He conjures a goblet, a dewdrop falls into it, and Gary snatches it, saying "I know what it is" (Book 10, Ch86 L47-50). Hero calls his choice the reason both are there (Book 10, Ch86 L53).
- **What it does**: Gary drinks, and the window says he has absorbed divine power belonging to the god of heroes, which will leave his soul unless he is isolated from the god's influence, and reforges his body into a gestalt (Book 10, Ch86 L59-63). His hammer, fire and iron essences become Divine versions at Gold 0 and his forge confluence is replaced by a Demigod essence (Book 10, Ch86 L67-72).
- **The aftermath**: Hero acts "like a proud but sad father" (Book 10, Ch86 L52). Jason, learning of it, speaks in a flat voice, and Farrah warns him not to do anything crazy (Book 10, Ch89 L26-40).
- **A gift to Jason**: afterwards Hero tells Jason he can only push the limits of his influence a little, enough to give him a gift as the Healer did: a Genesis Command: Source, a transcendent orb with "the authority to link power" (Book 10, Ch89 L77-83). Hero says "It is the best I can do" and is gone (Book 10, Ch89 L83).
- **On Purity**: Hero guesses Purity turned himself into an artefact because the continental war made Purity seem a dark god, and says that is why he himself is wary of changing his own nature (Book 10, Ch89 L70-75).
- **How he sees himself**: "I am the god of heroes. I, of all, understand that actions, not power, are what makes one worthy of respect. And all I do is kill heroes" (Book 11, Ch68 L326, L334).
- **His planned self-sanction**: Gwydion Remore tells Gary Hero has decided to sanction himself, as he has considered for longer than any of them has been alive. It will not be as drastic as Purity's. He wants to add "another miracle option. Something less powerful than the Cup of Heroes, with less of a price", by making the relics of heroes who drank the cup usable again, "if only for a short time", so that "the stories of heroes past live on in heroes of the future" (Book 11, Ch68 L707-709). Gary is one of the reasons (Book 11, Ch68 L711).
- **Hero's church**: Gwydion Remore is a priest of Hero (Book 11, Ch60 L24). The church has collected the relics of dead demigods for millennia (Book 11, Ch68 L709).

### 3. Using this in a story

Hero is a god of tragedy: the god who is asked to choose between dying and becoming something that dies slowly. His church is respectful, and its priests tend to carry guilt. A story that wants a god's help in a desperate hour can use him, but only for a heroic sacrifice, and he will say plainly that it will cost the hero. His self-sanction is a hook for a changed Hero, a new miracle and a church that has to adapt.

---

## Knowledge

### 1. Summary

The goddess of Knowledge is the god Jason meets first and speaks to most. She is detached, polite, honest in form and a planner at heart, and she knows everything anyone in her world knows. Her church is scholarly and wealthy and funds research, and from Book 6 on it is shown mustering armies. By Book 13 the books reveal she has worked for centuries to invade Earth.

### 2. Facts

- **Appearance**: in the Divine Square a glorious light appears in front of a temple and the people fall to their knees (Book 1, Ch45 L31). In her temple she takes the form of a woman with colourful clothes and Mediterranean features, "beautiful, yet there was something detached and untouchable about her" (Book 1, Ch46 L16). She says "I am Knowledge. Everything that is, or ever was known in this world" (Book 1, Ch46 L22).
- **Omniscience, limited**: she knows what anyone in her world knows, including what Jason brought with him (Book 1, Ch46 L22). Jason says in a recording that deities are gender fluid, "heard from the goddess of knowledge herself" (Book 1, Ch77 L8), and jokes that she knows his Mario Kart shortcuts (Book 3, Ch57 L87).
- **The church**: acolytes of the church check Adventure Society assessments, "don't try to slip anything past them, because there isn't any point" (Book 1, Ch38 L68). Gabrielle Pellin introduces herself as an acolyte (Book 1, Ch101 L72). Danielle Geller will send her scholarly relatives to the temple's library, as "the goddess always welcomes seekers of truth" (Book 2, Ch21 L129).
- **Gifts to Jason**: a token the goddess claimed would send him home (Book 2, Ch63 L48) and books on dimensional transgression, which Clive annotates (Book 3, Ch3 L14).

### 3. Later developments, Books 4 to 9

- **Answers**: Knowledge gives answers people need rather than those they want. In the Vitesse temple she tells Sophie, "Now is not the time to pursue this goal" (Book 6, Ch47 L614-616).
- **Temples**: the Rimaros temple is an important resource for magical researchers and has a symbiotic relationship with the Magic Society (Book 7, Ch9 L4).
- **Jason's survival**: Jason hopes it will not be a big deal that people knew he was alive because "Knowledge told people I was alive" (Book 7, Ch4 L58).
- **Armies**: Knowledge's church has been mustering forces around the world (Book 9, Ch42 L69), with a small holy army near Yaresh (Book 9, Ch36 L21; Book 9, Ch42 L80) that waits to strike the Yaresh force from behind (Book 9, Ch104 L76).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **Teasing**: she appears to Jason as a bookish woman in brown robes beside an expedition crawler, and he is still piqued that she did not tell his friends he was alive. She answers, "I'm the goddess of knowledge, Jason, not of very confident guesses" (Book 10, Ch67 L19-23).
- **Funding**: the Church of Knowledge is one of the churches that funds the Magic Research Association (Book 12, Ch1 L58). Armies of nations and other gods lacked her forewarning (Book 12, Ch24 L3).
- **The plan**: in Jason's briefing Knowledge helped Disguise pose as Purity, and in return he brought the Network founder into his church. She promised the messengers' leader a chance to invade Pallimustus and claim Purity's relic, and spent centuries preparing Earth for invasion (Book 13, Ch1017 L15-29). Jason says he was "exactly what she needed" and that she tried to recruit him (Book 13, Ch1017 L32, L38).
- **Annexation**: the Church of Knowledge annexes the island that anchors the bridge on the Pallimustus side, seizing Storm Kingdom territory (Book 13, Ch1020 L95; Book 13, Ch1022 L25).
- **Gabrielle**: a priestess of Knowledge protests that she is not of Deception or Conquest (Book 13, Ch1023 L131), and a cube leaves her chest into the goddess's hand (Book 13, Ch1023 L139).
- **Confrontation**: Knowledge tells Jason the time has come "to fulfil your destiny... and open the gateway that I might claim your world" (Book 13, Ch1024 L133). She says he cannot sanction her, since that is for other gods (Book 13, Ch1024 L141), and he answers that he will kill her (Book 13, Ch1024 L146, L153).

### 5. Using this in a story

Knowledge is helpful in the way a very good librarian is helpful: she answers the question that was asked, and also the question behind it, and she never lies. Her motives are the issue. A scene with her should feel civil and slightly chilling, because she has seen how the scene will go. Her church is wealthy, careful and influential, and a priest of Knowledge is both a source of information and a possible agent.

---

## Pain and Discord

### 1. Summary

Pain and Discord belong to the "hidden" gods, the gods people pray to for what they want to avoid. The books mention them only in passing. This file records every thing the text says, so that a story using them knows how much is open.

### 2. Facts

- **The hidden gods**: Carlos says many gods fall into two camps: those whose temples are anywhere there are people, and "the gods whose priests dwell in the hidden places. Gods who you pray to not because of something you want, but something you want to avoid. Pain, Discord, Deceit" (Book 8, Ch48 L51). These are the "dark gods" who "will do very well" if the Purity deception becomes public, and Carlos does not like "the idea of my actions serving the God of Discord" (Book 8, Ch48 L47).
- **Pain, a god or a goddess**: a soldier thinks of Pain as a god, but Kerr answers, "Where I come from, they know that Pain is a woman", and refers to "the Goddess of Pain's firstborn daughter" (Book 7, Ch25 L113-115). Gods are gender-fluid in the books (Book 1, Ch77 L8).
- **A byword for fear**: Trenchant says that against an affliction skirmisher he would "run like the God of Pain was chasing me" (Book 7, Ch44 L23).
- **Discord**: it is called out as "in particular" the god the deception benefits (Book 8, Ch48 L53).

### 3. Not in the text

The text gives no scene with either god, no named priest, no temple and no description of their clergy or appearance. The wiki's list names them as evil or hidden gods (wiki).

### 4. Using this in a story

Both gods work best as names that characters fear to say. If a story needs a church of Pain or Discord, it should be hidden, small and rarely seen, matching Destruction and Undeath, with priests who live where the text puts them: out of sight.

---

## Purity and Disguise

### 1. Summary

Purity is the god of cleanliness, with both gentle and extreme aspects; his church is rich, strict and prominent in Greenstone. For centuries the god in the Church of Purity was not Purity but Disguise, who masqueraded in his place with Knowledge's help. The church's collusion with the cult of the Builder, Disguise's role in the Order of Redeeming Light, and the real Purity's relic are the revelations behind the Book 3, 8 and 10 plots.

### 2. Facts

- **The church**: Anisa Lasalle is a priestess of the God of Purity (Book 1, Ch20 L80), and a priest of Purity in clean robes attends the Adventure Society inquiry team (Book 2, Ch17 L31). The temple has church militants who guard its interests (Book 2, Ch37 L105).
- **Collusion with the Builder cult**: when the church's involvement with the cult comes to light, a number of its key members vanish on "previously scheduled sabbaticals", including the archbishop Nicolas Hedron (Book 3, Ch1 L106). The people from the church are detained under the authority of the ecumenical council (Book 3, Ch5 L67).
- **Hendren**: the archbishop calls out, "You think afflictions can take down a priest of Purity?" in the fight (Book 3, Ch59 L45).

### 3. Later developments, Books 4 to 9

- **A bargain with the Builder**: Dawn says "the god Purity has struck a bargain with the Builder": Purity lays the groundwork and the Builder helps him cleanse the world of what he has come to see as unclean, taking the abundant astral spaces and leaving Purity to rebuild civilisation in his image (Book 4, Ch68 L139). Clergy of the Order say their "so-called God of Purity handed our world to a being that would taint our very souls" (Book 7, Ch16 L53).
- **Purification ability**: converts of the Builder cult have a purifying ability that comes ultimately from the god, passed along a chain from the god to a purified clockwork king, a purified core, and the converted (Book 8, Ch10 L24).
- **Carlos's theory**: the priest of the Healer argues that Purity has been replaced by one of the deception gods, most likely Deceit or Disguise (Book 8, Ch48 L14). Disguise is "the lord of illusion, manipulating assumptions and walking unnoticed in plain sight", and "if the god of disguises chooses to take on a disguise, even Knowledge or Truth cannot reveal it" (Book 8, Ch48 L16, L22). The gods have rules governing how they relate (Book 8, Ch48 L22-26).
- **The ecumenical council**: it was convened by the churches to judge the church's behaviour, and found it had been operating well outside its dictates for some time (Book 8, Ch48 L32).
- **Unanswered**: Emir says people everywhere are trying to learn exactly when and why the original Purity was sanctioned. The churches either haven't been told or aren't saying, and the diamond-rank community has been digging into it (Book 9, Ch51 L15-17).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **The Order of Redeeming Light**: Carlos and Arabelle conclude that the Flames of Redemption are an extreme modification of lesser vampirism, and that part of it comes from Disguise, "the god who was pretending to be Purity", with the order founded within the church only after Disguise took on Purity's mantle (Book 10, Ch39 L45-46). The Flames instil an absolute faith in Purity as a safety mechanism against deprogramming (Book 10, Ch39 L55-56).
- **Death on Disguise**: Death confirms that Disguise moved slowly, shifting the clergy over generations towards the extreme aspects of Purity's remit, and rejected the priests who knew the original (Book 10, Ch85 L33-35). She says the gods were frustrated but could do nothing, since "the hidden gods operate differently" (Book 10, Ch85 L40).
- **Hero on Purity**: he guesses that the god of purity has positive and negative aspects, and that a war over a human empire's concept of purity put him in danger of being seen as a dark god. The Order of Redeeming Light's seed was planted then, before Disguise (Book 10, Ch89 L71-73).
- **The "fake god"**: a character refers to a deal made "with the fake god of Purity" (Book 12, Ch32 L74).
- **Jason's account**: Purity was in conflict within himself, as he tends to be, about five hundred years ago. He was likely to sanction himself, retiring and being reborn, but Knowledge persuaded him to leave a divine relic instead. She hid it until about a quarter of a century ago, and she aided Disguise in masquerading as Purity in return for his help (Book 13, Ch1017 L15-18).

### 5. Using this in a story

The Church of Purity is the best example in the books of a faith that can be sincere and betrayed at once. Its people believe, and their god is a fraud, so a scene with them should respect their sincerity. For a villain, Disguise is a patient, careful trickster who builds a long con out of a real faith. The real Purity is an absent god whose relic is still waiting to be found.

---

## The Healer

### 1. Summary

The god of medicine and healing, the Healer is kind, modest in manner and strict with those who exploit the sick. His church runs clinics, hospitals and research. In Book 1 he casts out the corrupt clergy of the Greenstone temple in person, and in later books his priests, among them Neil, Carlos and Arabelle, are central members of Jason's team.

### 2. Facts

- **Corruption in Greenstone**: Neil Davone makes a stand in the Greenstone Temple of the Healer, saying "This isn't about serving the Healer", and is told he is no longer welcome in the church (Book 1, Ch94 L3-7).
- **The god arrives**: the Healer appears at Jory's clinic, tells his clergy that merely not being shunned from his temples is "mercy enough", and refuses to restore their essences: "For that, I shall give you no salve. But you may turn to another" (Book 1, Ch95 L84-86). He says the power-seekers are of no use to him and hands them to Dominion, who takes those willing (Book 1, Ch95 L90-95).
- **A blessing**: he declares the clinic a sanctuary for healing, accepts that Jory's alchemy includes "togetherness jelly" ("I'm not going to begrudge people a little... togetherness"), and promises rituals of sanctification and a healer to staff it (Book 1, Ch95 L120-126).
- **Those who repent**: he answers a plea from a priest with "You blame others for your failings?", and gives a slight nod of assent to those who accept responsibility (Book 1, Ch95 L106-109).
- **The church in practice**: Neil reminds enemies he is "part of the church of the Healer" (Book 3, Ch21 L46), and Carlos introduces himself, "First and foremost... I am a priest of the Healer. Before anything else, I'm here to help you" (Book 3, Ch22 L73). The church opposes forms of punishment such as necromancy techniques (Book 3, Ch32 L101).

### 3. Later developments, Books 4 to 9

- **Attackers' banner**: some of those who attacked the Order of the Reaper's fortress wore Healer robes, which Jason finds at odds with the picture of the church as intolerant, calling it "revisionist history" (Book 2, Ch58 L77-78).
- **Specialists**: Carlos specialises in soul damage from star seeds (Book 8, Ch17 L45). The church takes over from Purity in handling them (Book 3, Ch21 L73).
- **Research**: Carlos and three assistants from the Church of the Healer live and work in Jason's astral space (Book 9, Ch28 L44), and Carlos, Arabelle and Neil advise on the design of the hospital in Jason's palace (Book 9, Ch71 L38). Hana Shavar is High Priestess of the Church of the Healer in Yaresh (Book 9, Ch74 L114).
- **Compensation**: Neil says the Healer gave healing powers that can no longer resurrect the ability to heal "on a body-matrix level" to compensate for what Death took away (Book 8, Ch39 L146).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **A friendly older man**: the god meets Arabelle as "a friendly older man, patiently listening", with no divine aura to crush her thinking (Book 10, Ch19 L61). He counsels her to walk beside Jason, not lead him (Book 10, Ch19 L50-51), and she talks to him about Jason's patterns of recovery (Book 10, Ch19 L57-62).
- **Hospital**: the Healer priestess runs a hospital in Jason's palace (Book 10, Ch3 L11).
- **Neil's choice**: Neil says he did not join the Healer's church by accident but to help people (Book 11, Ch68 L1084).

### 5. Using this in a story

The Healer is the gentle god whose gentleness has teeth. He does not argue and does not punish more than needed, but he does not give a second chance to those who treat the sick as a business. His priests are skilled and usually modest, and a team with one has a better chance of surviving a fight and a reason to listen to its healer's conscience.

---

## Undeath

### 1. Summary

Undeath is the god of the unliving, the dark counterpart of Death. His church lies dormant for generations and strikes when it has saved up the god's chances to intervene. In Book 10 it nearly destroys the Cardinas expedition, and in Book 11 Jason sanctions the echo of Undeath's authority left in an avatar. Undeath is a menacing but brisk god who compromises with other gods, including the high priestess of Destruction whose grandson serves in his church.

### 2. Facts

- **Early notice**: Gary says "Undeath is bad" (Book 1, Ch20 L21). A character recalls a zombie plague with a Temple of Undeath at its heart, whose high priest was the local mayor (Book 7, Ch9 L97-99).
- **How the church acts**: Hana Shavar says the Church of Undeath "does not act frequently. We don't give them the chance", so it lies dormant for generations and strikes when it gets one. "It's like their god has been saving up his chances to intervene in the world. Expect to see some dark miracles" (Book 10, Ch78 L38).
- **Garth and Jameela**: Garth, a zemravore, leads the church's priests in Cardinas (Book 11, Ch8 L20), and with Jameela commands the undead (Book 10, Ch88 L70-73). Garth's tactic: "The harder-fought the battle, the more we have to work with when it's done", and every battle that does not crush them makes the church stronger (Book 10, Ch88 L73).
- **Claiming territory**: Jason sees the god seeping into the ground and making it his domain, marked by purple light (Book 10, Ch85 L63; Book 10, Ch87 L19). Death says "Undeath has been liberally spending his influence in this place" (Book 10, Ch85 L70).
- **Appearance**: in Cardinas Undeath appears as a living man in simple black robes with empty sockets containing a crimson spark, and a deep voice "like gravel being dumped into a silo" (Book 10, Ch88 L74-76).
- **His manner**: he accepts that Death and Hero's interventions at the critical moment need a response, tells Garth he will not punish him for following instructions, and complains that his priest Jeff's grandmother is a high priestess of Destruction: "When dealing with other gods, compromises must be made, even by me" (Book 10, Ch88 L77-85). He says "we are forced into another compromise" over animating a vessel that will hold only a fraction of his power (Book 10, Ch88 L89-91).
- **The avatar**: he allows an avatar to be drawn into the transformation zone to aid his priests, and it fights Jason and loses (Book 11, Ch65 L43). It is "just power and the echo of intent", with no active will behind it, since the god's will is locked out (Book 11, Ch33 L99). Jason sanctions its authority and turns it into a divine weapon (Book 11, Ch35 L42-47; see `../Authority_and_Sanctioning.md`).
- **Jason's reaction**: his aura becomes anathema to the priests of Undeath (Book 11, Ch28 L16).
- **A visit in Greenstone**: the god leaves when told to by Jason, and when Jason calls him "Steve" the others whisper (Book 11, Ch62 L28, L39). The text says "The god of Undeath's name is Undeath" (Book 11, Ch62 L77).
- **Hidden strongholds**: he is among the gods who keep only hidden strongholds (Book 10, Ch85 L40).
- **Jason's view**: Jason calls Undeath "a complete prick" in a conversation about the gods, noting that some others have been kind to him (Book 12, Ch7 L14).

### 3. Using this in a story

Use Undeath as the patient storm. His church is a threat that arrives once in a generation and has been preparing. His own manner is more businesslike than evil, and he does not rant. A villain in his church believes the cost of every battle is an investment, and that is a more frightening mindset than bloodlust.

---

## The All-Devouring Eye

### 1. Summary

The All-Devouring Eye is the great astral being of annihilation. It does not communicate with the others, gives no blessings, and stands apart from the pacts. Its realm in the deep astral is where Gordon and the apocalypse beasts come from, and the great astral beings believe it created Gordon for the purpose of repairing the Cosmic Throne.

### 2. Facts

- **Among those interested**: it is one of the handful of great astral beings that take an interest in physical realities (Book 2, Ch21 L92).

### 3. Later developments, Books 7 to 9

- **Its realm**: "The realm of the All-Devouring Eye" is where Gordon comes from, and Colin comes from the border territory with Legion's realm (Book 4, Ch32 L36).
- **No blessings**: Legion and the All-Devouring Eye "didn't hand out blessings" (Book 7, Ch11 L75).
- **Region**: it is "where I, and your friend Gordon, come from, and it abuts the realm of Legion, the great astral being whom administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself. Your sanguine horror comes from this place, where life and annihilation are neighbours" (Book 8, Ch55 L92).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 11 (spoilers)

- **A silent being**: the Eye "is not one for communicating, even with other great astral beings", and the great astral beings believe it created Gordon for the throne repair (Book 11, Ch64 L91). "There is little point asking questions of the All-Devouring Eye" (Book 11, Ch64 L93).
- **Apart from the pacts**: it stands apart with the Keeper and the Word in the Silence (Book 11, Ch64 L49). Its stance is "least active of us all", a vessel says, and its last intervention is long ago (Book 11, Ch22 L38).
- **Avatars of doom**: they "are the exclusive domain of the All-Devouring Eye"; it has never employed its reality assassins for any task, instead loaning them to the Sundered Throne, for reasons nobody knows (Book 11, Ch34 L97).
- **The seed that grew**: Jason is "a seed that the World-Phoenix planted, but he has grown in ways only the All-Devouring Eye anticipated" (Book 11, Ch22 L29).
- **Its vessel**: an orb of leathery flesh, larger than a person, draped in a dark green cloak, whose front is an open mouth ringed with needle teeth and a single huge eye inside (Book 11, Ch68 L2526).
- **Its connection**: a speaker suggests Gordon's potential comes from "the connection of his kind to the Sundered Throne or the All-Devouring Eye", but will not elaborate (Book 10, Ch5 L94).

### 5. Using this in a story

The Eye is the great silence behind Gordon. Keep it unreadable: no speeches, no demands, only effects. Anything it has caused looks like a coincidence until someone realises the pattern, and the beings who know it best are least willing to talk about it.

---

## The Celestial Book

### 1. Summary

The Celestial Book is the great astral being of the understanding of magic, venerated by researchers and ritualists. It gives blessings, is friendlier than the Reaper and more cheerful than most of its peers, and in the Book 11 battle it is the one great astral being who enjoys being mortal. It locked essence combinations after the sundering.

### 2. Facts

- **Veneration**: "I venerate the Celestial Book," Clive says, describing a blessing that triggered a racial gift evolution, changing the human special-attack affinity to a spell affinity, like the elves (Book 1, Ch85 L22). It is "fairly common for those of us heavily involved in magical theory" (Book 2, Ch21 L94).
- **Not a god of books**: Jason first asks if it is "the god of books, or something" (Book 1, Ch85 L26). It is named among the great astral beings interested in physical realities (Book 2, Ch21 L92).
- **Approachable**: its stones are described as "a lot more approachable than the Reaper" (Book 2, Ch56 L94).
- **A word on proportionality**: the World-Phoenix reminds the Builder, "The Celestial Book wanted me to remind you about proportionality... The ritualist is one of his", meaning Clive, and the book will not tolerate a gold-ranker sent to kill the boy out of spite (Book 3, Ch69 L278).

### 3. Later developments, Books 9 to 11

- **A network**: those who venerate the Celestial Book "maintain a loose network, with ties to the Magic Society and the Church of Knowledge", and its symbol is commonly recognised (Book 9, Ch65 L28-30). A man on Jason's world venerates it (Book 9, Ch27 L21).

- **The sundering and combinations**: the Celestial Book and the Seeker of Songs "were both against the sundering from the start" (Book 11, Ch65 L75). After the sundering the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations, so that each combination has only one confluence; the restrictions unravel as Jason repairs the throne (Book 11, Ch68 L1580). A great working of authority for healing would also have involved the Celestial Book (Book 11, Ch33 L112).
- **In the jungle**: in a mortal body the Celestial Book "merrily plundered each new food cart" (Book 11, Ch68 L443), asks if the Reaper's joke was any good (Book 11, Ch68 L1333), and finds the battle "a petty squabble. It's kind of fun" (Book 11, Ch68 L174). It is delighted at the surprise of the gathering (Book 11, Ch68 L178), although it later gives Jason accusatory looks (Book 11, Ch68 L260).
- **Its warning**: it tells Jason that if he loses, his mind will be destroyed and he will be a new person with no memory (Book 11, Ch68 L227). Later it says "all of our judgements are compromised" by the vessels Jason gave them (Book 11, Ch68 L2166), and that the battle is done and he lost (Book 11, Ch68 L2158).

### 4. Using this in a story

The Celestial Book is the friendly face of the cosmos. It likes discoveries and cleverness, and it reacts to mortal pleasures with the delight of a student on a trip. A story that needs a patron for a researcher, or a great astral being who is on the player's side without being a tool, can use it. Its history of locking off essence combinations is a hook for anyone investigating why combinations are fixed.

---

## The Keeper of Moments

### 1. Summary

The Keeper of Moments, also called the Keeper of the Sands, is the great astral being that governs time. It opposed the sundering from the beginning and refused to join the pacts, and it polices attempts at time travel. Its prime vessel is Raythe, who in Book 13 bargains with Jason over what he may try to do with time.

### 2. Facts

- **Domain**: "Even the Keeper of Moments, the great astral being that governs time, cannot [affect the past]" (Book 6, Ch14 L80).

- **Policing time**: it "comes down hard" on anyone who comes close to time travel, "in terms of bad ideas, even on a cosmic scale, time travel is the worst" (Book 11, Ch63 L98).
- **Names**: a speaker confesses "a soft spot for the name 'Keeper of the Sands'. I like the hourglass imagery", and Jason says he once heard the master called "the Underclock" (Book 11, Ch22 L21-22).
- **Vessel**: Lady Raythe is the prime vessel of the Keeper of Moments (Book 11, Ch64 L9). She says her master "opposed the sundering from the beginning and refused to participate in any of it", which gives her freedoms others lack (Book 11, Ch64 L47). The Keeper stands apart with the All-Devouring Eye and the Word in the Silence (Book 11, Ch64 L49).
- **Interventions**: Raythe's master took an interest in Jason (Book 11, Ch22 L29-32), and its prime vessel killed Mah Go Schaat to protect him (Book 11, Ch42 L87). Velius warns that the Keeper and the All-Devouring Eye waging war in Jason's soul would be bad even if they were on his side (Book 11, Ch65 L47).
- **Why the link was left**: Clive reasons that the Builder's synchronising of two universes' timelines can't have pleased the Keeper (Book 11, Ch63 L100).
- **Raythe on time**: she says her relationship with time is not linear. Time is "a series of interconnected points" and "any given node... can only be directly changed by those within it" (Book 13, Ch991 L7-11). She asks Jason not to attempt time travel or time looping, saying that section of the time pattern is too damaged to tell whether he would succeed or cause a cascading paradox (Book 13, Ch991 L60-62). She did not kill him earlier because eliminating the one who would repair the throne would be a massive disruption, and Dawn talked her out of it (Book 13, Ch991 L66-68).
- **An offer**: the Keeper's rules hold sway even in Jason's realm. Raythe offers to find him when no one else can (Book 13, Ch991 L84-86).

### 3. Using this in a story

The Keeper is the quiet auditor of causality. Do not make it the one who rewrites the past. It prevents others from doing so. A story with time travel will bring in Raythe or her kind, and she will be polite, patient and immovable.

---

## Legion

### 1. Summary

Legion is the great astral being that administers the cosmic rules governing life itself. It is one of the beings that joined the pacts after the sundering, then came to think the sundering a mistake. In the Book 11 battle it appears in a mortal body as a deep-voiced man with antlers and a beard.

### 2. Facts

- **No blessings**: Legion and the All-Devouring Eye are not known to hand out blessings (Book 7, Ch11 L75).
- **Domain and realm**: Legion "administers the cosmic rules that govern life itself", and its realm abuts the All-Devouring Eye's region, a place "where life and annihilation are neighbours" (Book 8, Ch55 L92). A sanguine horror was summoned from a "nightmare realm where the Limitless Legion met the Final Domain" (Book 9, Ch62 L23).

- **Position on the sundering**: Legion is among those who "have come around and will fight" (Book 11, Ch65 L75).
- **In a mortal body**: "the man with the antlers" (Book 11, Ch68 L159). It speaks in a "deep, rumbling voice" and objects to vessels that Jason provided: "There are rules" (Book 11, Ch68 L161). It looks impassive behind its beard (Book 11, Ch68 L178).
- **Its view of the plan**: it tells Jason that he could have given them far more advantages (Book 11, Ch68 L229), and says "We do not get 'used in turn'" (Book 11, Ch68 L238). Fighting beside him, it says "You are throwing away a chance we have waited eons for" (Book 11, Ch68 L261).
- **Against the World-Phoenix**: it says Jason agreed to help and that "we exploited that to come here", and explains that it is easier to make an immoral choice when you are not doing so alone (Book 11, Ch68 L2162, L2181).

### 3. Using this in a story

Legion is a being of law: it cares about the rules of life, expects them to hold, and prefers a disciplined plan to improvisation. It is a good voice for a great astral being who is more worried about consistency than about people.

---

## The Seeker of Songs

### 1. Summary

The Seeker of Songs is a great astral being whose domain the books never state. It was against the sundering from the start. It appears in Book 11 in a mortal vessel as a woman with blue eyes, and likes music from Jason's world.

### 2. Facts

- **Position on the sundering**: Raythe says the Celestial Book and the Seeker of Songs "were both against the sundering from the start" (Book 11, Ch65 L75).
- **Appearance**: "the woman with blue eyes" among the great astral beings in mortal bodies (Book 11, Ch68 L159).
- **Manner**: it identifies a phrase as "a song from Asano's world: 'Rumble in the Jungle' by Fugees, featuring A Tribe Called Quest, Busta Rhymes and John Forté" (Book 11, Ch68 L175). When the others complain at being used as a training tool it says "this man is hosting the largest gathering of great astral beings since the sundering, and he's using us as a training tool?" (Book 11, Ch68 L236).
- **Against the World-Phoenix**: it calls hijacking Jason's soul while his willpower is diminished "unconscionable" (Book 11, Ch68 L2164), and in the throne room, when the Reaper calls ceremonies pointless, says "I rather like them" (Book 11, Ch68 L2530-2531).

### 3. Not in the text

No domain, vessel, church or cult is described. The name suggests an interest in music, and the being is shown enjoying it, but the books do not state its sphere.

---

## The Builder

### 1. Summary

The Builder is the great astral being of construction, whose work is forging universes. There have been two. The first built the twin universes of Earth and Pallimustus and was sanctioned for it. The second, the Builder of the present, is a mortal messenger who was raised to the office and whose authority is held on conditions. He is obsessed with physical reality, runs the cults that hunt astral spaces, and is building a universe of his own.

### 2. Facts

- **Obsession and method**: "obsessed with physical reality while, by its very nature, being unable to co-exist with it", the Builder recruits people to carve off the astral spaces connected to their world, then steps in and claims them (Book 2, Ch21 L106-112). He gathers followers rather than crossing the World-Phoenix (Book 2, Ch25 L69).
- **Tools**: star seeds, tokens, cults, constructs and clockwork animals (Book 2, Ch21 L26-36; Book 2, Ch25 L37-45).
- **The three-way meeting**: the Builder meets the Reaper and the World-Phoenix, grandly says "I will be worshipped by an entire universe... A god beyond gods" (Book 3, Ch69 L261), and is told that "we are the rules" (Book 3, Ch69 L258). The Reaper's terms bar him from interfering with Jason's birth world or producing new star seeds, tokens or vessels (Book 3, Ch69 L288-292). In return the World-Phoenix will offer Jason a power at the cost of no further resurrections (Book 3, Ch69 L295).
- **Observers**: the Builder's observer constructs accompany a group at a test, and Shade reads this as the Builder testing them (Book 3, Ch63 L45).

### 3. Later developments, Books 6 to 9

- **The compact**: Dawn says Jason's killing by Shako violated the compact between the Builder, the Reaper and the World-Phoenix (Book 6, Ch18 L6).
- **The Book 8 deal**: the Builder, speaking at the table, says "Authority must be traded" (Book 8, Ch54 L19). Jason trades the authority token for the opening of the fundamental realm and the Builder's withdrawal from the planet, and the Builder replies "Accepted. Deal struck" before the World-Phoenix can object (Book 8, Ch54 L89-94). His voice is "like the grinding of stone" (Book 8, Ch54 L19).
- **Vessels**: Shako is the Builder's prime vessel until the Sundered Throne takes him (Book 10, Ch15 L5).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **The first Builder**: experimenting once the throne was sundered, he made the twin universes, one rich in magic and one poor. It was "a step too far", and the other great astral beings took his power and authority and gave it to a mortal (Book 13, Ch1017 L9-11).
- **The second Builder**: "His name is Zithis Carrow Vayel. He was a sixteen-year-old diamond-ranker when the great astral beings recruited him to replace the old Builder" (Book 10, Ch26 L55).
- **A new prime vessel**: Erigo Fin Desca, a messenger heavily modified by the Builder, with silver wings and amber glass eyes, is the new prime vessel (Book 10, Ch15 L5). He leads the move of a planet with the world engineers (Book 10, Ch15 L3-4).
- **The conditions**: the Builder says that when he was ascended, "they took precautions to control me": they can revert his mind to the state it was in at sixteen, brash, impetuous and arrogant, though he keeps his memories (Book 11, Ch68 L450-454). He believes they intend to restore his predecessor and move his authority back (Book 11, Ch68 L460).
- **His own kingdom**: he is building his own universe, "not from a seed but something different, belonging to only me", so that when the others move against him he has a refuge. He wants to be "the greatest of astral kings" (Book 11, Ch68 L460-464).
- **Why he fights**: he fights to restore the throne because the great astral beings could only do this to him by being unbound from their purposes (Book 11, Ch68 L468). Jason calls him a worse person than Thadwick Mercer, whom the Builder used as a vessel (Book 11, Ch68 L447, L467).
- **A weak replacement**: of the new Builder, Jason says "it turns out that he's... not great" (Book 13, Ch1017 L27).

### 5. Using this in a story

The Builder is a great power with a mortal's resentments. He is arrogant, impatient and bound by pacts, and what he cannot do directly he does through cults, constructs and vessels. His plans have an expiry date because the other beings may revert his mind, and a story can use that fear.

---

## The Reaper

### 1. Summary

The Reaper is the great astral being of the finality of death. It is distinct from the god of Death of Pallimustus, who only guides souls into the astral. Cold, dry and a lover of rules, the Reaper is the mediator among the great astral beings, the father of the shadows that serve as familiars, and in Book 11 the reluctant opponent of Jason's plan to restore the throne. Its vessel is Velius.

### 2. Facts

- **Domain**: "The Reaper is very big on the finality of death. Some consider it the true god of death, as all our god of death governs is the passage of the soul into the astral" (Book 2, Ch25 L67).
- **Items and orders**: the Way of the Reaper is a set of skill books (Book 1, Ch50 L40), and the Order of the Reaper's teachings are collected in its legacy (Book 2, Ch60 L15). The Order of the Reaper used ancient knowledge of how to anchor such realms, "provided by the Reaper itself" (Book 2, Ch44 L91). Reaper awakening stones give mostly aggressive utility and conjuration powers (Book 2, Ch67 L45).
- **Speaking through Velius**: when the Reaper takes over its vessel, the warm voice becomes "cold and bleak" (Book 3, Ch69 L251). It tells the Builder that Jason "carried the World-Phoenix's token. Those pacts are older than you and I will not violate them" (Book 3, Ch69 L254).
- **The rules**: "We are the rules. To deny them is to deny ourselves" (Book 3, Ch69 L258). It arranges the compromise between the Builder and the World-Phoenix and makes its own concession, because it fears being made a farce if Jason is resurrected over and over (Book 3, Ch69 L284-304).
- **Shade**: "Of all my children, Shade has ever followed his own path", the Reaper says, with a brief fatherly smile (Book 3, Ch69 L305-306).

### 3. Later developments, Books 5 to 9

- **A favour**: Dawn says the Reaper offered to bring Farrah back, because it wanted to stop the World-Phoenix sending Jason's soul back and forth across the astral with tokens (Book 5, Ch20 L41).
- **The cult**: the Cult of the Reaper requires authentic veneration. It was among the first to notice its former offshoot order moving again, but is hard to infiltrate (Book 9, Ch27 L57).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **The resurrection**: Jason says "The Reaper resurrected her, not me. The World-Phoenix convinced him because she was worried I'd go nuts and let the whole planet die" (Book 10, Ch57 L60).
- **The throne**: through Velius the Reaper says many of those who took part in the sundering now think revisiting it would be prudent (Book 11, Ch64 L66), and later fights Jason in his soul as one of the opponents (Book 11, Ch68 L2430). Its servant Velius is a fertility doctor on Earth in the aftermath (Book 11, Ch68 L776-778).
- **A joke**: Jason calls everyone to hear that the Reaper made a joke, and the Celestial Book asks whether it was any good (Book 11, Ch68 L1329-1335).
- **A walk with the World-Phoenix**: afterwards the Reaper and the World-Phoenix walk an empty road for two years (Book 11, Ch68 L2244). The World-Phoenix accuses it of raising its vessels "like pets instead of using them like tools", and it answers that she got sad when her boy left home (Book 11, Ch68 L2328-2329).
- **Sanctioning**: when Shade sanctions himself, the Reaper warns that "Sanctioning can so easily go wrong" (Book 11, Ch68 L2220).
- **Bending a rule**: Jason says the Reaper decided to "bend his own rules, one last time, before the rules were locked in once more", allowing Gary to reincarnate near people who knew him (Book 13, Ch963 L57).
- **Its children**: Shade and Umber are the Reaper's children and brothers who drifted apart (Book 13, Ch981 L37, L62-64).

### 5. Using this in a story

The Reaper is a stern parent with a dry streak. It follows its own rules strictly, bends them rarely and thinks in eons. It has no interest in grand speeches. If a story needs a great astral being to say no, or to set limits, the Reaper is the one.

---

## The Whisper in Corners

### 1. Summary

The Whisper in Corners is a great astral being Jason had never heard of before meeting Raythe and Velius. It joined the fight against the consequences of the sundering and appears in Book 11 as a veiled woman in lace whose voice comes from every direction.

### 2. Facts

- **Position on the sundering**: it is among those who "have come around and will fight" (Book 11, Ch65 L75).
- **Appearance**: "the woman in lace" (Book 11, Ch68 L159), laced and veiled, "not a great astral being Jason had heard of" before (Book 11, Ch68 L231).
- **Voice**: "Her mouth did not move, her voice instead a susurrus of whispers all around them" (Book 11, Ch68 L2160).
- **On forcing souls**: it warns the World-Phoenix that there are lines even great astral beings should not cross, and asks "Will you become like the Builder, World-Phoenix? Forcing your way into unwilling souls" (Book 11, Ch68 L2160). It later asks why she would entice others to stand against her (Book 11, Ch68 L2180).

### 3. Not in the text

No domain, vessel, church or cult is described. The name hints at secrets, but the books do not state its sphere.

---

## The Word in the Silence

### 1. Summary

The Word in the Silence is a great astral being named only once. The text lists it among the beings that "stood apart" from the rest, even before the sundering.

### 2. Facts

- **Apart from the pacts**: Velius says of those who stood aside from the sundering, "They have ever stood apart from the rest, even before the sundering. The Keeper, the All-Devouring Eye, the Word in the Silence" (Book 11, Ch64 L49).

### 3. Not in the text

No domain, vessel, appearance, church or cult is described, and the being does not appear in the Book 11 battle or throne room.

---

## The World-Phoenix

### 1. Summary

The World-Phoenix is the great astral being of dimensional integrity: it keeps universes from tearing, and it set Jason's journey in motion. It prefers to plant seeds rather than act, has a sense of humour, and fought Jason in his own soul in Book 11. Its prime vessels are called First Servant or First Sister, and Dawn, a former vessel, is its hierophant.

### 2. Facts

- **The mark on Jason**: his first status screens carry a symbol of a fire bird, and an ability labelled "Authority of the World Phoenix" (Book 1, Ch1 L86). Jason says the World-Phoenix gave him "a gift as his soul passed through the astral", and that he is an outworlder through "happenstance" (Book 3, Ch69 L266-267).
- **Its role**: "the integrity of dimensions is mine. It is only with my permission that you can conduct your little game" (Book 3, Ch69 L272). The Builder will not cross it (Book 2, Ch25 L69).
- **The meeting of three**: the World-Phoenix attends in a celestine vessel with alabaster skin and ruby hair, "a teasing smile and an amused twinkle in her red, gemstone eyes" (Book 3, Ch69 L262). She calls Jason "a pleasantly effective little seedling" (Book 3, Ch69 L276), and negotiates with the Reaper over terms that forbid the Builder from interfering with Jason's world (Book 3, Ch69 L288-295).

### 3. Later developments, Books 4 to 9

- **How it acts**: "The World-Phoenix does not like to act directly. It prefers to set things in motion that will ultimately achieve the end it desires" (Book 4, Ch3 L66). Jason receives "the blessing of the World-Phoenix" (Book 4, Ch2 L39).
- **The cult**: its head is the First Servant, the ultimate arbiter before the World-Phoenix itself (Book 3, Ch69 L962). Dawn says she cannot sneak past the World-Phoenix (Book 5, Ch20 L52), and that it and she as its representative have always sought to sanction interference with the physical-astral boundary (Book 5, Ch66 L36).
- **Avoiding confrontation**: the World-Phoenix is "notoriously averse to direct confrontation" (Book 6, Ch35 L42). It crafts a bridge for Jason as compensation, Dawn says, "a sliver of hope in his darkest hour" (Book 6, Ch18 L65).
- **A tool that fails**: Dawn says the World-Phoenix "doesn't care about me or my wellbeing because it can't. What it can recognise is when a tool... is not functioning the way it should" (Book 8, Ch19 L54).
- **Speaking through Dawn**: at the table in Book 8, the World-Phoenix speaks through Dawn, "a lot more sultry than I expected", and thanks Jason for reminding Dawn of her mortality (Book 8, Ch54 L24-29). It grins and the vessel's eyes return to normal (Book 8, Ch54 L112).
- **Former servant**: Dawn is no longer First Sister, and her successor is Helsveth (Book 7, Ch63 L111; Book 9, Ch78 L28).

### 4. Later developments, Books 10 to 13 (spoilers)

- **Not a friend in the soul**: Jason says the World-Phoenix "had to know what she was doing to me" (Book 10, Ch5 L100). In Book 11 Raythe says it prefers the current state of affairs and will be his antagonist in the battle for the throne (Book 11, Ch65 L34-36).
- **The battle**: the World-Phoenix leads a horde of monsters in Jason's soul, asks him why he struggles (Book 11, Ch68 L244, L1755), and says his will is in tatters in a matter-of-fact voice (Book 11, Ch68 L2082). When the great astral beings are given mortal vessels, it realises "he is trying to infect us with mortal morality" (Book 11, Ch68 L2175).
- **The Boundary**: she explains that before the sundering she was the Boundary, who sanctioned herself because she wanted to be more than her role (Book 11, Ch68 L1793-1795).
- **After**: for two years the World-Phoenix and the Reaper walk an empty road together, with one pause when she says "I miss food" (Book 11, Ch68 L2244-2248). When Jason arrives, she is surprised, and he talks about the Rumble in the Jungle (Book 11, Ch68 L2339-2342). The restored throne takes her current state as its baseline (Book 12, Ch60 L16).
- **In Book 12 and 13**: the cult of the World-Phoenix opens the universe to gold-rankers at Jason's request (Book 12, Ch60 L19-20), and the World-Phoenix leaves Jason a message through Helsveth, who has fought him before (Book 13, Ch1024 L90).

### 5. Using this in a story

The World-Phoenix is the patient gardener of the cosmos: it plants seeds, trims branches and tolerates a great deal so long as the dimensions hold. It speaks in a teasing, almost friendly way, and will use a friend against a friend without malice. A scene with it should leave the character feeling both looked after and managed.
