## Abilities and Attributes

### 1. Summary

An essence ability is a power an essence user has from an essence. Each essence gives five; one is awakened at absorption and the rest are awakened later by stones. Each ability has a type, a cost, a cooldown and a rank, and gains a new effect at each rank. Four attributes, Power, Speed, Spirit and Recovery, each bond to one of the four essences and rise in rank as that essence's abilities are mastered. Abilities and attributes together decide when a person can move up a rank.

### 2. How it works

**The five abilities.** An essence "imbues 1 awakened essence ability and 4 unawakened essence abilities" (Book 1, Ch20 L52). The awakened one is a function of the essence and the person: Jason's dark essence gave Midnight Eyes at absorption (Book 1, Ch8 L35), blood gave Blood Harvest (Book 1, Ch21 L7), sin gave Punish (Book 1, Ch21 L50) and doom gave Inexorable Doom (Book 1, Ch21 L62). Further abilities come from awakening stones (see `Awakening_Stones.md`). A full set is twenty.

**Types.** The System sorts abilities into types that show on each ability's description, with keywords after them. The types visible in the books are special attack, spell, special ability, aura, conjuration and familiar (with summon and ritual tags), plus a separate list of racial abilities. Examples from Jason's screens:
- Special attack (melee, drain, wounding, blood): Leech Bite (Book 1, Ch27 L28).
- Spell (drain): Blood Harvest (Book 1, Ch21 L15).
- Special ability (dimension, teleport): Path of Shadows (Book 1, Ch22 L116).
- Aura (holy, unholy): Hegemony (Book 1, Ch40 L37).
- Conjuration (darkness, light, dimension): Cloak of Night (Book 1, Ch8 L62).
- Familiar (ritual, summon): Sanguine Horror (Book 1, Ch23 L62).

**Cost, cooldown, rank.** An ability screen lists a cost in mana, stamina or both, in words (low, moderate, and so on), a cooldown (none, or a time such as forty seconds) and a current rank with a percentage: "Current rank: Iron 0 (00%)" (Book 1, Ch22 L117-119). Mirage Step costs "low stamina and mana" with a forty-second cooldown (Book 2, Ch8 L174-175).

**Rank within an ability.** Within a rank an ability also has a level and a percentage, so the same spell reads "Iron 0 (00%)" when first awakened (Book 1, Ch34 L39) and "Iron 1 (19%)" a few chapters later with a stronger effect (Book 1, Ch39 L70-71). An ability keeps one effect per rank, so its description lists an iron effect, a bronze effect, and so on, and the later effects add to the earlier ones (Book 5, Ch25 L23-25 shows Cloak of Night). The full ladder for each of Jason's twenty abilities up to gold is in `Jason_Power_Set_Reference.md`.

**Ranking an ability.** An ability reaches its next rank as a separate event: "Ability [Midnight Eyes] (Dark) has reached Bronze 0 (00%)" (Book 3, Ch15 L47). Several abilities reach Bronze 0 in the same stretch of Book 3: [Sanguine Horror] (Book 3, Ch21 L121), [Hegemony] (Book 3, Ch21 L136), [Path of Shadows] (Book 3, Ch29 L23) and [Blade of Doom] (Book 3, Ch38 L5). An ability can be held back: "Ability [Cloak of Night] (Dark) cannot advance further until all attributes have reached silver rank" (Book 5, Ch25 L26).

**Attributes.** The four attributes are Power, Speed, Spirit and Recovery. Each essence bonds to one of them and raises it from normal to iron: "[Blood Essence] has bonded to your [Power] attribute" (Book 1, Ch21 L6), dark to Speed (Book 1, Ch8 L34), sin to Recovery (Book 1, Ch21 L49), and doom to Spirit (Book 1, Ch21 L61). "Master all blood essence abilities to increase your [Power] attribute" (Book 1, Ch21 L6). Once an essence's abilities are all awakened, the linked attribute "will advance in conjunction with lowest-rank" ability of that essence (Book 2, Ch8 L171).

**Rank progress.** Progress to the next rank counts essences complete: "Progress to bronze rank: 50% (4/4 essences complete)" (Book 3, Ch14 L98) and a smaller fraction for fewer completed essences (Book 1, Ch99 L65). All of a person's attributes must reach the new rank before an ability can go further (Book 5, Ch25 L26). See `Ranks_and_Advancement.md`.

**Knowing what an ability does.** Ordinary essence users must feel their way into a power by instinct; "unlike other essence users, Jason had never been forced to fathom out his abilities by feel", because he has System messages (Book 3, Ch20 L17). The Magic Society keeps records of what abilities do at later ranks, and Clive urges Jason to look them up (Book 2, Ch9 L31-35).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Cost versus effect.** An ability may cost nothing, or may allow a higher spend for more effect: Punition at silver can be raised from a base cost to high, very high or extreme mana, which shortens its cooldown to twenty seconds, ten seconds or none (Book 12, Ch67 L331).
- **Passive powers.** Auras are passive and projected; Jason notes that an aura power common to the force confluence is able to move things physically, which none of his can do (Book 8, Ch60 L5).
- **Racial gifts.** Races have gifts that interact with abilities: humans' aptitude for special attacks over spells (Book 1, Ch87 L91; Book 4, Ch40 L72), Kylie's vision confluence letting her awaken a perception power from each essence (Book 4, Ch42 L44).
- **Variable subtypes.** A spell can have "variable subtypes, contingent on effect" (Book 2, Ch50 L57).
- **Abilities that outgrow their text.** Jason notes that the wording of Cloak of Night has changed from earlier iterations and wonders whether his own perception shaped it (Book 5, Ch25 L27).
- **Execute and retribution.** Some abilities hit damaged targets harder (execute), such as Verdict, "deals transcendent damage. Scales with injury level of target" (Book 12, Ch67 L335).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Jason's twenty.** Dark (Midnight Eyes, Cloak of Night, Path of Shadows, Hand of the Reaper, Shadow of the Hegemon), blood (Blood Harvest, Leech Bite, Feast of Blood, Sanguine Horror, Haemorrhage), sin (Punish, Feast of Absolution, Sin Eater, Hegemony, Castigate) and doom (Inexorable Doom, Punition, Blade of Doom, Verdict, Avatar of Doom) (Book 12, Ch67 L169-192).
- **Sophie.** Mirage Step is the last of her five mystic abilities (Book 2, Ch8 L170-171), and she awakened confluence abilities before her essence abilities, which Clive calls "quite unusual" (Book 2, Ch8 L45).
- **Clive.** His Enact Ritual makes drawing and performing rituals more convenient (Book 2, Ch6 L43).
- **Gary.** His replaced abilities Craftsman's Gaze and Stoke the Forge become All-Seeing Eye and First Son of the Leonids when he takes divine essences (Book 10, Ch86 L71-72).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Strong abilities are better.** Farrah and Rufus both lay out a scale from individually strong abilities to abilities that "underwhelm in isolation, but used together become very dangerous", with affliction specialists at the second end (Book 1, Ch22 L88-93). "Simple doesn't mean bad" (Book 1, Ch22 L90).
- **Combat power matters most.** Gary: "just having a bunch of destructive combat powers makes you less useful to a team", and a few good utility powers help one get jobs (Book 1, Ch22 L111).
- **An ability is its description.** The description may not reveal all later effects, and costs for lower-rank effects are removed when abilities rank up (Book 5, Ch25 L27).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 2:** Abilities scale with rank into effects the earlier text hints at, like Path of Shadows from a single teleport to portals across regional, continental and global distances (Book 12, Ch67 L224-227). Jason's Interface gift gives the same display to others in his party (Book 12, Ch67 L197).
- **Level 3:** Jason's gold-rank sheet in Book 12 records twenty abilities at gold 3 to gold 5, with attributes at gold 3 and 4 and progress to diamond at 38 percent (Book 12, Ch67 L155-160, L169-192). See `Jason_Power_Set_Reference.md`.

## The Adventuring Profession

### 1. Summary

Adventuring is the work of killing monsters and clearing hazards for pay. In practice an adventurer is a licensed contractor: they take posted notices and contracts from a jobs hall, work in a team, and are paid in spirit coins and loot. Most are not heroes in the story sense, and the profession is as much about judgement and bookkeeping as combat. This file describes how the work runs. The organisation is described in `05_Organisations/Adventure_Society.md`.

### 2. How it works

**What an adventurer does.** Rufus: "The bulk of our job as adventurers is hunting them down before they reach that stage", meaning the aggressive end of a monster's life (Book 1, Ch19 L36). Farrah and Rufus both reject the idea that adventuring is "just going places and killing everyone you find" (Book 1, Ch19 L37-38).

**Notices.** A monster notice, "whether from a notice board or the Adventure Society directly, has three pieces of information, so long as that information is known. The name of the monster, or a description. The number of monsters, and the approximate location" (Book 1, Ch57 L33).

**The jobs hall.** The jobs hall is "an annex of the main administration building", "a moderate-sized room divided into rows by standing bulletin boards" with a desk where a clerk records contracts (Book 1, Ch63 L54; Book 1, Ch64 L5). Contracts for areas near the city are in the hall; "those further afield were posted on each town or village's noticeboard", and every month the Society sends people to patrol those areas for a full month away, "not a popular task" (Book 1, Ch64 L3). A director can change how notices are posted: Greenstone's new director stopped keeping a separate board for incentivised contracts (Book 1, Ch63 L81).

**Pay and bonuses.** The Society pays iron spirit coins for an iron-rank monster contract, ten up to a hundred depending on number, travel and difficulty; bonuses can run "all the way up to an awakening stone, although such a reward was extremely rare" (Book 1, Ch64 L12). The Society "was known to give out awakening stones for exceptional service, although rarely" (Book 1, Ch64 L81). As a rule, "we don't give out awakening stones to people for killing monsters above their rank. It would just incentivise people getting themselves killed trying to jump ranks" (Book 1, Ch91 L34).

**Badges and stars.** A new member gets a badge, a circular iron medallion embossed with a sword and rod crossed over a shield, "one-star, iron rank" (Book 1, Ch62 L61, L66). The ranking system "has two parts": the first is the member's essence rank, and the second is stars, "not an assessment of your power, but your judgement" (Book 1, Ch62 L68-70). Everyone begins at one star and the maximum is three (Book 1, Ch62 L70). One-star contracts "are pure monster hunts, with no complicated elements to deal with" (Book 1, Ch62 L70). Two stars mean "at least some level of actual, unsupervised responsibility", investigating "potentially dangerous situations or unknown phenomena", and leading small expeditions of one-star members (Book 1, Ch62 L82). Three stars means "they trust you to handle yourself when things get political", and three-star members are "expected to anticipate and manage consequences at a higher level" (Book 1, Ch62 L85-86). "You can expect to drop a star rank each time you increase a tier in power" (Book 1, Ch62 L91). The badge confers prestige, not authority: "any actual authority comes from the contract you are carrying out" (Book 1, Ch62 L64). Society officials are outside the rating system (Book 1, Ch62 L72). The badge does not track the wearer if their aura resists tracking (Book 1, Ch62 L55-59).

**Teams.** "Rick's team had an archetypal distribution of roles, with a couple of resilient front-liners, some damage specialists and a healer. Not every team could find a good healer... team dynamics were as much about the balance of personalities as the balance of powers" (Book 1, Ch66 L60). When a team loses a front-liner it needs a new one (Book 2, Ch15 L38; Book 2, Ch29 L8). A group works "as a team, instead of as individuals" against a bronze monster, directed by a leader (Book 1, Ch77 L60).

**Specialist or generalist.** In Rimaros the culture prefers specialists: Jason, with stealth, utility, mobility and summoning powers beside his afflictions, "in Rimaros, you aren't" an affliction specialist, "you're a dabbler; a dilettante" (Book 7, Ch5 L25). A Rimaros assessor reads him as "an affliction-using generalist" while another corrects it (Book 7, Ch44 L7).

**Loot.** Teams split loot as a group (Book 2, Ch21 L14) and keep records for splitting later: Jason "took out a notebook and recorded all the loot for splitting up later" (Book 2, Ch48 L61). Choices can reflect need: the team lets Jason and Henrietta split an elemental's loot because each has expensive summoning rituals to pay for (Book 3, Ch14 L79). Rufus gives spare summoning materials to Jason when dividing loot (Book 2, Ch63 L111).

**Retirement and longevity.** Silver-rank arena professionals "keep going until silver-rank longevity is no longer enough, at which point they retire and make their way to gold for the extended life span" (Book 2, Ch73 L14). Gary retires after Book 3 to become a full-time weaponsmith (Book 3, Ch69 L895). Silver-rankers in low-magic Greenstone are "semi-retired at best" (Book 1, Ch61 L32).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Guilds.** Guilds are private organisations of adventurers (Book 1, Ch38 L52). During the Book 7 surge, in a city like Livaros "about three in ten adventurers are in a guild. One in ten is in what's considered a high-end guild... Yet guilds are given sixty percent of the quotas to fill" (Book 7, Ch12 L23). The Society handles guilds' quotas and leaves them to manage on their own (Book 7, Ch38 L7).
- **Surge quotas.** During a surge every adventurer has an action quota; contracts over and above it earn contribution points, tallied on weekly and overall leaderboards with rewards (Book 7, Ch12 L15). Portal users earn more points because of the demand for transport (Book 7, Ch20 L23).
- **Rule of thumb.** Rufus's rule of thumb is to handle monsters one rank up only with a good match-up (Book 2, Ch47 L59).
- **Arena sport.** Iron-rank monster-hunt events judge teams on performance against identical monsters (Book 2, Ch73 L37).
- **Non-adventurers.** Many portal workers "aren't even adventurers and do storage space transport for a living" (Book 7, Ch20 L23).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Rick Geller's team**, with front-liners, damage dealers and a healer (Book 1, Ch66 L60).
- **Jason's first contract** logged at the jobs hall desk (Book 1, Ch64 L5).
- **Team Work Saw**, whose defender Henry holds a gold-rank converted at the Book 8 Purity attack (Book 8, Ch12 L5).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **The badge is authority.** It is not; the contract carries it (Book 1, Ch62 L64).
- **Higher stars mean more power.** Stars measure judgement, not power (Book 1, Ch62 L70).
- **Adventuring is killing for sport.** Rufus refuses to work with those who relish it (Book 1, Ch19 L38).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 1:** Jason's one-star iron badge is the starting point (Book 1, Ch62 L66); Greenstone's jobs hall changes with a new director (Book 1, Ch63 L77).
- **Level 2:** In the Book 7 surge, orders and quotas replace ordinary contracts, and guilds carry most of the load (Book 7, Ch12 L15, L23).

## Afflictions, Boons and Damage

### 1. Summary

An affliction is a condition that harms its target for a time; a boon is a condition that helps. Both are named in brackets in System messages, carry tags (poison, disease, curse, holy, unholy, magic and others) and can stack. Defence against afflictions is a game of resisting, cleansing and negating: a cleanse removes an affliction, resistance reduces the chance or strength of one landing, and some afflictions are built to defeat both. In this world a character who understands which tool beats which condition has a large tactical advantage, and Jason's power set is built around that interplay.

### 2. How it works

**Naming and tags.** Afflictions and boons appear in brackets with tags: "[Leech Toxin] (affliction, poison, blood, stacking)" (Book 1, Ch29 L15); "[Mark of Sin] (affliction, holy)" (Book 1, Ch87 L99); "[Resistant] (boon, holy)" (Book 12, Ch67 L303). A tag may be a type of harm (poison, disease, curse, wounding), a moral colour (holy or unholy) or the nature of the effect (magic, drain, stacking).

**Stacking.** Many conditions stack, each "instance" adding to the effect, as for Vulnerable: "Additional instances have a cumulative effect" (Book 1, Ch88 L132). Some stacks decay, like Penance, "Stacks drop off over time" (Book 12, Ch67 L281).

**Resistance.** Resistance is a chance and strength modifier. Jason's Sin Eater increases his own resistance to afflictions and gives him Resistant each time he resists or cleanses one (Book 1, Ch28 L93). His Hegemony aura raises allies' resistance and lowers enemies', and lowers it further for each instance of Sin (Book 1, Ch40 L41). In battle only a fraction land: "as many as one in three afflictions were taking hold" against a flesh monster in Book 2 (Book 2, Ch52 L51), and "almost half" against a lizard after resistance-lowering stacks (Book 3, Ch8 L76).

**Cleansing.** A cleanse removes afflictions. Jason's Feast of Absolution removes "curses, diseases, poisons and unholy afflictions", plus holy afflictions if the target is an ally, from a target other than himself, and it "circumvents all effects that prevent cleansing" (Book 1, Ch34 L40); a few chapters later, at Iron 1 (19%), the same spell removes holy and unholy afflictions from an ally or an enemy and "circumvents any resistance or immunity to cleanse effects" (Book 1, Ch39 L70-71). Cleansing triggers other abilities: "Cleansing afflictions has triggered [Sin Eater]" (Book 1, Ch34 L47). A cleansing aura, such as Cleansing Breeze, adds resistance to curses, diseases, magic afflictions, poisons and unholy afflictions and negates poisons in the air; it is a holy effect (Book 2, Ch9 L119).

**Cleanse conditions.** Many afflictions are written to resist cleansing: Mark of Sin "cannot be cleansed while target retains any instances of Sin or Legacy of Sin" (Book 1, Ch87 L99). A curse can protect another: a patient arrives with two curses, one adding poison to the other, and "the curse that kept making more of the other two couldn't be cleansed until the other curse was cleansed" (Book 1, Ch103 L130).

**Negating immunity.** Some afflictions remove an immunity: Weakness of the Flesh "negates immunities to disease and necrotic damage" and that "includes intrinsic immunities, such as from not having a biology or corporeal form" (Book 5, Ch31 L181). Blood From a Stone does the same for blood and poison, so "entities without blood can bleed" (Book 5, Ch31 L176), and Mortality does it for curses, even for the not alive (Book 5, Ch31 L179). Inevitable Demise, an aura Knowledge tried to give him, treated "any affliction immunities, including inherent immunities, as complete resistance" (Book 2, Ch13 L69).

**Healing interaction.** Bleeding "soaks up healing, negating its effect" and is removed only after absorbing enough; Leech Toxin reapplies it when negated, "leaving any healing stopped cold" (Book 1, Ch29 L15-16). Weight of Sin deals transcendent damage to anyone subjected to a holy boon, recovery or cleanse effect (Book 12, Ch67 L289); Sanction reduces healing (Book 12, Ch67 L339).

**Holy and unholy.** Effects carry a holy or unholy tag, and some effects cannot touch them. Hendren's ongoing cleansing powers "could not eliminate holy effects", and he had only one power that could (Book 3, Ch59 L38). Another ability grants resistance to curses, magic and unholy afflictions, and bars unholy boons (Book 3, Ch67 L93). Hegemony is "both a holy and unholy ability at the same time", which fascinates Jason (Book 1, Ch40 L42).

### 3. Damage types

- **Physical and elemental.** Normal cutting, piercing, fire and similar damage. Rank gives damage reduction against lower-rank sources (Book 1, Ch21 L67).
- **Necrotic.** The damage type of rot, drains and death magic. Sin, Creeping Death and many of Jason's afflictions raise or deal it (Book 12, Ch67 L215, L278).
- **Disruptive force and resonating force.** Two force types for special cases. Spell Breaker adds disruptive-force damage, "highly effective against magical defences and incorporeal entities" (Book 1, Ch56 L54); Stone Cutter adds resonating-force damage, "highly effective against physical defences" (Book 1, Ch56 L53). A defensive gift can reduce disruptive-force damage by a large amount (Book 2, Ch7 L162). An unarmed ability adds resonating-force damage and negates damage from actively intercepted attacks (Book 2, Ch8 L44). Gary's hammer for fighting constructs delivers "a resonating-force explosion" with each hit (Book 7, Ch31 L10).
- **Transcendent damage.** "Transcendent damage ignores all forms of physical and magical defence, damage reduction and resistances" (Book 1, Ch99 L169). Vincent is astonished at seeing an iron-rank ability deal it (Book 1, Ch99 L166). Jason's Castigate at iron already deals "slight transcendent damage" (Book 1, Ch87 L97), and execute effects like Verdict scale it with injury (Book 12, Ch67 L335).

### 4. Examples from the books

Definitions from the Book 12 appendix, as of gold rank (Book 12, Ch67 L349-387):

| Condition | Type | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Bleeding | affliction, wounding | Ongoing bleed damage; absorbs healing; cannot be cleansed but removed after absorbing enough healing |
| Leech Toxin | affliction, poison | Reapplies Bleeding when negated |
| Creeping Death | affliction, disease | Ongoing necrotic damage; stacking |
| Rigor Mortis | affliction, unholy | Penalty to Speed and Recovery; adding to the stack inflicts necrotic damage |
| Weakness of the Flesh | affliction, magic | Negates immunities to disease and necrotic damage |
| Sin | affliction, curse | Necrotic damage taken increased; stacking |
| Mark of Sin | affliction, holy | Turns the target's aura into a beacon; cannot be cleansed while Sin or Legacy of Sin remain |
| Weight of Sin | affliction, holy | Transcendent damage if subjected to a holy boon, recovery or cleanse |
| Penance | affliction, holy | Ongoing transcendent damage; stacks drop off over time |
| Legacy of Sin | affliction, holy | Execute abilities have a greater effect on the target |
| Vulnerable | affliction, unholy | Resistances reduced; stacking |
| Resistant | boon, holy | Resistances increased; stacking |
| Integrity | boon | Ongoing life force and mana recovery; stacking |
| Blood Frenzy | boon, unholy | Bonus to Speed and Recovery |
| Harbinger of Doom | affliction, unholy | The target conjures butterflies that spread all its afflictions to other enemies |

(The full alphabetised list is at Book 12, Ch67 L349-387.)

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Healing beats damage.** Bleeding soaks up healing and Leech Toxin reapplies it (Book 1, Ch29 L16).
- **Cleansing is always available.** Afflictions like Mark of Sin and Persecution are written to block it (Book 1, Ch87 L99; Book 12, Ch67 L317).
- **Immunity is permanent.** Weakness of the Flesh, Blood From a Stone and Mortality cancel even intrinsic immunities (Book 5, Ch31 L176-181).
- **Rank is a wall.** Resistance and damage reduction from rank can be bypassed by transcendent damage (Book 1, Ch99 L169).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 1:** Early iron-rank afflictions are described plainly, like Vulnerable's "All resistances are reduced" (Book 1, Ch88 L132). Later versions gain extra clauses, such as the cleanse restriction and the intrinsic-immunity text (Book 5, Ch31 L176-181).
- **Level 2:** A speaker in Book 13 says Bussinger's Tribulation Lightning purges her own afflictions at the cost of harming her (Book 13, Ch980 L93).
- **Level 3:** By the end of Book 12 Jason's ability set is built around holy-tagged transcendent effects, such as Penance, Weight of Sin and Sanction (Book 12, Ch67 L281, L289, L339).

## Alchemy, Artifice and Magical Materials

### 1. Summary

Alongside essences and stones the world has a layer of working magic that does not need an essence: quintessence gems, spirit coins, potions, ointments, enchanted tools and growth items that rise in rank. This file describes what these materials are and how they are used. It does not list individual named items; those are in `09_Items_and_Artefacts/`.

### 2. How it works

**Quintessence.** Quintessence is "kind of like chunks of essence" and "gets used a lot more" than essences: "Ritual magic, alchemy, weapon forging" (Book 1, Ch19 L47-52). It appears as small gems named for their theme: dark quintessence is "small black gems" (Book 1, Ch7 L68). Water quintessence forms when magic-rich water from an astral space reaches the sea and condenses "huge quantities of magically-imbued water into a little crystal" (Book 1, Ch24 L40). Villages along the coast live by finding it (Book 1, Ch24 L48). Gary says he goes "through quintessence by the pile" for weapons and armour (Book 1, Ch19 L53). A quintessence gem can be used directly in an item: a bracelet "keeps the wearer cool and refreshed" with a water gem, and a gem refills its energy (Book 1, Ch31 L27-28; Book 1, Ch68 L114). A quintessence pile cannot be made into an essence (Book 1, Ch19 L48-50).

**Spirit coins.** A spirit coin is a crystal in the colour of a rank; the iron-rank coin "had the metal-grey colour of iron but was actually made of crystal" (Book 1, Ch22 L77). Eaten, it "dissolved with an intense fizzing sensation... tangy and energetic" and restores power (Book 1, Ch22 L77). Ranked people "sustain themselves on spirit coins and go without food entirely" (Book 3, Ch1 L5). A coin an hour or so can replenish reserves, with no food for a day or more (Book 3, Ch14 L18), and captors give an unconscious captive a coin to eat to keep him healthy (Book 3, Ch17 L26). Coins are grown on farms, where "special moulds cause magic to crystallise", and changes in ambient magic can ruin whole batches (Book 1, Ch80 L21, L43). A vehicle runs on coins fed into a slot (Book 1, Ch80 L104). The currency role is in `Economy_and_Money.md`; the exchange rates are "a full hundred lesser coins to one iron-rank coin, after which denominations went up in multiples of ten" (Book 1, Ch36 L72).

**Spirit coins and rank.** Eating a coin of one's own rank, or ten of one rank lower, restores recovery in low-magic zones (Book 12, Ch27 L19). A coin can briefly boost attributes to offset rank disparity, but it "will leave you weaker once the strength fades" (Book 1, Ch19 L43).

**Potions.** A recovery potion restores health, stamina and mana; "until the remnant magic fully dissipates, consuming further health, stamina or mana potions will result in toxic side-effects" (Book 1, Ch6 L53-54). Potions come in ranks: Jason's first is a bronze-rank, rare Recovery Potion (Book 1, Ch6 L46). Healers' patients are limited by cost: both ritual magic and alchemy have ways to heal, "but the cost and expertise required placed both out of the reach for most people" (Book 1, Ch35 L22).

**Alchemy.** Alchemy is brewing potions and elixirs. Jory's "true calling was alchemy", and his research is to make products cheaper and simpler: "If I can make alchemical products affordable to everyone, not only can it help a huge number of people, but it will open up huge new markets" (Book 1, Ch35 L10, L21). Alchemy and weapon forging use quintessence (Book 1, Ch19 L52). Alchemists belong to the Alchemy Association, which Jory joins alongside the Adventure Society (Book 1, Ch36 L28; Book 1, Ch38 L52). Alchemy sits beside medicine as an everyday tool: the shaving cream Jason mentions came from "an alchemist friend" (Book 1, Ch59 L8).

**Artifice.** Artifice makes magical items and devices. Farrah and Clive see "interdisciplinary crossover" between formations and artifice (Book 4, Ch25 L20). Clive mentions "some rather sophisticated artifice" used to tamper with carriages (Book 1, Ch82 L57). The Artifice Association sells good kitchen devices such as stand mixers (Book 1, Ch91 L58). Skilled people mix disciplines: a friend of Clive's has "solid ritual magic, a bit of artifice" and upgraded a mirage chamber (Book 2, Ch23 L72).

**Crafting.** Monster materials are crafting inputs: snakeskin and dark quintessence are crafting materials (Book 1, Ch7 L68). Gary makes weapons and armour (Book 1, Ch19 L53). Magic craftspeople range from leatherworkers and weapon-smiths to engravers and alchemists (Book 2, Ch42 L86).

**Growth items.** A growth item gains forms and powers as its rank rises when fed the right materials. Emir's cloud palace "is a growth item" (Book 2, Ch40 L61). Jason's cloud flask is "iron rank [growth], legendary", bound to him, and its upgrade to bronze needs 1000 bronze air quintessence, 1000 bronze water quintessence, 200 bronze dimension quintessence and 10,000 bronze spirit coins (Book 2, Ch74 L40-50). Legendary growth weapons come in matched sets (Book 2, Ch51 L98; Book 2, Ch53 L70).

**Soul-bound items.** A soul-bound growth item "cannot be used by anyone else" and "tends to take on" its owner's properties as it advances; Clive says that "if you meet someone who seems like a good person but has a hideous and twisted soul-bound item, stay clear" (Book 2, Ch74 L41, L72-74). Emir's cloud palace, "outrageously grandiose, yet welcoming and beautiful", reflects him (Book 2, Ch74 L74). Soul-bound items "are rare, even compared to other growth items", and "The advancement requirements are usually quite prohibitive" (Book 2, Ch74 L45).

**Communication.** Long-distance speech runs through the Magic Society's water link chambers: "Communicating through watery clones was the most accessible form of long-distance communication and a major use for the magical stone that Greenstone exported" (Book 6, Ch47 L843). The people on the other end appear as water clones "indistinguishable from her actual parents to the eye", although magical senses show them to be projections (Book 7, Ch40 L54). In a surge the Adventure Society takes over the links and cancels bookings (Book 6, Ch47 L922; Book 7, Ch28 L106). A carried device like "a water link chamber you carry around in your pocket" is mentioned as a communication network item (Book 7, Ch10 L38).

**Other tools.** Crystal wash is an odourless cleaner that "clears off everything"; its absence is a running problem (Book 1, Ch32 L57). Recording crystals capture images, messages and fights (Book 1, Ch54 L52; Book 1, Ch61 L129). Dimensional storage includes bags (Book 1, Ch17 L21); Jason's inventory has forty spaces, with stacking (Book 1, Ch61 L40).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Low-magic zones.** Coin farms work only where magic is stable: "No activity, no life. Very stable ambient magic" (Book 1, Ch80 L21).
- **Divine supply.** A church can supply healing essences and stones (Book 1, Ch35 L23).
- **Prices.** Coins bought in bulk go through brokers; an adventurer can be paid in coins up to an awakening stone for a contract (Book 1, Ch64 L12).
- **Hydra whip and other loot.** Monster-part weapons keep some properties: a hydra whip "had the hydra's property of regeneration" (Book 5, Ch1 L49).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Bracelet with water quintessence** (Book 1, Ch31 L27).
- **Skimmer powered by coins** (Book 1, Ch80 L104).
- **Cloud palace and cloud flask** (Book 2, Ch40 L61; Book 2, Ch74 L40-50).
- **Jory's clinic**, an alchemy lab and medical clinic in one building (Book 1, Ch35 L63).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Quintessence can replace essences.** It cannot (Book 1, Ch19 L48-50).
- **Healing potions are always safe to chain.** They cause toxic side effects until the remnant magic dissipates (Book 1, Ch6 L54).
- **Soul-bound items are interchangeable.** They are bound and reflect the owner (Book 2, Ch74 L41, L72).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 1:** Greenstone's market for essences and stones fell to an all-time low after the astral space was plundered (Book 3, Ch1 L100).
- **Level 2:** Cloud constructs advance with Jason's rank (see `09_Items_and_Artefacts/Cloud_Constructs_and_Palaces.md`).
- **Level 3:** In Book 12 Travis offers to build weapons for the cloud flask, saying he has "done weapons for your cloud flask before, but that was years ago" (Book 12, Ch23 L25).

### 7. Item types and where they are described

Each item type in `09_Items_and_Artefacts/` is explained here in one line and then in its own file. Rows from later books are under level tags.

| Dimensional bags and storage | Bags have a rank and add slots to an inventory in proportion to it (Book 1, Ch76 L43, L49); portal abilities open only to places the user has visited (Book 1, Ch113 L58) | `../09_Items_and_Artefacts/Dimensional_Storage_and_Portals.md`; see also Unusual_and_Unique_Magic.md |

## Astral Spaces, Transformation Zones and Surges

### 1. Summary

Three kinds of event reshape territory in the series. Astral spaces are pocket worlds attached to a physical world through apertures. Proto-astral spaces are short-lived, unstable versions of them that Earth suffers from. Transformation zones are sealed events that rewrite a place and the people in it. Monster surges are periodic increases in monster numbers across a world. All four are driven by the same source: raw magic leaking through from the astral.

### 2. How it works

**Astral spaces.** Farrah: "Astral spaces are pretty common, but normally they're sealed off and you need magic to track one down and break in. Being naturally open like this is rare, especially with so many apertures" (Book 1, Ch24 L38). Greenstone's river comes out of a large aperture (Book 1, Ch24 L38). An aperture connects a place on the physical world to the astral space; an astral space may have many apertures, and the mayor of one town notes theirs is "only one of many places with an aperture leading to that astral space" (Book 1, Ch31 L4). An astral space can be a rainforest island chain, with a sun that "just moving around on a circuit in the sky" and no night (Book 1, Ch104 L61). It can be far smaller than the world it is attached to: "the astral space is only a fraction of the size of the world it's attached to" (Book 1, Ch111 L24). Expeditions enter through the aperture, making camp, searching in teams and retreating through it for triage (Book 1, Ch104 L60-61; Book 1, Ch111 L28).

**Why they are attached.** Clive: "Astral spaces form attached to worlds, without which they immediately break down. Without a real world to anchor them, they cannot exist. But if an astral space is given the ability to sustain itself, even for just a brief period, the Builder can take it and anchor it to the world the Builder is creating from stolen parts" (Book 2, Ch21 L110). The Builder's process preserved the astral space at the cost of catastrophic destruction to the physical reality (Book 2, Ch21 L114).

**Surges.** "Every ten years there's a massive increase in the spawn rate of monsters. All across the world, all at the same time. Whole villages evacuate to fortified towns" (Book 1, Ch31 L71). The last one was eleven years earlier; "it's never exactly ten years. It's been as little as eight or as many as thirteen. The last few have all come pretty late" (Book 1, Ch31 L73-74). Most of the delta's population "comes into the city during monster surges" (Book 1, Ch35 L31). The Book 7 surge is "some five years overdue, during which time monster activity had gradually increased. Once the surge proper began, it was expected to be more brutal and last longer than any in history" (Book 7, Ch1 L56). During a surge adventurers earn contribution points instead of direct payment, and guilds use it to scout talent (Book 7, Ch38 L6).

**Proto-astral spaces (Earth).** A proto-astral space is "unstable dimensional pockets attached to the world" (Book 4, Ch37 L63). Their usual duration is "forty-three hours"; an anomalous one in Book 4 lasted "less than a second" and was the size and shape of a person, though its rated strength still registered above five (Book 4, Ch5 L127). The aperture to one "wasn't visible to the naked eye, although magical senses made it extremely easy to see. It was a more tenuous bridge across dimensional boundaries than a normal aperture and appeared... as if it might collapse at any moment" (Book 4, Ch40 L33). Entering one is announced by a System message: "The ambient magical saturation has increased. Your recovery rates will remain at normal levels without spirit coin consumption" (Book 4, Ch39 L55). Spirit coins cannot be formed in them: "Earth doesn't have the magic and coin formation takes months, so you can't do it in the proto-astral spaces" (Book 4, Ch37 L79).

**Transformation zones (Earth).** In the Russian city of Kostroma the whole city "was sealed off in a dome", actually a sphere that extended underground; "forty-three hours after the sphere moved into place, it vanished, revealing a city vastly changed" (Book 5, Ch44 L48). The changes remake the area "in the image of worlds used as patterns when the original Builder created this universe" (Book 5, Ch44 L52). Buildings look weathered with years of age (Book 5, Ch44 L51). On Earth many normal-ranked people were transformed into other races in accordance with the zone they were in, humans becoming "leonids, celestines and other races native to neither Earth nor Pallimustus" (Book 11, Ch1 L36).

**Zones as spaces to be claimed.** A transformation zone that Jason enters contains a genesis space, which his System names: "You have established a spirit domain. Expanding your spirit domain will define and stabilise unstable genesis space but trigger anomalous reactions from genesis space outside the spirit domain" (Book 6, Ch2 L15). Territories are claimed by defeating anomalies and then a final one: "You have overtaken a genesis space territory and purged all anomalous elements" (Book 6, Ch5 L32). See `Monsters.md` for the anomalies.

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Why zones happen on Earth.** "Transformation zones on Earth were the result of the World-Phoenix intervening in eons past, to prevent Earth from breaking under the influence of magic." Pallimustus has no such need, so the dimensional rupture there required "another hand to trigger the transformation zone" (Book 11, Ch1 L17).
- **Jason's three zones.** In the first he "had broken into a zone already in place" and it forcibly evolved an outworlder power into Spiritual Domain; in the second he could reshape it from the start and raised the base level of magic on Earth, so that "magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world"; the third is on Pallimustus (Book 11, Ch1 L15-17).
- **The special zone.** The System describes the Book 11 zone: "This special transformation zone must be unified to restore stability, reintegrate it with physical reality and re-establish an astral space", unified by "claiming all non-central territories" (Book 11, Ch1 L38-39). Each territory is claimed by eliminating a final anomaly, and if several are present it "must be ceded to one individual through conflict or forfeit" (Book 11, Ch1 L40).
- **Nitra.** A transformation zone at Nitra in Slovakia forms as a "glimmering dome several kilometres across" that stays closed for days (Book 5, Ch68 L68). The Chinese forces under Li Li Mei claim a site around it (Book 6, Ch5 L48).
- **Low-magic zones.** In a low-magic area, "consuming a spirit coin of your rank or ten spirit coins of one rank lower will restore your recovery rates to normal for eight hours" (Book 12, Ch27 L19).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **The desert's water-source astral space** in Book 1, an island-chain rainforest (Book 1, Ch104 L60-61); more in `06_Places/Astral_Spaces/`.
- **Kostroma** in Book 5, the first transformation zone, 43 hours long (Book 5, Ch44 L48).
- **Bankstown, Sydney**, a zone with lava streams (Book 5, Ch57 L11).
- **Nitra**, a Book 5 to 6 dome (Book 5, Ch68 L68).
- **The Cardinas zone** in Book 11 (Book 11, Ch1 L38-42).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Astral spaces are the same as other worlds.** They are small pockets attached to a world (Book 1, Ch111 L24).
- **Proto-astral spaces last forever.** They last about forty-three hours (Book 4, Ch5 L127).
- **A surge is exactly ten years.** It ranges from eight to thirteen (Book 1, Ch31 L74).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 2:** The first zones on Earth are 43 hours long and remake places in the pattern of other worlds (Book 5, Ch44 L48-52).
- **Level 3:** After Jason's second zone, "The base level of magic had risen; magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world. He had begun a new age of magic, where monsters and essences manifested directly in the world" (Book 11, Ch1 L16).

## Auras

### 1. Summary

An aura is the projection of a ranked person's soul. It grows with rank, is read by other ranked people as a sense of danger, strength and mood, and is how adventurers judge each other before words are spoken. Controlling the aura is a skill with three basic parts: projecting it, restraining it and suppressing other people's. Auras can be hidden, masked, aimed at normal people to intimidate them, and, at silver rank, begin to lift the body off the ground.

### 2. How it works

**Aura sense.** A new iron-ranker gains the ability to sense auras (Book 1, Ch21 L69). Jason's first impression of other ranked people is a feeling of danger, which Rufus explains is "our auras. Now that you're iron rank, you can sense them", and which gets more reliable as he learns to tell "a monster from an essence user from a regular person" (Book 1, Ch22 L31-33). The sense is "not completely reliable" because "some monsters can hide their auras. People can too, if they have an aura power" (Book 1, Ch22 L35). Ordinary people are "faint, barely detectable, while those with essences were much clearer"; a village normally has one or two with an essence, and a full-set iron-ranker "radiated out like a beacon" (Book 1, Ch35 L50).

**The three controls.** Farrah teaches Jason to control his aura "in three ways": "projecting your aura and restraining it", then "using your aura to suppress the auras of other people", which is "harder than the others", to be left alone "until you reach a certain level of proficiency" (Book 1, Ch40 L64-70). Projection is "pushing your aura out to affect people"; restraining is "drawing it in, whether to hide it, or just not be rude" (Book 1, Ch40 L66). Everyone projects until they learn not to: "It's what makes people with no aura control easy to read" (Book 1, Ch40 L74). Later the text repeats that "all aura control techniques were variations or extensions of those three" (Book 4, Ch74 L10).

**Why it matters.** Anyone with a perception power will eventually see auras clearly, so an uncontrolled aura reads like signs, including location and emotions, and "know when you lie" (Book 1, Ch40 L50). The skill with which an aura is controlled "is how adventurers make their first impressions on one another. If you can't do it properly, people won't take you seriously. Excellent aura manipulation marks you as an adventurer of training and distinction" (Book 1, Ch40 L80). Farrah calls the lack of an aura ability a serious gap: "anyone who hits bronze rank and can't manage their aura is a second-rate adventurer" (Book 1, Ch39 L152).

**A gold-ranker's aura.** At gold an uncontrolled aura is dangerous to normal people: "If you reach gold rank and can't control your aura properly, you can hurt normal people just by going near them" (Book 1, Ch40 L44). Such people are required to wear a suppressor: Farrah once saw "a gold ranker who forgot to put on an aura suppressor before going to a market. People were passed out, bleeding out their ears" (Book 1, Ch40 L46-48).

**Aura weapons.** Control can be turned on normal people. Jason, in Book 4, slowly unleashes his aura in a room: "Normal humans couldn't detect auras unless they were projected in a specific way. It was a simple use of basic projection control... a tool that essence users employed to intimidate normals" (Book 4, Ch7 L92). Higher-rank auras can be pointed at lower-rank ones: a bronze-rank woman suppresses Jason's with her own, which is "the very height of rudeness" (Book 1, Ch65 L91). A silver-ranker's weight can be felt without being a suppressing force (Book 1, Ch101 L16).

**Blending in.** A gold-ranker can use aura control to pass through a crowd unnoticed, and a high-end silver can do the same (Book 4, Ch74 L6). The technique blends projection and retraction to merge the aura into the ambient magic, with delicate suppression to blunt others' aura senses (Book 4, Ch74 L12-13). Normal people "were aura blind unless someone with aura control didn't want them to be" (Book 4, Ch74 L14). Jason's inspirations are Farrah's orthodox teaching, his own experience, Vermillion's use of aura on normals, the Mirror King's aura that "had felt like a part of the world around it", and Shade's masking (Book 4, Ch73 L95-100).

**Masks and suppressors.** Magic items hide or damp an aura. Farrah mentions aura suppressors (Book 1, Ch40 L46); a thief's methods include "aura masking" (Book 1, Ch100 L85); an aura mask is breached by using essence abilities or failing to keep a strong aura suppressed (Book 1, Ch102 L93); aura masking will not work against a tracking effect on the aura (Book 1, Ch103 L16). A suppression collar can negate a target's powers; Jason is able to "completely negate the effects of an iron-rank suppression collar" after practice, and holds off a bronze one for a few moments (Book 3, Ch24 L30).

**Silver and levitation.** "Levitation, Jason had discovered, was a perk of reaching silver-rank. It was an intrinsic property of a silver-rank soul, allowing the aura it projected to physically affect the environment" (Book 4, Ch73 L92). Farrah warns that it is "not even a practical ability. It requires intense concentration, has minimal effect, and is easy to disrupt with just some basic aura suppression" (Book 4, Ch73 L93). At silver it was "mostly just a power to levitate that helped their increasingly heavy bodies walk on weaker surfaces or even water" (Book 6, Ch14 L6).

**Aura signatures.** An aura has a signature that places can record: Emir's cloud palace stores Jason's signature in its registry (Book 2, Ch24 L13) and cannot let him in when it changes (Book 2, Ch66 L8). A soul crest carries a unique imprint on the aura that stays the same even when the aura changes, "impossible to track or falsify through even the strongest magic" (Book 2, Ch70 L37).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Aura powers.** Some abilities are auras (Hegemony, Cleansing Breeze), which are a different thing from the aura itself: they are passive effects projected around the user (Book 1, Ch40 L37-41; Book 2, Ch9 L115-119). A person can have only one (see `Awakening_Stones.md`).
- **Physical force.** Most aura abilities cannot move objects. "An aura power common to the force confluence famously allowed auras to move things physically", and Jason's cannot (Book 8, Ch60 L5).
- **Perception and silver.** Farrah says her perception power does not improve her aura sense until silver rank (Book 1, Ch40 L52).
- **Monsters.** "Higher-rank monsters can" manipulate their auras; at low ranks the most to expect is "a few stealthy monsters that restrain their auras to hide better" (Book 1, Ch40 L76).
- **Transcendent echo.** Soul damage from gods can change an aura: after multiple divine presences press on him, Jason's "aura has been damaged by the direct, concerted focus of multiple transcendent-level entities", the recovery refines it, and it now carries "an echo of transcendent power" (Book 2, Ch65 L86-87).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **Titles from soul scars** (full list in Titles_and_Blessings.md). Jason's Interface uses titles to translate soul scars into game terms (Book 4, Ch2 L26). Resolute raises resistance to suppression from higher-ranked auras (Book 3, Ch14 L82); Indomitable enhances resistance and "ignores rank disparity", and adds a resistance bonus to allies in his aura (Book 4, Ch2 L23-24); Spirit Warrior increases both suppressive force and resistance, lets him resist other magical suppression, and lets him "attack their soul directly" after fully suppressing their aura (Book 3, Ch21 L151-152); Godless Prophet records the refinement after gods press on him (Book 2, Ch65 L85-86). Each changes his aura signature (Book 3, Ch14 L83; Book 3, Ch21 L153).
- **Rank disparity.** Aura strength is "the inherently superior strength of higher-rank auras", which some of Jason's titles do not cancel (Book 3, Ch21 L110).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Auras are just a feeling.** They can be used as weapons and as disguise.
- **Normals cannot feel them.** Normals can sense strong, directed auras on some level but are "aura blind" unless the wielder allows it (Book 4, Ch74 L14).
- **Suppressing an aura is simple.** Farrah calls it the hardest of the three controls (Book 1, Ch40 L70).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 1:** In Book 3 Jason refines his suppression until he can hold off an iron-rank collar entirely (Book 3, Ch24 L30).
- **Level 2:** After his Book 4 return to Earth, Jason rebuilds his aura control from scratch to use on normal people with "art and finesse" (Book 4, Ch72 L38).
- **Level 3:** The Numen gift in Book 12 makes his avatar immune to rank suppression and lets him negate aura abilities by fully suppressing the user's aura (Book 12, Ch67 L196).

## Awakening Stones

### 1. Summary

An awakening stone is a consumable crystal that awakens one essence ability the user has not yet awakened. It is the third kind of non-living magic Rufus lists, after essences and quintessence (Book 1, Ch19 L56). The stone does not choose the ability; it steers toward a theme, and what comes out depends mostly on the essences the user holds. Stones are how a new essence user fills out the twenty abilities that a full set carries, and they are bought, auctioned, given as rewards and kept as family wealth.

### 2. How it works

**What a stone does.** Each stone's description says the same thing: "Awakens an essence ability", with the requirement "Unawakened essence ability" (Book 1, Ch22 L99-102). Jason is shown a count of how many abilities he still has to awaken, such as "You have 10 unawakened essence abilities" (Book 1, Ch22 L132). Stones can also be used in other kinds of magic: "sometimes awakening stones get used as part of very powerful rituals" (Book 1, Ch22 L45), as the cult did with its feast stones in the sacrifice chamber (Book 1, Ch19 L57-58).

**What decides the ability.** Farrah: "the biggest determinate of what ability you get is the essence it comes from" (Book 1, Ch19 L67). A stone has a theme, and the theme sets the range of powers: a feast stone is "related to the concept of a feast, but that can manifest in any of hundreds of powers" (Book 1, Ch19 L63), which Farrah corrects to "thousands" (Book 1, Ch19 L64). The abilities a person has already, and the essences they have used, steer the stone. This is why Farrah and Rufus advise taking every essence before using stones: otherwise "your abilities will lack focus" (Book 1, Ch21 L36-37).

**Rarity and specificity.** "The more rare an awakening stone is, the more specific the powers" (Book 1, Ch19 L64). A common stone "can give you any ability the rarest could", it just draws from a larger pool; "rare stones don't give out better abilities, just more specific ones" (Book 1, Ch19 L66). The stones people seek are those with a desirable specialty, and "stones with desirable specialties tend to be the most expensive" (Book 1, Ch22 L104). A mid-rarity stone is "almost always a useful utility power" (Book 1, Ch22 L110). A high-rarity stone is "more specialised" (Book 1, Ch39 L147-148) and restricts the possible abilities to just one or two types (Book 2, Ch57 L36).

**Grading.** The Magic Society grades stones on a scale of one to five stars "based on how frequently they are known to appear world-wide", working with brokers and the Adventure Society; Jason's ability also sorts them into five stages of rarity: common (one star), uncommon (two stars), up to epic (four stars, "the second highest rarity") and legendary (Book 2, Ch9 L9, L17). In the Adventure Society's wording, a stone of the apocalypse is "unranked, legendary" (Book 1, Ch22 L128) and a stone of omens "unranked, epic" (Book 1, Ch39 L137).

**Using one.** The stone melts into the user's hand or arm and sinks in without fanfare (Book 1, Ch22 L71, L112, L152), and Jason's system confirms "You have awakened the blood essence ability [Leech Bite]" (Book 1, Ch22 L72). Most people need a ritual for each stone, and a person with a whole row "going through a half-dozen rituals would take hours" (Book 1, Ch22 L38-42). Clive's essence ability, Enact Ritual, makes drawing and performing the circles more convenient (Book 2, Ch6 L43). Clive draws the circle and completes the ritual when a team member uses an uncommon stone of preparation (Book 2, Ch66 L66).

**Hunger afterwards.** A stone of the feast leaves Jason ravenous: "I think the stone of the feast made it worse" (Book 1, Ch22 L75). The cure is a spirit coin (Book 1, Ch22 L76-77).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Themes by name.** Stones are named for a theme or concept. The text names many: feast, adventure, apocalypse, omens, wrath, absolution, judgement, hand, foot, eyes, sky, purgation, preparation, rebirth, karma, avatar, celestials, moment, surge, champion, the stars, the Reaper, magus, fish, rain, ruin, focus, defiance and more. Jason's first stone is the "Awakening Stone of the Stars" (Book 1, Ch4 L40). A shopping list includes awakening stones of the eyes, the hand and the foot (Book 2, Ch5 L105-107). Neil and Jason select awakening stones of the avatar, and Humphrey selects an awakening stone of rebirth (Book 2, Ch63 L25). One speaker mentions an awakening stone of defiance (Book 9, Ch78 L129).
- **Tendencies of a theme.** The text gives these: eyes "a good shot at giving a perception power" (Book 2, Ch5 L105); hand awakens empty-hand abilities and attacks; foot, unarmed attacks and movement abilities (Book 2, Ch5 L108-110); sky, a very good chance of a flight power, though "it could just as easily give you a special attack effective against enemies in the air" (Book 2, Ch9 L29, L38); purgation, "almost certainly some kind of cleansing ability" (Book 2, Ch9 L47); magus, "a common awakening stone, especially with humans... almost guaranteed a spell, which humans rarely awakened, with an outside chance of a coveted summoning or familiar power" (Book 1, Ch87 L91); omens, a hope for an aura power (Book 1, Ch39 L150).
- **Human aptitude.** Humans have an aptitude for special attacks and rarely awaken spells without a magus stone (Book 1, Ch87 L91).
- **One aura only.** A person can have just one aura ability; the stone that would give a second does not work (Book 2, Ch13 L70). A tablet can remove an existing aura ability (Book 2, Ch13 L76-78).
- **Divine stones.** Gods craft stones for a specific outcome. Knowledge sends Jason two: a Divine Awakening Stone of Inevitability, to bestow an aura power (Book 2, Ch13 L60-62; the ability is [Inescapable Doom] in one line and [Inevitable Demise] in another, Book 2, Ch13 L62, L66), and a Divine Awakening Stone of Persistence, to bestow a specific spell (Book 2, Ch13 L83-85), with a Soul-Purgation Tablet to make room (Book 2, Ch13 L71-76). Jason shuts the case, calling it "a shiny red apple" and a poison pill (Book 2, Ch13 L96, L122). A god can take back what it gave: Jason says "the idea of some god repossessing my magic powers doesn't appeal" (Book 2, Ch56 L93).
- **Great astral beings' stones.** "The stones the astral beings produce aren't divine stones that the astral beings can revoke. They're just ordinary awakening stones whose aspect aligns with the great astral being in question" (Book 2, Ch56 L94). Relatively common from the Reaper and the Celestial Book, not from the World-Phoenix (Book 7, Ch11 L75).
- **Non-essence uses.** The same stone items fuel rituals (see `Rituals_Arrays_and_Formations.md`).

### 4. Examples from the books

Jason's own awakening record, with the stone where the text says which:

| Ability | Source | Seen at |
|---|---|---|
| Midnight Eyes | Dark essence, at absorption | Book 1, Ch8 L35 |
| Cloak of Night | Awakening stone of the stars | Book 1, Ch8 L51-57 |
| Blood Harvest | Blood essence, at absorption | Book 1, Ch21 L7 |
| Leech Bite, Feast of Blood, Feast of Absolution, Sin Eater | Stones of the feast | Book 1, Ch22 L72, L83-85 |
| Path of Shadows | Stone of adventure | Book 1, Ch22 L99, L114 |
| Sanguine Horror | Stone of the apocalypse (his arm turns blood red as it sinks in); the ability appears in the next chapter | Book 1, Ch22 L128, L152; Book 1, Ch23 L61 |
| Hegemony | Stone of omens | Book 1, Ch39 L137, L154 |
| Blade of Doom | Stone of absolution | Book 1, Ch88 L118-125 |
| Shadow of the Reaper, Hand of the Reaper | Stones of the Reaper | Book 2, Ch63 L73, L115 |
| Avatar of Doom | His final stone, awakened with eyes closed | Book 2, Ch64 L3-5 |

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Rare means better.** Farrah and Rufus both deny it (Book 1, Ch19 L66; Book 1, Ch22 L104).
- **A stone can be aimed.** "There are no guarantees when it comes to awakening powers, not even with the rarest of stones" (Book 1, Ch22 L107). Clive: "I'm just managing expectations" (Book 2, Ch9 L40).
- **A stone saves you from needing a full set.** Rufus's advice is to take all four essences first (Book 1, Ch21 L36-37).
- **Stones are only for abilities.** They also fuel rituals (Book 1, Ch22 L45).

### 6. Later developments

- **Level 1 (Book 2):** Stones are rewards. The Adventure Society raised the bounty on Jason to a four-star stone for each person on the team that caught him, with a cap of six after people formed giant groups (Book 2, Ch9 L17-18). The Society gives out stones for exceptional service, rarely, and as rewards for contributions in open contracts (Book 1, Ch64 L81). A Geller family tradition supplies scions "with enough awakening stones to get started" (Book 1, Ch64 L80). As a rule, "we don't give out awakening stones to people for killing monsters above their rank", so that people are not tempted to jump ranks (Book 1, Ch91 L34).
- **Level 2 (Book 9):** Stones keep their reputation for surprising results. In a joking exchange, one speaker admits to using a stone of defiance and a companion teases that they expected an ability from a chef-type essence (Book 9, Ch78 L126-129).
- **Level 3:** After the throne is restored, stones continue to be used; the fixing of confluences, not stones, is what changes (see `Confluences.md`).

## Confluences

### 1. Summary

A confluence is the fourth essence a person receives. It is not picked, bought or found. It is produced by the three essences already absorbed, and it arrives the moment the third is used. In the main run of the series a given trio of essences always gives the same confluence, and the Magic Society keeps a list of the known trios. Confluences are rated and talked about as if they were essences in their own right, and many of the best-known power sets belong to a confluence.

### 2. How it works

**Arrival.** Farrah explains that "once you use your third essence, a fourth one manifests itself on the spot" and that confluences are "a result of the three essences you already have"; her own fire, earth and potent gave the volcano essence (Book 1, Ch19 L30). Confluences "only manifest after three essences are used", and cannot be found loose: "You can't find a volcano essence anywhere" (Book 1, Ch19 L31).

**The scene.** When Jason uses his third essence, three shimmering cubes rise from his torso and merge into one new cube; the System tells him the "confluence of your essences has produced the doom essence", which he "may claim or reject", and that a refused confluence "will not be available to you again" (Book 1, Ch21 L53-54). Rufus's practical advice is that refusing means one "can only replace it with a normal essence" and "I promise you that is not the way to go" (Book 1, Ch21 L57). Only the clergy refuse, because their gods give them divine versions of regular essences (Book 1, Ch21 L57).

**Looking them up.** The Magic Society's living document carries every essence and every combination it knows. A person can look an essence up to see what combinations are known and which are restricted (Book 1, Ch20 L97-104). Jason's dark, blood and sin is found there and produces doom, which is not restricted (Book 1, Ch20 L110). Clive can name a result from memory, as he does for swift, balance and wind (Book 2, Ch5 L83). The Society's common-combinations list is the basis for many choices, such as Ian's ministration confluence (Book 4, Ch71 L30). A larger list of "thousands of known essence combinations" is offered for sale to Jason by the Network's envoy (Book 4, Ch35 L123).

**Many routes, one result.** Some confluences are produced by many combinations. Mystic is common because "so many combinations produce it" and because "a lot of useful abilities come out of the mystic essence" (Book 2, Ch5 L87). Undeath comes from "many combinations", "almost all of which involve the death essence" (Book 1, Ch20 L19). Garuda has at least two routes, might, swift and bird (Book 4, Ch65 L22), and might and wing, which Jason secures instead of the plan to give Taika renewal and the immortal confluence (Book 4, Ch64 L57; Book 4, Ch65 L28).

**Confluence abilities come late.** It is "quite unusual to awaken the confluence essence abilities first", and some advocates of a theory say people with a very strong sense of self do it (Book 2, Ch8 L45-49).

**What a confluence does to a person.** A confluence can carry a racial or personal gift with it. Kylie's vision confluence lets her awaken a perception power from each essence, "where other essence users only had the one" (Book 4, Ch42 L44). An aura power common to the force confluence is able to move things physically with an aura, which is unusual (Book 8, Ch60 L5).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Adventurer's confluences.** Farrah calls chimera "an adventurer's confluence", unsuited to a civilian such as Kaito, who is given a combination of common essences: vehicle, wind and swift, forming the soaring confluence, a known non-combat flight combination (Book 4, Ch71 L4-5, L36).
- **Surprising results from the user.** Greg's magitech confluence did not look like the Network's high-tech magitech users; Jason and Ketevan remark that he ended "all steampunk Tesla" (Book 5, Ch7 L64-66). The same confluence can play very differently.
- **Rare essences, common results.** Sword, myriad and adept give master as readily as sword, swift and adept, in a different style: Lance, a spell-using elf, shares the confluence with Valdis, who relies on special attacks (Book 3, Ch1 L89-90).
- **A deliberate choice.** Jason and Farrah pick sets by the kind of power wanted. Erika is given feast, knife and dance, producing bounty, a food-magic confluence (Book 4, Ch69 L102, L106), and Yumi takes blood, flesh and bone, which give the avatar confluence and let her remake her body into an idealised younger one (Book 5, Ch31 L147). Jason's two sets for the former Engineers of Ascension are sun, blood and life (avatar, "about as perfect an anti-vampire set as you'll find") or gun, hand and adept (master) (Book 6, Ch26 L94).

### 4. Examples from the books

Further named confluences in the text include Medusa (Jason's joke about a hair essence plus snake and earth, Book 5, Ch3 L77), phoenix (Humphrey's sister, Book 6, Ch13 L69), and the lotus set Jason imagines for a Japanophile friend (Book 4, Ch72 L83).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **You can pick your confluence.** Only the three essences are chosen; the fourth follows from them. People do pick a set to aim at a confluence, with the Society list as guide (Book 2, Ch32 L67-72).
- **Refusing the confluence frees the slot for a better one.** Rufus: "I promise you that is not the way to go" (Book 1, Ch21 L57).
- **A confluence guarantees a role.** Clive taught Jason to shape a power set "by aiming for powers within a certain scope" rather than seeking specific powers (Book 4, Ch65 L29), and the same confluence plays differently by user (see section 3).

### 6. Changes over time

**Level 3. The fixed pairing ends.** Rufus is told that essence combinations have "only one potential confluence" and "before the Cosmic Throne was sundered, things were different. More flexible", that an essence combination could once "produce different confluences, from person to person" (Book 11, Ch68 L1574). After the sundering, "the Celestial Book locked off essence combinations" (Book 11, Ch68 L1580) and, if Jason repairs the throne, "all those restrictions will be undone"; the restrictions "are already starting to unravel" (Book 11, Ch68 L1580). The first reported case is Emi, whose vast, myriad and harmonic should produce unity and instead give resonant (Book 11, Ch68 L1559, L1568). A speaker in Book 12 reports that "the previously fixed essence combinations are starting to add variety to the confluence essences they produce" (Book 12, Ch10 L91), and that some people refuse the confluence, "especially now that the combinations are becoming less reliable" (Book 12, Ch10 L88).

**Level 3. Gary's Cup of Heroes.** When Gary becomes a demigod his essences are replaced by divine ones, and his forge confluence by a Demigod essence, with abilities replaced to match (Book 10, Ch86 L67-72). The effect on others is not shown.

## Magic on Earth

### 1. Summary

Earth has the same magic as Pallimustus in a much thinner form. Through most of its history essences and monsters did not exist there at all; magic leaked in through short-lived proto-astral spaces, and a small number of secret societies used the powers that people could earn from them. When Jason returns in Book 4, Earth's magic is low and rising, with a planetary Grid of rituals monitoring and containing the leaks. The monster waves of Book 5 and the transformation zones that follow end that system. By Book 11 the rules have changed.

### 2. How it works

**The old magic.** Craig Vermillion: "Magic has always been a difficult and esoteric thing. Some five centuries ago, a new kind of magic appeared. People with no connection to the old ways could suddenly wield a variety of easy-to-use mystical powers. At that time, they were a limited threat. They were collected into various secret societies around the world, hoarding their knowledge" (Book 4, Ch11 L4).

**Tiers.** The shared numeric rank system runs from zero up: "Whether you call them tiers, categories, realms, or ranks, like you, the same numbers are recognised across the board" (Book 4, Ch11 L8). Tier zero is people without enough magic to "cross the first, transformative threshold" (Book 4, Ch11 L10). Blood servants can reach the first or second tier temporarily by ingesting vampire blood (Book 4, Ch11 L14). Vermillion says he and Jason are "tier two of five", that he has heard of tier-four Cabal figures who "entered forms of hibernation, hidden away for centuries", and that the fifth tier is "the limit of mortal power" (Book 4, Ch11 L19-22). In Network usage the ranks are called categories after spirit coin colours: category one is iron, two bronze, three silver (Book 4, Ch21 L33; Book 4, Ch31 L48). See `Ranks_and_Advancement.md`.

**The Grid.** The Grid is the Network's planet-wide monitor of dimensional incursions. "The grid infrastructure isn't like a normal formation array of permanent ritual circles. Each node is enormous and not made from a ritual circle at all. It's like the landscape is somehow operating as a series of interconnected rituals, creating a magical array from the natural features of the world itself. We're talking about nodes the size of cities, with elements made up of mountains, hills and rivers to form a magical array covering the entire planet" (Book 5, Ch5 L11). Its "express purpose is to identify and monitor dimensional spaces" (Book 4, Ch51 L35). It is "designed to be accessible to anyone with the requisite knowledge", so that once Jason knows about it he may tap into it himself (Book 4, Ch43 L33). It registers events by category: an incident in Book 4 "registered as being above category five" (Book 4, Ch5 L13). A local branch once hid the Saint-Étienne astral space by disabling the Grid in that area and "claiming that there was an infrastructure collapse" (Book 4, Ch51 L35).

**Where magic comes from.** Dawn explains: "The link between worlds ... It's been siphoning off magic from Pallimustus to this world for centuries. It was slow, at first, but the rate of transfer has been rapidly escalating over the last century and a half. Each proto-space that breaks down without the anchor creatures being destroyed deposits its magic into your world... after centuries, the magical density of your world has started to rise. This strengthens the link, which feeds the loop" (Book 4, Ch68 L59-61). The founders of the Grid and the Network "failed to prepare a response to proto-spaces appearing deep in the oceans", so the Network "slows the rate at which your world's magical density has risen" without stopping it (Book 4, Ch68 L63-65). See `Astral_Spaces_Zones_and_Surges.md` for the proto-spaces themselves.

**Supplies.** Earth has no spirit coin farms: "Earth doesn't have the magic and coin formation takes months, so you can't do it in the proto-astral spaces" (Book 4, Ch37 L79). Quintessence is called affinity gems: "We call them affinity gems. I'm pretty sure the Network is the main supplier" (Book 4, Ch23 L26). The Network gives its executive staff essences to reach category one and reserves cores for frontline staff (Book 4, Ch36 L77). Magical technology exists, built on leaning "on the magic as little as possible. Let the technology do the work and use magic to skip over the places where the tech would otherwise bottleneck" (Book 4, Ch46 L90).

**Characters on Earth.** Essence users on Earth are mostly category one to three in Book 4 (Book 4, Ch16 L108; Book 4, Ch18 L122). Vampires are the Cabal's classic power; the Engineers of Ascension are a radical group (see `05_Organisations/Earth_Powers.md`).

### 3. Variations and exceptions

- **Low-magic rule.** Entering the vicinity of a proto-astral aperture raises ambient magic enough that "your recovery rates will remain at normal levels without spirit coin consumption" (Book 4, Ch39 L55); outside such places Earth's magic is thin.
- **Core use as policy.** Network members are given cores according to role and rank rather than by ability (Book 4, Ch36 L77).
- **Training divergence.** The Network's own training is human-derived; Jason and Farrah introduce training "from the ground up" in Book 5 (Book 5, Ch1 L51-53).

### 4. Examples from the books

- **The Starlight Rider and the Network's tactical teams** (see Book 4 timeline).
- **Kostroma**, the first transformation zone, in Book 5, Ch44 L48.
- **Nitra, Slovakia**, a zone at the end of Book 5 (Book 5, Ch68 L68).
- **The Quilido Procedure**, Book 13's cure for core taint (Book 13, Ch1001 L9).

### 5. Common misconceptions in-world

- **Earth has no magic.** It has a trickle, increasingly large (Book 4, Ch68 L59-61).
- **The Network can contain it.** Jason concludes that the Network's mission of containment "was completely stuffed from the start" because the oceans hide leaks, and Dawn agrees (Book 4, Ch68 L63-65).
- **Tier five is a myth.** Vermillion has "never seen proof" of it (Book 4, Ch11 L21).

### 6. Changes over time

- **Level 2:** In Book 5, grid failures and monster waves begin (Book 5, Ch14 L3; Book 5, Ch16 L78); the Network becomes publicly known as the Global Defense Network (Book 5, Ch17 L7). Zones such as Kostroma remake places (Book 5, Ch44 L48-52).
- **Level 3:** After Jason's second zone, "the base level of magic had risen; magic no longer manifested in proto-astral spaces before spilling into the world. He had begun a new age of magic, where monsters and essences manifested directly in the world" (Book 11, Ch1 L16). Many normal-rank people on Earth are transformed into other races (Book 11, Ch1 L36). By Book 13 the Asano clan's training and the Quilido Procedure give it influence over national essence-user programmes (Book 13, Ch1001 L8-9).

## Essence Catalogue

### 1. Summary

The books name far more essences than the wiki lists give with evidence. This file collects those the text actually shows, with who holds them and what the text says of their behaviour. Rarity statements come from the text; where the text gives none, none is invented. It is intended as a quick reference for building a character's power set, not as a mechanical list. The full set of essences the Magic Society knows is in its living document (Book 1, Ch20 L97).

The wiki's fuller lists of essences, confluences and combinations are in `../Appendices/Wiki_Reference_Lists.md` (wiki tier), with a cross-reference to the first book line for each entry found in the text. Where the wiki gives a rarity, it agrees with the text so far: sin is Legendary, renewal is Epic (the text's "second-highest rarity", Book 6, Ch13 L68) and rune and vast are among the highest.

### 2. How to read it

- An **essence** is named here by its concept. A **confluence** is a fourth essence produced from three others (see `Confluences.md`).
- "Seen with" lists a person or group for whom the text names the essence and gives a line.
- Rarity is only given where the text gives it. The text uses five stages for stones: common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary (Book 2, Ch9 L9; Book 2, Ch9 L17 puts four-star at the "second highest rarity"). Essences are discussed with the same words.

### 3. Rarity as the text gives it

| Might, shield, magic | Common and desirable, "could all have been traded for some quality awakening stones" (Book 1, Ch73 L51) |
| Gathering | A rare essence (Book 4, Ch21 L135) |
| Growth, life | Uncommon (Book 4, Ch2 L18) |

### 5. Variations and misconceptions

- **Names and concepts.** An essence name is a concept, not a promise of power: the bird essence might give "the power to talk to birds" rather than a combat power (Book 4, Ch65 L27).
- **Same essence, different user.** The vehicle essence gives drones to Kaito (Book 5, Ch7 L8) and a conjured limousine to Wesley Asano (Book 12, Ch59 L9) and a helicopter to another (Book 11, Ch68 L1526).
- **Wiki lists.** The fan wiki grades many essences by rarity; those grades are not used here when the text gives a different one. Where the text and the wiki conflict, the text is followed (for example renewal, above).

### 6. Later developments

- **Level 3:** Gary's essences are replaced by divine versions (Divine Hammer, Divine Fire, Divine Iron) and his forge confluence by Demigod (Book 10, Ch86 L67-70). See `Confluences.md` for the end of fixed pairings.
